AN ANTI-BOOMER. A Plea for the Farm Rural Simplicity Preferred to the Rushing Dummy, Tinkling Cable, Smoky Smelter or Odoriferous Packing House. To the Editor Kaxsas City Daily Gazette : Please insert a cry "from out of the depths." To begin with, Mr. Editor, we are anti-boomers, a minority which I represent. Now we don't want to be considered as lacking in patriotism nor to injure the welfare of the country, neither do we ob- ect to grand "booms," both general and ocal. We object not to the city "boom" nor ooomer. cut we protest against the farmer who has taken up the "pro- ession," who, having a beam in his own eye, yet attempting to dislodge the mote he seeks in his brother's, would destroy that brother's eyesight. We would only echo the cry of Patrick Henry when he said "There is no peace." Now what we poor fossilized creatures want is to be allowed to remain on the and of our birth. We are children of Nature, who love the Kentucky bluegrass that grows to our doors and covers our walnut grove pastures. We plead with hose "boomers" that swoop down upon us as a hawk on a poor defenseless chicken, and ask what have they to exchange or this? They say that possibly we may obtain a corner lot 25x50 or some such stupendous dimensions, and enjoy, instead of Gods sunshine and Nature's beauties, the scenery of a canning factory, instead of the per- ume of the violet and of the wild- rose inhale the order of a packing house, our society shall be enlivened and culti vated by the close proximity of car shops and, heaven of heavens, a smelter may adorn our front door yards, but we wish to forego such luxuries; then propose that we be removed to a reservation farther west; they insist the sand hills are just as productive and nature just as inviting, but we like the poor Indian prefer our own hunting ground. We are accus tomed to measure land by section not by foot. We are asked to exchange our dusty, turf-bordered roads for the bliss of mortgaging our premises to meet the expense of constructing a creaking, break ing sidewalk, and that conglomeration of mud and stone called a street. We are simple cleatures of the dust and prefer clean dirt. Again they tell us that we are a hin drance to the grand onward march of civ- llzation, that we are unfriendly toward Kansas City (I mean of both states), which is already the metropolis of the west. Now, Mr. Editor, ever since Kansas City was Westport landing and Shawnee town flourishing city, before the raids of the bush whackers, we entertained kind ly feeling toward Kansas City, and con tinue to do so. Mr. Editor, some of us are beginning to note silver threads among the raven tresses of that period, and others that years have not vet bur dened can note the same, the result of this progressive spirit that has infested these hills-of ours. This boom of ours has as many lives as the proverbial cat. lne boom de-clineth elsewhere, yet it declineth not here. It is a progressive boom; it has progressed from nothing to nothing. Its birth is an obscure date of some two years past. it sun breathes. uur boomers, unfortunately, possess the rich loamy soil of several hillsides, and nature has not been gracious; she has disclosed huge boulders of some remote geological period. The power of erosion has drawn boundary lines over which the plowman cannot pass, and the lowing herd would be engulfed. It would seem that a smelter or car shops plant might take root here, even if the succulent faileth, yet it seems to fail even in that product, so they cast their eyes southward toward our land of Canaan. They say, "Here we will use rule for general average conned in the arithmetics of our boy hood, the formula we will arrange thus : acres x acres acres x cash amount x acres general average, which in equity gives us of the hillsides an equal piece of pie as those hostile, rascally fellows on the level land beyond, who persist in working for a living." So these mathematicians of ours count off our possessions and count one to theirs. Now we don't object to them booming their own property, nor disposing of it. They may start a London or a Paris if they choose, but we don t want to boom; we don't care to exchange rural simplicity for such urbane splendor as they depict. We admire government patents; we love to note Uncle Sam's signature to our land tales; this dear old relative of ours has a pretty good financial standing. We prefer such old fogy investments to wild hog schemes of wealth in shady speculations. Our lands neither die, burn up, nor run away, neither can our Kansas blizzards or clycones move them, they are a solid investment and a sure interest. But our home boomers cause us to feel depressed. We want to stay. We don't want filthy alleys back of us nor mixed mud in front of us. We don't care to exchange elm trees for telegraph poles. We don't need telephones. Some of us are young and some are old, but we are all old fogies, we are cranky, we are queer, we are fossils of a by gone age. But we believe in reform, we are temperate, we are good citizens and try to deal honorably with all men. We use the cash system both ways. We don't want canning factories, car shops, smelters, packing houses nor steel works any nearer. They are all around us. We regulate our time-piece by their whistles, our wives prepare our dinners and we unhook our teams at the notes of the "old growler." We are content with it so. We, care not for the rushing dummy, the tinkling cable car, nor even a mule proder nor mule car would elevate our spirits, to see them crossing our fertile fields and defacing our lawns. We enjoy the Arabian railway, we have tried means of locomotion on foot, on horseback and by wheeled vehicles; when we tire of these and wish swifter transportation we have but a few rods to. traverse before we reach the roaring steam car. Mr. Editor, as a word of warning to our persecutors, we would cite a biblical instance of two boomers' financial failure. "Annniasand Sapphire," we are told, "in attempting to get a corner on a piece of real estate were compelled, through their illegal procedure, to go into bankruptcy." Now we are not alluding personally to any one, all our motives are entirely pure and free from malace aforethought. And lastly, Mr. Editor, although we 1 are a niinoruy anu uus is a cry oi .Les Miserables," yet we are patriotic, we simply want a permit from the people to be allowed to stay. We ourselves are "farm products." We wish to peaceably cultivate our orchards, Vineyards, wheat fields and "bog oranges." As a closing remark, I will say that our boom has been only in the fertile brain of our visionary boomers. We ask but to retain our own and to receive the benefit resulting thereto instead of enriching our interested friends at our own expense. But if we are scooped out by the onward swoop of civilization and are compelled to move our tent poles to some Alaskan reservation, yet our last cry will f be "Long live the Kepublic and a lie-publican administration. One of the Persecuted. MORE UUILDINGS. The Board of Education Take Steps to Provide More School Buildings. The Board of Education met last night for the purpose of considering the question of providing more room to accommodate the rapidly increasing school population of the city. The committee on buildings submitted a report in which they recommended that the Armourdale building should be increased from six to twelve rooms; that four more rooms should be added to the Barnett street building; that four rooms should be added to the Long building; that one room be added to the Gray building, and that work on the new colored school building on Washingtpn avenue should begin as soon as possible. The committee also reported upon the crowded condition of the schools in the northern part of the city, and asked the board to take some action in the matter. The clerk was instructed to advertise for bids for the sale of the frame building on the property on Washington avenue recently purchased by the board. County Superintendent Taylor asked for the privilege of using four rooms in the Central school building for the summer Normal, which will begin June 10. The superintendent called the attention of the hryrd to the fact that tfe basement room in the Central building was unfit for use, and that the health of both teacher and pupils was greatly endangered by continuing its use as a school room. He suggested that the Gray building be used instead of the one in the basement at the Central school. On motion of Mr. Northrup the president and clerk were instructed to have a room in the Gray building fitted up and the grade transferred as soon as Dr. Gray vacates. The attention of the board was called to the rules fixing the date of holding examination for teachers in the city schools, and on motion of Mr. Northrup the rules were suspended and the time fixed for July 5 and 6. The clerk was instructed to furnisn no more pens or slate pencils for use in the city schools, except slate pencils for the 1st and 2d grades, which are to be furnished as usual. Mr. W. L. Hackney was chosen architect for the board. The architect was instructed to prepare plans for a 12 room building to be located on Washington avenue, six rooms to be erected this year. The system of heating to be used in the new buildings was quite generally discussed, and on motion, was deferred till the next meeting of the board. Adjourned till Monday, April 8. DON'T MACADAMIZE MINNESOTA. To the editor of the Kaksas City Gazette : As a citizen we respectfully protest against the further use of macadam on streets ueed by street cars. It may do on side streets where there are no cars, but not elsewhere in the city. The frequency of carriages, the crowded condition of the streets, and the rapid move ment of the cars necessitate at times the quick movement of vehicles, and drivers ought to be able to go eyery where, and at any angle across the tracks, and this they can't do if the roadway is paved flush with the rail. When there is ma cadam it settles down, and the rail is or dinarily from four to six inches above the roadbed and becomes a great impe diment to travel and a source of danger If the wheel strikes it obliquely your waeon is slewed about, to the peril and annoyance of the occupant. If you strike the rail perpendicularly, perhaps the loss of the steel tire of your buggy is the con sequence. Upon a substantial concrete base, block pavement is cheapest and best. It can be easily taken up for repairs. It is pleasant to drive on, less wearing upon horses and carriages and less jarring upon the nerves of our people. If, after four or five years of use, the old blocks need to be replaced by new blocks the expense is not large. Then let us have Minnesota avenue, between Fourth and Eighth streets, paued with cedar blocks placed upon a substantial concrete base and not macadamized, as desired by some property holders; and we shall then have the finest street of the two cities. The common council hss a discretion in this matter and ought to exercise it in behalf of the people of the whole city. Publtus. THE NEW CHIEF OF POLICE. WESTIXGllOUSE TO EDISON. THE ALTERNATING SYSTEM IS DEFENDED. A Reply to the Wizard's Article on the Dangers of Electric Lighting. The Pittsburgher Comes Out Strong for Underground Wires. ' George Westinghouse, Jr., contributes an article to the North American Review for December in which he shows how electric lighting may be nvule absolutely safe in Sew York. This article of course is a reply to one by Thomas A. Edison published in the same magazine on the subject, "the dangers of electric lighting," in which the inventor sets forth the claims of his direct current system of supplying incandescent light from central stations, and at the same time attempts to cast discredit upon the converter or alternating current system, of which the Wesf-iughouse Electric Company is the principal promoter. Mr. Westinghou.se is a Arm believer in underground distribution of wires, as the following will show: "The placing of the wires under ground would eliminate many of the causes of accidents from electric currents, and they may all be prevented by the employment of reasonable and well-understood safeguards. Mr. Edison's statement that the putting of the wires under ground will, instead of diminishing, increase the danger to life, is little less than amazing, at least when considered in connection with his advocacy of his own underground System. The repeated and violent explosions of gas in the manholes of the Edison system, and in connection with the underground systems of the telephone and telegraph companies, have certainly Bhown that electricity from any source may be the cause of a serious catastrophe. Inasmuch as Mr. Edison's arguments against underground wires generally are equally applicable to his own system, it would seem logically that, if his views are to prevail, all electric wires must cease to serve the public. The experience of the cities of Chicago and Philadelphia in the use of underground cables for high-tension currents, to say nothing of the large number of cables laid under ground in Home, Iierlin, Milan, and in other cities, indicates that the success of properly constructed underground systems, whether . for currents of high or low tension, has been established beyond question.'' In speaking of the superior safety of the alternating system Mr. Westinghouse denies that the same amount of electricity is carried in the house wires as in the main, as in the Edison system. This disconnection of street and house wires gives per- i feet safety, he contends. It has been shown that in the alternating system the street mains are absolutely disconnected and detatched from the house mains, while the low tension system necessitates the meshing of all underground mains into one network and the supply of a current to that system by a series of feeders. In ' fact it necessitates at times the supply of an enormous electrical energy to supply the demand. "With the alternating system the practice is not to mesh the wires, but to run independent pairs of wires connecting the switch lioard in the station with the thin wires of the converters. There is not on record a solitary instance of a person having been injured or shocked from the consumers' current of an alternating system. This is wholly due to the fact that the converted current within the buildings supplied need not exceed 50 volts, and that the street mains and the house wires are absolutely detached from each other, so that there is no possibility of a shock being received from leakage or short-circuiting in the high-tension street mains. As to the safety from fire insured by the converter system, Mr. Westinghouse says: "The fire risk from electricity is the one most to be feared. With the continuous current, wherever there is occasion to put out a number of lights by the movement of a switch, it not. infrequently happens that a dazzling arc of blue flame is formed which has to be blown out. With the alternating system it is impossible to form any considerable arc, even if the switch controls a thousand lights, the rapid re versal of the current having the effect of preventing its establishment." Mr. Westinghouse goes on to prove, out of the mouths of Mr. Edison's own friends, that a system of arc lighting has become a necessity. He says: "Mr. Edison's observations concerning the efforts of his competitors in the direction of savins; an investment, are no less applicable to the desires of the supplies of Jus own system. J. lie author quotes trom the proceedings of the annual convention of Edison companies to show the need of aa efficient and cheap arc light system. Mr. Westinghouse concludes as follows: "A careful consideration of the whole subject proves that it is possible to lisrht all the buildings within a city by means of electricity distributed by an underground system, wherein there shall be no connection whatever between the underground system and the wires within the buildings. It has been demonstrated that an incandescent, lamp operated by a 50-volt current will give more light at a given cost than a 110-volt tamp; and, these two things being admitted, it follows that, if there are to be any restrictive regulations with reference to electric lighting, they might more properly be. first, that the electro-motive force within any building shall never exceed one hundred volts: second, that no underground system shall be placed in electrical connection with the wires in the buildings: third, that no underground system shall be permitted which does not provide for the renewal and repair of the mains without digging up the streets. "In conclusion, it is worthy of note that for three years past the purchasers of a p-paratus for electric lighting, who are at perfect liberty to buy from any company, have for the most part preferred to use the alternating system, so that to-day the extension of that system for central-station incandescent lighting is at least five times as great as that of the direct curient. If the opinion of these persons, who can have no interest except to purchase that which they believe to be the best, is of any value, then the alternating system has been demonstrated to be the one which can give to the public that which they so strongly desire a perfectly safe, cheap, efficient and universally applicable system of incandescent electric lighting." is

Woman In The Year 2000. l!Y edwa hd Bellamy It is assumed that the year 2,000 will see Nationalism fully established as the basis of the industrial system and of society, so far as dependent upon it. Judsinz from the signs of the times, I think it would he quite safe to make the date seventy-five years earlier but for the benefit of those weak in the faith it is well set ahead. As there are doubtless some who do not understand vnrv clearlv what Nationalism is, it may be well enough just here to ex plain, so far as may be done in a phrase, it proposes turning over all the bust ness of the country to a single firm, of which all the people, women as well as mpn. shall he emnlovees. and m the proceeds of which all shall be equal partners. Leaving wholly aside, for the present purpose, all explanations as to thfi details of this plan, and all questions as to its feasibility, it is sim ply proposed to point out certain ways in which the positiou of women would tin RfTfifltprf bv its successful introuuc tinn w nm tn snniiose that every adult woman in the United States while re quired, like every adult man (except as modified by sex conditions,) to perform some self elected useful work- had coming to her a regular annual in come in the form of credit, to be ex- nenrlfld as she pltases. eaual. say, to the present purchasing power of $1000, $3,000 or $3,000, more or less, according to the prosperity of the national turn, said income to be the same in amount as that received by her brother, hus band or father, but not to come to her through them or through any other in termediary, but directly from the national administration, as a matter of constitutional right. Now, considering the fact that wo man, owing to her comparative physi cal disqualifications as a worker, has hitherto been, as a rule, wholly or partially denendent on the favor or af fection of men for the means of a se cure and comfortable existence, it is evident that a system like that describ would, by rendering her entirely independent of man in this respect, make a great alteration in her position. Obviously the most important single respect in which it would be altered, as to her attitude toward marriage. She would no longer be obliged, as the most women now are, to look forward marriage as offering, if not absolutely her only means of support, yet at least as constituting her hope of a secure and comfortable life. The only possible motive which would impel her give herself to a man would be that loved him. May and December might still mate, Beauty might still the Beast, but the sourest cynic would no longer be able to attribute an unworthy motive to the bride. However sordid she might become under the temptation, then there could be none, not only would she be under no necessity of marrying at all, but the wealth of all her possible suitors being same, she could have no motive save love or admiration for marrying one, more than another. Not only, however, would Nationalism guarantee woman dignity and independence before a marriage, but equally afterward. That event would in no way affect her rights as a citi.en at.d a partner In the national concern The humiliation of complete pecuniary dependence upon their husbands, being obliged to ask tor all they have beyond bare bread and meat, which the best and noblest of wives now have endure, the wife of the year 2,000 would never know. Let us suppose, on the other hand that her heart remaining untouched she had preferred to remain single. At the present time, a popular pre- sumption exists that all girls wish to marry, and fail to do so only because they lack an eligible opportunity. This presumption exists on account ot the obvious fact that women, being able with difficulty to support themselves have in general a greater material in terest than men have. Surely there can be a few incidents of an unmarried woman's condition more exasperating than her knowlebge that because this is the undeniable fact it is vain for her to expect to be popularly debited with the voluntary choice of her condition She must endure with a smile, howev er she may rage within, the coarse jest or innuendo to which it would be worse than vain to reply. Nationalism, by establishing the economic independence of women, without reference to their single or married state, will destroy the presumption referred to by making marriage no more obviously desirable to one sex than to another. Would you gain a realization of the "old maid" in the year 2,000? If so, look at the lordly bachelor of to-day, the hero of romance, the cynosure of the drawing room and of the promenade. Even as that bright being, like him self-poiser, serenely insouciant. free as air, will the "old maid of the year 2,000 be. It is altogether probable, by the way, that the term "old maid" will by that time have fallen into dis use. But while the unmarried woman of the year 2,000, whether young or old, will enjoy the dignity and indepeud ence of to-day, the insolent prosperity at present enjoyed by the latter will have passed into salutary, if sad. eclipse No longer profiting by the effect of the pressure of economic necessity upon woman to make him indispensable, but dependent exclusively upon his intri sic attractions, instead of being able to assume the fastidious airs of a sultan surrounded by languishing beauties, he will be fortunate if he can secure by his merits the smiles of one. In the year 2,000 no man, whether lover or husband, may hope to win the favor of maid or wife saving by desert. While the poet, justly apprehending the deal proprieties, has always persisted n representing man at the feet of wo man, woman has been, in fact, the de pendent and pensioner of man. Nationalism will justify the poet and satisfy the eternal fitness of things by bringing him to his marrow-bones in earnest. But, indeed, we may be sure that in the year 2,000 he will need no compulsion to assume that attitude. It implies no dlsloyality to the wo manhood of to-day believe that the personal dignity and moral freedom, un known before to her sex, which will be the birthright of woman in the twen tieth century, cannot fan to react most favorably upon herself, ennobling her graces, clothing with a new majesty her beauty and making her every way moie worthy of the reverence and de votion of man. There is another and profoundly tragic aspect of the relation of the sex es which by no means may be passed over in considering what Nationalism will do for women. The same economical pressure which brings the mass of women into a relation of dependence upon men, rendered more or less toler able according to the degree of mutual affection, reduces a great multitude of women, wno are not iortunare enougn to find adequate masculine support, to a form of slavery more morally de grading than any other and more complete in its indignity. This most ancient form of bondage, which has grown up with the race and flourishes to-day in the face of civilization and Christendom as widely and vigorously as eyer, whicii no wisdom oi tne economist, no zeal of the philanthropist has ever availed to diminish, Nationalism, Dy the necessary operation of its fund amental principle, will at once and forever extirpate. Want on one hand will then no longer drive the virtuous woman to dishonor nor on the other will wealth in the hands of unscrupu- ous men, tempt her frivolous sister. Ladies' Home Journal. The recent arrest in this city of three men on the charge of trafficking in indecent photographs has resulted in developments which give rise to the belief that they are simply part and parcel of a gang that infests nearly every large city in this country. Their methods are to get possession of the photographs of well known and prominent society women and then attach to the head of the picture the photograph of the half or whole of a nude body. It is said that this traffic has been indulged in on an enormous scale.

The other day I was seated in the park watching the string of wheelmen whirling past Lemon hill on their way up the drive. "Did it ever occur to you what infernal nuisances those confounded bicycles are?" asked a communicative man, limping up and depositing himself on the bench beside me. "No; it did not," I replied. "Well, they are," he continue, "the worst kind of a nuisance. They should bo driven from the streets. I walked up Broad street ono afternoon a few weeks ago and every stop I took I heard the bell on one of the Infernal things ring, ordering me out of the road. At last I got tired of it; so when I saw the next one coming I just stopped right in the middle of the street and waited for it. On she came and the fool on the machine rung the bell. I didn't get out of the road." "No?" "No, sirree! I just stood there and yelled to tho fool that it was as easy for him to get out my road as it was for me to get out of his." "Indeed!" "Yes, sir! 'And remember,' I said. 'I'm going to stand right 'here and If you run into me I'll break your confounded machine and he came." "No." "Yes, sir. On he came and there I stood." "Well?" "I didn't get out of his road. He ran into me." "Is that so?" "Yes, sirree!" "Well? And then?" "I broke the machine." "Impossible!" "Not a bit That's just what I did." "What did he do?" ' "He ran into me." . "And you-?" "I broke the machine." "Well I mean after that what did he do?" - "Oh! He gathered it together." "But what did he do with you?" "Oh," with a sickly smile; "they gathered me together, too." And then he relapsed into silence. Burdette, in Philadelphia Press. -

Some good people who have been poorly informed continue to grumble because the United States will not enact rigid restrictions on immigra tion. That it will not do so is very clear. Of the two new projects of law proposed since the Immigration Commission's report the one which is least drastic is certain of adoption. The other has been 6ent to the limbo to which a free country should consign all illiberal measures. In the Forum, Edward Atkinson, the well- known economist, devotes a few crisp pages to ridiculing the notion far too popular nowadays that we have no more room for immigrants. He shows very clearly that the five and a quar ter million of immigrants who have come to this country since 1881 are scarcely noticeable in the vastness of territory through which they are scattered. We have still, he cries in a burst of enthusiasm but enthusiasm backed up by statistics incalcul able room for immigrants!

SPECIAL , DISEASES. Ills to Which Several Classes Are Liable. THE BICYCLER'S STOOP. The Telephone Ear Gum Chawar'a Cramp The PauIlUt's Fat Neck Why John I Sullivan Lost Hie Last Battle , A New Theory. From the New York Herald. "In this fast age we are a prey to some mighty funny diseases." "The man who said this, one of the widely known physicians of New York, went on to explain as follows : VThe other day my son asked me to buy him a bicycle, and, while I would like to do it, I have been hesitating because I know if he rides very much he will become afflicted with the 'safety stoop. Catarrhal laryngitis is the latest disease charged up against the bicycle. "I was going along the street the other day and I saw half a dozen young men who were neither straight nor crooked. They were all bicycle riders, as I could tell at a glance, and they were all afflicted with the 'safety stoop.. Now the 'safety stoop' is a mighty bad thing. "It is different from the scholastic stoop. It is different from the round-shouldered stoop. "The man with the 'safety stoop.' as it is called, often suffers impaired vitality. There is a peculiar hump on his back that cannot be explained in words. It looks something like the stoop of the fellow who does the single scull act. To ride the bicycle is no doubt heathful recreation, but like everything else in this world it has its drawbacks and one of them ia the 'safety stoop.' " THE TELEPHONE EAR. "The other day," went on the doctor, "a young woman called on me at my office and said: 'Doctor, I don't know what is the matter with my ear. I am getting deaf in my left ear!" I inquired into the case and found the voung lady had been troubled only about six months. I applied the usual instruments and found that the inner ear was perfectly normal. I then asked the young lady if her mother had ever boxed her ears excessively in her youth, and she said no, although she admitted that while she was at school the school ma'am used to twist and screw her ears considerably. "Well, it was a case of 'telephone ear. "You would be surprised if you knew how many of our young women are becoming partially deaf through the constant use of the telephone. It is such a common case now that aurists have coined the name 'telephone ear' to designate the peculiarties of the case. The 'telephone ear' is the result of the never-ending use of one ear in listening . at the receiver of the telephone. "I advise all young people, and old ones, too, who are afflicted in this way, to vary tha ears in listening through the 'phone'.' If they do not, sooner or later the hearing of the ear that is worked too much will become seriously, perhaps permanently impaired. " Look out for the girl with the telephone ear. She is abroad in the land. You can tell her in the street car by the way she cranes her neck." i THE " GUM CHEWEHS' CRAMP." ; "Another strange case," went on the man, " is found among our girls, who are altogether too much, addicted to the use of chewing gum." The scribe smiled as he heard this. " No, no ; you need not smile. It is a fact. Any physician will tell you of the circumstance. " Now, a girl who chews gum on every occasion is working her jaws too much in connection with her average amount of talking. The result is, the muscles of her jaws are overstrained. There is a reaction. Her jaws become set and well-nigh immovable. Her speech then takes the form of monosyllables. I ,do not want to be misunderstood in this matter. I say that the girl who chews gum to excess will, sooner or later, find that her jaws refuse to act with their usual freedom. "In other words, she becomes afflicted with 'gum chewers' cramp.' " "Funny, isn't it ?" "Not at all ; you must remember that there are compensations in nature. The inordinate use of one muscle or one set of muscles tends to abnormally expand them, overtax them or impair them, as the case may be. "Thus it is that there is no pastime or labor which, pursued steadily to excess, will not result in some malady. "Now, then, it is widely known that the dentist's diseese, for illustration, is a kidney complaint. Nine dentists out of ten suffer with it. This is because their work compels them to stand hour after hour rooted to one spot The strain falls on the small of the back, and as it happens, develops kidney trouble. I mention this as an illustration of what I am driving at." TIIE PCGILIST'S TAT NECK. "As the result of the recent prize fisrht between Sullivan and Corbett, some unique conclusions were drawn as to why the. famous man had not won. All sorts of theories, more or less scientific, were advanced by the friends of John L. Sullivan. To my mind, however, the real explanation has yet to be advanced. "John L., to my mind, went into the ring with too mud: rrrebral fat on his neck. You know the seut of muscular activity is in the cerebellum. "I advance the startling theory that the trouble with John L. was that he had too fat a neck. This prevented him from striking a rapid blow. "Now, then, why isn't it possible to train a man down so fine in the neck that his blows will be simply lightning-like in succession ? If a man has a fat neck, he might have all the science in the world, yet his blows would be so slow that they would not amount to very much. He might be able to think quick enough, but before he . could turn his thoughts into blows his name would be mud. "I give you thia theory for what it is worth." I"

NEWSPAPERS BLAMED. An Assertion That They Are a Power for Evil, Not Good. To the Editor of The Timks: There are hundreds of trivial reasons that prevent men from going to church or have a tendency to lead them to go elsewhere, but It Is my Intention to mention but oneout of the many, leaving the rest for the other readers of The Times to talk about. That reason is Sunday newspapers. It Is sad to note that nearly all of the great metropolitan dallies now print a Sunday edition of bulky size to be sold at a very low rate. Every possible effort Is put forth to make the Sunday Issue excel any week-dav number, and to accomplish this end the other IsBues of the paper are Impaired In many cases. All special articles and such matter as will " keep" are reserved for Sunday and every resource Is strained to it utmost tension to gain success tor the Sunday edition In preference to all others. The hubltual reading of these 8unday newspapers Is Just what draws the attention of many men from divine worship. This I know to be a fact from real practical Illustrations which have been seen, and never in one Instance have I known them to nave any Influence for good, nlthough I hove made this subject a special study, ever observant of all examples which came to my view. it is a shame that the great minds of the country should allow themselves to become so powerless (for good) In the hands of that unfathomable greed and hunger and thirst atter mis worm s goods as to be led to become discontented with six days out of seven, and thus steal the seventh. In the estimation of all conscientious readers of the week-day edition of The Timks It is my opinion that this Impertinent question (from such a source) will receive nothing but scorn and ridicule, and I hope that it will. I venture to predict that when the day dawns in which all men attend church, Sunday newspapers will have passed away forever. William L. Packard, Jr. Elmeh, N. J.

TELEPHONE EARS. One of the Many Curious Ills of Man. HELLO GIRLS' BETE NOIR. A Disease That Affects Only a Small Portion of the Inhabitants of a Great City. There is a disease that Is at present quite prevalent in the city of which very little is known by the outside worlu. SE3S It is called, lor want of a better name, the "telephone ear," and only attacks the operators in the "centrals," the ones who answer you when you givo two rings to your telephone-bell and ask to be connected with your butcher or baker. These long-suffering mortals, who do nothing but strain their ears for eight or nine ami sometimes ten hours a day, are beginning to feel the effects of the constant application to their work, which they are compelled to give to satisfy their employers and the public. This disease first makes its approach felt by severe headaches. Nearly all the operators have these when they first enter lit, service, but those with a strong constitution soon overcome this and do not feel any evil effects from their work. These, however, who aro not as strong as they might be, especially the girl?, who form a large force ot operators, soon find their headaches followed by it peculiar buzzing sound in their head when they go home at nicht. it steadily becomes worse, aud at last the operator is obliged to take a day or two off work to recover. But this day or two seems of no permanent benefit to the sufferer, and at last the "hello-girl" gives in to the Inevitable and gees steadily on with her work, until at last an abscess forms in the ear and a most painful and sometimes dangerous operation has to he performed. This latter has been the case witn several of the young ladies who are at present operators in this city. Several of them were seen yesterday by a Call reporter, and cave their opinions as to what caused their trouble. Miss .Mamie McClosky, who has been an operator for the I'acifie Telephone Company for some rears, and is now chief operator at the central office on Bush street, said : "1 have been an operator for a good many years, and numbers of cases of 'telephone ears' have come under my notice. You see, the operator has to sit fir eight hours a day with the rubber eartrumpet strapped to the head by a sleel band, and at first the unnatural presssure makes one veiy nervous and subject to headaches. When this first nervousness wears off, as of course it dues when one becomes accustomed to the work, the headaches do not seem to wear off with it. "Whether it is the almost constant talking and bell-ringing that goes on In our ears, or whether the lact of the steady pressure on the outer ear causes it. It is a fact that nine-tenths of our cirl operators are affected with some kind of ear trouble. Usually an aim st constant earache and a biizziug in the ears when off duly is the extent of the injury, but frequently it is a more serious matter. 1 myself, a short time ago, found tint my ear was fiiving mo constant trouble, and consulted an aurist. The consequence was that 1 found an abscess had formed in the inner ear, and it was only removed after a most painful course of treatment Of course, I had to lake a vacation for a time, as my ear was so sore that I could not stand the pressure of the ear-trumpet." Julia Valentine is another snfferer from this most peculiar disease. She has only been doing telephone work for a year and a half, and already the evil effects of her employment are making themselves felt. "huyou call it n telephone ear, do you?" said she. "I am glad to hear what it i«, for I've had it several mouths now and didn't know -hat it was. ••Of course, when I first st.trtej to work I had Ihe usual headaches a first, and have them yet, but they have become so common now that 1 pay mi more attention to them. In fact, I am more worried when my Ilea' l . does not ache than when it doe.', for It has become mv normal condition now. "But this telephone oar is another matter 1 have never hud any serious trouble with it, such as an abscess forming, bat it constantly annoys me, and at times my left ear, over which we operators usually wear our cap, as the ear-trumpet Is called, becomes so sore, both inside and out, that 1 have to change and use my right ear for a tmie. "The only effect that this has is to make the right ear as soro as the other, and then it is a case of taking a week or so to recover. "We also find that after a few years' service we are gradually becoming deaf. Why this is I can't imagine, but it is so. "1 have known ever so many eiris who have had to take several days off to allow their ears to regain tlieir former condition. I have not been without a peculiar buzzing sound In my ears, such as one has when one takes luo much quinine, lor a lunger time than I care to remember, and time and again I have decided to consult a physician, But I suppose I won't tllljl get so sick 1 can't work at all." The abovo is the condition of a great majority of the "hello-girls." Xot one in twenty escapes the disease, if such it can be called, and no wonder, with the hard tvork they are Culled on to perform. One of the most prominent aurists was spoken to on the subject, ami said he bad seen and treated several cases of It. "We have no special name for Ihe disease at present," said lie, "except that of the 'telephone ear,' which seems very appr.pri.tt,'. "Its cause is rather hard to state. It may be brought on by the pressure of the ear-trumpet on the outer ear, causing a corresponding pressure on tho tympanum, or the constant and intense straining of the nerves to catch every sound that passes over the wires. "The ear, as every one knows, Is one of the most delicate organs of the body. Next lo the eye. there is probably no part so easily affected and deraDged. Indeed, I think 1 can safely say that it is more sensitive than the eye and more likely to damage. "Being so sensitive, you can readily see that it does not take much to put it out of its usual working order. When this occurs, even in the slightest degree, serious effects are almost sure to follow, "1 had one case a few months ago of a young man, who was an operator for the Pacific Telephone Company. He had been steadily at wore for eight years, arid had paid no attention to the fact that his oars were giving him almost constant trouble. The consequence was that when at last he was compelled to consult au aurist 1 found that a largo abscess had formed in the drum of his ear. "He told me that for three years he had not missed a day nt his table, except the regular day off. la all that time there had been a constant buzzing in his head, ns though owing to the presence of a set of clock-works" which ihad been mislaid there, bad got . out of order and were steadily running down. Of course, in time this became worse, with the result that lie was housebound for ten weeks. He is now at his table again, but will be careful about getting another case of the 'teleiihoneear.' •'; "As for the fact of the constant use nf tho telephone causing: deafness, 1 think that It is almost purely imaginary. Ifiersons have been accustomed to hearing well for years and suddenly find that they do not hear as well as formerly. It is not because they are becoming deaf, but usually that they are finding out that they did not hear as well as they thought they did. This may sound strange, but I will try to explain it to you. "Our senses are given us to perform their natural duties only. If we strain them, or abuse them in any way, they soon lose their natural ucuteness. Take the Indian, for example. You will never, hud one near-sighted, for they do not strain their eyes by reading at close quarters, as their Caucasian brothers do. "So it is with this telephone deafness. The ear is under a constant strain, trying to natch sounds at long range, and when, after a year of such work, an operator finds that he has trouble in distinguishing other sounds it is not because of deafness, but' that the ear has-been used for purposes other than those that nature intended. "But the .'telephone ear' is making rapid headway among tho operators in this city, and also all over the country. .'.Whether it will become more prevalent in tho future depends wholly on whether those affected take proper care of themselves or nut." L,e t the next man who "rings up central" and thinks he lias a grievance against the demure "hello-girl," who repeats his number after him, rellect that he may be growling at a girl who is unique in her way, for she is probably affected with "telephone ear a distinction which . the ordinary Individual could not obtain '. even II he anted to. The Elevator Sickness. "Cases of elevator sickness are on the increase," said Dr. E. C. Knowl-ton, of Chicago. "When physicians first began to claim that there was such a thing as elevator sickness their statements were usually discredited, but it is now becoming well defined. Its effects are found in an increased nutn- ber of cases of brain fever aud disordered nervous systems. Every one has felt a sense of emptiness in their heads, a sensation as if they were falling when riding rapidly in an elevator, especially if it was going down. This creates a dizziness, slight it is true, but the constant repetition of which brings on headaches and often brain fever. If not so serious then it is felt in the nerves. Those who habitually ride up and down eight or ten stories cannot fail to realize that it is bringing on a disordered condition of the nerves. For this reason elevators should be run slowly, especially whoa descending. Cincinnati Enquirer,

THE WEAK POINT OF THE BIOYDLE. In the recent article in the " St. James's Giusetie " on cycling aa a pursnit for women no reference was made to the general question, Is bicycling healthy or not? A vast deal (writes "A Medical Man" to 'the same jenrrnai) has been written on this subject, chiefly in praiso of the inariiine by enthusiastic admirera : voimg men have been exhorted not that thev need "much eihortation to take it up as a prcMmmently wholesome occupation for mmd and body alike, and fnicfi as are of riper years have (been assured that it will give them a new lease of life. Doctors have recommended it right and left "in moderation "we always recommend everything in moderation and they are rrot a little responsible for the increasing prevalence of the practice among the upper and middle classes. But it may -ba doubted whether they have really paid very much attention to the subject ot taken serious pains to ascertain the nature and efieets of the exceedingly peculiar form of exercise involved in riding a bicycle. Certainly experience is lieginning to reveal the existence of some very grave disadvantages which have been hitherto generally overlooked, possibly because time was required to bring them to light. Now that cycling seems likely to become more popular than ever, attention may be opportunely drawn to them in the public interest. At first sight it looks as if the -bicycle ought to be the greatest boon to town-dwellers of moderate means. It offers at once fresh air, change of scene, mental recreation, and physical exercise, more easily and completely than any other athletic or semi-athletic pursuit. One would expect to see those who use it bearing the same obvious signs of benefit to health whioh are always associated with outdoor occupations and pastimes such as boating, ridin" cricket, golf, and so on. But it is matter of common observation that the very reverse is the case. On the outskirts of LondoA and every largo town you constantly see strings of young men scouring tho country road with ease and swiftness, filling their lungs with fresh air, and performing all the orthodox sacrifices to HVgieia. Ton expect to see them looking tiie better for" it, but are often disappointed. They frequently wear an anxious look and an unwholesome mllo- which are so characteristic that one may almost speak'of the "bicycle face." Watch them descend at a roadside inn; a good many exhibit anything but the exhilaration of healthy exercise. Some are more than pale; their faces have the peculiar grey .me which betokens nervous exhaustion. And they complain or. headache-a singular complaint for young men engaged in an athletic pastime. Of course, this does not apply to all but it is true of so many as to be quite noticeable, 'and to make people ask why bieyclisM always "look so secdv." It is at-tritmted to the hunehed-up attitude in which most of them nde, or to their over-taxin" their strength in speed and distance: but inquiry shows thai riders who take their wheeling in ail moderation and sit upright often suffer in the same way. One constantly meets with people wiio have given up bicycling because it does not " agree ' with them. Thev" find that, so far from being refreshed by a ride, 'headache and increased weariness are apt to result. Certain it is that some people who aro sound in wind and limb and can enjoy other exercises, do get mora barm tbaa frood from the bicycle., and there are reasons for thinking that such people are numerous if they do not exactly form the majority. The fact that the ill-effects associated with the two-wheeled machine are not experienced with the tricycle, although the latter entails far more exertion, gives a clue to what I believe the explanation. -the distinguishing feature of the bicycle, and especially of the safety, is the difficulty of maintaining the equilibrium. "Learning" to rido means mastering the art of keeping the machine upright. It lias a tendency to fall to one side or the other all the time, which has to be counteracted by a special effort. The learner knows it very well to his cost; but once having iearnt, he forgets about it and does his balancing more or less automatically. Nevertheless tho effort is still there, and it puts a constant, though unconscious effort upon his brain and nervous system. The reason why tho bicycle has to lie " learnt " at all is that the centre of equilibrium in the brain requires to lie taught the business of doing its duty under novel circumstances. The falling bicycle is maintained upright by a constant series of small muscular movements, which, unconsciosly. adjust the weight in the proper position, and are themselves controlled by a special brain -centre situated at, the back of the head. Tho strain upon this centre is incessant, though unmarked, and some people cannot stand it for more than a short time. This it is that causes the headache and nervous exhaustion. Probably it does not affect those who begin very young whose brain, that is to say, has grown to meet tho requirements made on it; and possibly it affects those with either very tough, or very dull, nerves but little. Most of us, however, are obliged to live in such :t way that our nervous systems become very susceptible to any unac customed strain, and those who are most likely to use the bicycle belong to the most susceptible classes, The urn-ens effort entailed hy balancing tho machine is too much for them. The explanation may strike some people as fantastic, but it is sound physiology and it squares with the facts. Experienced cyclists often say that the tricycle, and even the old high bicycle which requires less effort to balance are less fatiguing for prolonged work, such as a tour, than the safety ; yet the latter is lighter, quicker, and superior in nearly every respect, save that of stability. It is a question of balance. The once popular amusement of roller-skating oa-used much headache among women, and considering how liable they are to that complaint and, indeed, a nervous affection generally they cannot be too cautious about the bicycle. "Wheeling" is not a pursuit that will suit everybody.

Medical Men Not of United Opinion Upon Effects of Using the .Modern Vehicle. The "bicycle face" is a joke, and the "bicycle hump" is a prediction. Is the "bicycle spine" a present and perilous reality? Some doctors say yes and some say no. The discussion brought about by the death of a young man in Oakland shows the customary differences of the experts, but the discussion has but begun. On a subject In which there Is so much interest as bicycle-riding the debate will travel wherever wheels are ridden and where are they not ridden? Four doctors of Oakland declare that the fccr . : : George N. Northey, or Giles, the Dead Rider. Vrawn from a recent photograph. meningitis which caused the death of Geo. N. Giles was the result of the use of the bicycle. These four are Dr. E. H. Woolsey, Dr. J. P. H. Dunn, Dr.' O. D. Hamlin and Dr. M. L. Johnson, all of whom participated in the post-mortem perusal of the body of the young rider. . VThere can be no question as to the cause of the death of this young man," said Dr. Woolsey yesterday, "and there can be no question in my mind or the minds of the gentlemen who were with me in this case as to the cause of the meningitis. It was simply the Jarring of the spine upon the spinal cord caused by the riding of his wheel There was nothing else the matter with fcim. for be was a well-developed man. "There is also no question in my mind but there are to-day hundreds of cases of 'bicycle spine' in this city, which are not recognized because of lack of information on the subject. I say this because it is true, and because It may warn some who are overdoing the sport. Reasonable exercise upon the wheel cannot be criticised, but I consider the bicycle more dangerous than any other of the many causes of disease in the human frame. The railroad train, the horse car, the bookkeeper's desk and the sewing machine have all produced diseases In the human organization peculiar to them selves, and now the bicycle has added itself to the list, and there are undoubtedly bi cycle diseases in course of development. "Bicycle riding is of so recent date that the effect upon the human system has not yet been fully observed, but we will have 'bicyclism' in a few years, with as distinct an individuality as the 'railroad spine,' or diseases caused by using the sewing machine. These will come from the excessive and back and down to San Jose It means more than they can afford to give for the pleasure. "A question has been raised as to the posture of the rider whether riding bent over the handle bars or riding sitting up straight is the more injurious. I believe that the bent position Is the more damaging for a very simple reason. In bending over the vertebrae of the spine are compressed in the front and widened In the back, so that the intervertebral cartilage Is compressed in the front and stretched in the back. This brings the vertebrae more Closely together in the front and makes a more nearly solid connection from the base, where the jar occurs, to the brain. I am not an artist, but a simple diagram will show what I mean. I have here shown what will stand for the vertebrae with the cartilage between. In bending the position assumed can easily be seen. Anal-most solid line of contact would be formed from the point .where the jar occurs to the brain. . ... ; "It is exactly the principle of the spring of a wagon. The cartilage is the spring. It you load down one end of the wagon until it rests on the axle you lose the value of the spring. "It is a common principle of physics that the smalller the' surface ot elasticity the greater the effect of the concussion. It can easily be seen that if the point of elasticity becomes compressed Into one small space in the front of the spinal column the concussion will be carried to the brain more severely than if the spine were upright and the entire cushion of the cartilage were used in breaking its force. That this cartilage can be compressed is easily shown by the difference in the helghth of a person between evening and morning, which sometimes amounts to nearfy an inch. "The future has much more of this in store for us. and the world is wheeling to its grave, and some ministers would have them wheeling to eternal destruction. This is simply the beginning of the end. These diseases are beginning to develop, and from now on tbey will be heard from. It is death on a bicycle if the pace that kills Is not stopped." Dr. Woolsey's assertions are confirmed by the physicians who aided In the post mor- tern examination of young Giles. "This has opened a big question," said Dr. J. P. H. Dunn. "Cycling has become so common the magnitude of the question cannot be underestimated. It is also such a recent amuse ment that the full effect that it has upon the human organism has not been studied. From my experience with what is commonly known as 'railroad spine,' in the railroad hospital in this city, and from such observations as I have been able to make of the effect of bicycling upon the human spine, I have no hesitation in saying that the bicycle disease Is infinitely more dangerous than this very serious and common disease of railroad men. The railroad spine is CURVEDBACK. bicycle riding upon a person who curves his spine. "I have ridden a bicycle a little, but' not to any great extent," explained Dr. Hamlin, "and I can festify to the serious results that may be expected from excessive use of the wheel. I have had several caBes where I have beep compelled to forbid bl. cycle riding. It. seems to have a particularly bad effect upon the lumbar nerves, and that carries with it danger to the future of the race. Women cannot be too careful In the use of the wheel, and long rides will prove most disastrous to them. The. position has much to do with the effect of riding upon thetpinal cord and the brain. The construction of the backbone Is intended to protect, the spinal cord more than anything else; For that reason cartilage cushions are placed between the vertebrae. Bend the backbone so that the front of the vertebrae touch or nearly touch, and you have a solid line of contact from the base to the brain. Jar must necessarily be felt along this very keenly, and much more keenly than if the spine were kept straight. Ths. constant jarring causes congestion, and congestion causes inflammation, and inflammation means meningitis and death. This is the case summed up as briefly as It can be stated." The funeral services over the body of young Giles will take place this afternoon at 3 o'clock at the house of his adopted father, 2013 Brook street, Oakland. , William C. Giles, the boy's step-father, was as fond of him as if he had been his own son. The boy had lived with him from infancy, and took Mr. Giles' name, though his right name was Northey. "1 am thoroughly convinced that too much bicycle riding caused my son's death," said Mr. Giles yesterday, "and It was a strange fact that he said that his bicycle would kill him. The doctors and I thought that he was suffering from some rheumatic trouble or a little cold, but he said : 'That bicycle is killing me.' . "He bad a magnificent constitution, and lived wisely. He was young, well developed and had always spent much time in the open air, taking abundant exercise. He had never a day's sickness in his life until bis bicycle trouble began to develop. He never drank or otherwise dissipated and rarely smoked and then only cigars. He was not a cigarette smoker. Everything was in his favor as far as health went. "He began bicycle riding about two or three years ago, but then he rode comparatively little. Sometimes ho would not be on his bicycle once a week. But he used his wheel more and more until last March, when ho commenced the regular use of his bicycle In his business. "At that time he was made the inspector of the pipe line of the Oakland Water Cora pany between here and the works at Alva-rado, and he JtouDdUfcat wheelirea a great aid to him. He -told me that he was going to use It to carry him over the ground that he had to cover each day, and I thought that it was a good idea, better, in fact, than making the trip In a buggy or wagon. "The first day that he made the trip be complained of being sore in the muscles, and for a day or so he used the buggy. Then he took to his wheel once more and as soon as he got used to the Increased muscular ex ertion he felt all right. "He had been riding about two months very regularly when he began to complain of his back, which he said was hurting htm This kept getting worse until the latter part of May, when he said that the pain was so bad that he could not stand It any longer. I told him to take a rest for a while. It was at this time that he made the remark: 'That bicycle is' killing me.' "He went away to the springs for a while and came back feeling better, but not cured. He used his bicycle a little, and then gave it up altogether, saying that it hur him too much and that the very sight of a bicycle made him sick. He positively refused to use the machine, .though the doctors did not attribute his sickness to it. "He was finally taken down two weeks ago to-day, and we had two different physicians wno aa not seem to aid him any. One treated him for lumbago, and the other for typhoid fever. At last I called in Dr. Wool eey, who said that he thought that he was suffering from cerebral spinal meningitis. But the boy was too far gone at that time and death came. I believe thoroughly that death resulted from his use of the bicycle, and what he used to say was true, though we did not believe It at the time." The great interest taken by the men of the medical profession in San Francisco in the report from Oakland of the cause of the dath of young Giles, or Northey, Is Indicated by the expressions of their opinions. Dr. C. G. Kenyon rides a wheel and is glad of It. He likes the exercise and the pleasure and he recommends bicycle riding to bis patients, although he finds that when the recommendation Is adopted he loses a patient, health coming with the wheeling. "Some physicians as well as laymen have foolish ideas regarding cycling," said Dr. Kenyon, "but you can always put it down that they are not familiar with the wheel. Any one who has jolted over the stone pavements of this city for twenty years in a buggy, as I have done, and then taken up the wheel would never say the bicycle is not beneficial." "People who ride on wheels do not look happy," said the doctor, "and I do not like any outdoor exercise in which the mind is not perfectly at ease. Dr. Gardner, Chief Surgeon of the Southern Pacific Company, is one who does not favor the wheel for exercise. "I am hardly In a position." said he. "to speak of the use or abuse of the bicycle, as comparatively few cases have come under my attention. although in the past few days thera have reached my notice more injuries and more patients from riding a bicytle than from the railroad. I should consider the wheel highly Injurious to children, especially any afflicted with any organic disease or who are prone to consumption. "Onlv yesterday." continued , the doc tor, "I advised two of my patients to dls continue the use of the wheel, 'simply be cause it develops only the lower limbs, and when there is any lung trouble the parts of the ' body necessary . to develop are not affected. In the case of hard smokers it Is also extremely Injurious, and I know of a case here where death was undoubtedly has tened by wheeling. The position that the majority of riders assume is extremely bad and can hardly help, sooner or later, giving the rider curvature of the spine. Ridingjt bicycle would have the same effect that riding on a train would have, and the constant Jolt over cobble-stone pavements of the city streets must. In my opinion, tend to destroy the tissue between the vertebrae of the spinal column. Country riding should not be nearly so injurious as riding over the stone pavements of a city. I must con fess," concluded Dr. Gardner, "I am not very well posted regarding the wheel, as I have never tried it myself, and base my objec' Hons on what I have seen." Dr. W. F. McNutt declares that he Is not a bicyclist. "That will do for younger men." said he, "but I am in favor of the use of the bicycle, not unequivocally still I think it is a good healthy exercise, though there might be a better. The trouble Is ths American people will not walk. We do not take half as much exercise in the open air as the English, in their cold, wet climate, If bicycling will induce people to go out of doors, to keep out, to take plenty of exer else and to appreciate the benefits of out door exertion, it will do a great service to the people by making them healthier. As for bicycling doing any barm, why should it ? If people are Indiscreet, take excessive ex ercise, overtax their strength, they will feel bad effects. Just as from an over-indulgence in any other physical exercise, but with or dinary care no harm need be feared. "The case of the young man Northey or Giles is interesting, but not proved; that is to say, not proved against , the bicycle. Railway spine.' as It Is called, is caused l7 much severer jolting than any bicycle rider would receive. The shock from riding the wheel is far less than from riding in a train The air-filled tires makes It slight. People who ride in buggies over cobblestone pave ments use air cushions to check the concus sion. Then, too, the "railway spine is due case of disease arising from bicycling, and do not believe that under normal conditions bicycling will produce any disease." Dr. A. L. Lengfeld hesitated to express a professional opinion, for though a qualified he Is not a practicing physician. He said, however, "I think there is less jar riding a bicycle than a horse. I opposed my wife's riding a horse, and I approved her riding a wheel, so that she bas given up the former and taken to the latter. I should think that where there is a strong predisposition to spinal meningitis bicycling might bring It on or hasten it ; but I do not believe that the disease would be occasioned by bicycling." "Railroad spine comes only as the result of years of railroad travel," said Dr. . E. Caldcron. "It is not the result of a single trip. Railroad conductors, whose business Is all but Incessant traveling, get it. In their cases there is not necessarily any pre disposition to spinal meningitis. That bi cyclists can contract the disease from riding the wheel I very much doubt. The roads would have to be in very bad condition. I have never heard of any disease of any kind resulting from bicycling. The only cases resulting from bicycle riding that I have treated have been injuries, bruised hands, feet and faces, hurt in disasters. I have new even heard of Internal trouble brought about by bicycling. I believe it Is no more harmful for a woman than for ii man. I believe that a woman's own good sense should tell her'when bicycling would be 'injudicious tot her". , The only people who to my mind should not Indulge In bicycling are those who suffer from heart affections. The exertion is apt to bring on falntness." Among the doctors of San Francisco who believe that the bicycle supplies a means of healthful exercise, is Dr. W. R. Cluness Sr., who came hither after gaining distinc tion In Sacramento. He remarked that the certificate of Dr. Woolsey declaring bicycle riding to be the cause of cerebral spinal meningitis, 'from which came the death of a young man in Oakland, Is the first infor mation that the bicycle causes disease that hag reached him from a reputable authority. Notwithstanding this compliment to Dr. Woolsey's ability, Dr. Cluness does not agree with all the conclusions of the Oak land surgeon. Indeed he cannot conceive lhat cerebral spinal meningitis could be - produced by the Jar of a bicycle. Dr. . Cluness bas never in his practice had a case of disease that in his opinion might be attributed to the bi cycle. "I believe in the use of the bicycle," he said, "for I regard the exercise as bene ficial to the physical condition of the rider. The bicycle may be abused, just as whisky or wine or bread or beef or any other good thing may be abused, and whatever evila come from the bicycle are due to abuse and not to rational use. The bicycle affords fascinating exercise. It Is to many novel. Hence people, particularly the young, are Inclined to excessive riding, and the overexertion may do some injury. But the injury to th'e few from abuse of the bicycle is much more than compensated by the benefits to the many from Its proper use. Suppose even that one person should die from over-riding. The lives of 100 are prolonged by reasonable riding. The bicycle has come to stay, and I believe it brings with it no ills that in any degree compare with Its benefits. "Referring to the case In Oakland, while I regard Dr. Woolsey as equally strong with myself much stronger very likely 1 cannot understand bow spinal meningitis could be produced by the Jar of riding a bi cycle. Meningitis is the inflammation of a membrane. I cannot conceive that a membrane can be irritated by the motion of a bicycle. Among trainmen there is a dis ease known as railroad spine, that comes from the constant jar of the locomotive or the car upon the rails. A person regularly riding long distances over the cobbles might acquire a disorder similar to railroad spine, though I doubt it; but such a disease would not be meningitis, but a disorder of the acrobatsj who suffer a great deal from heart failure, and seldom live long. "People with weak hearts or. unsound lungs should not ride. For healthy people of sedentary habits cycling Is an excellent exercise. Dr. Winslow is a distinguished "alienist," that is, he is supposed to know, and probably does know, a great deal about mental derangements. But this does not prove that he is free from prejudice, or that he is so sane that he can look on all sides of a new question with impartial vision. It does not prove that he is not a fogy when it comes to innovations that run counter to his preconceived opinions. He has allowed himself to be interviewed in regard to the use of the bicycle by women. Incidentally, he also gave his views on horseback riding for women and on bloomers. He doesn't like any of them. Not a bit. In fact, he loathes all of them and he prognosticates dire calamities to follow the New Woman's predilection for them. Listen to this: "My disapproval of women using the bicycle is most positive. No woman ehould ever be allowed to exercise in that manner. It is dangerous to health and it is injurious to morals. "The physical nature of woman is snob that bicycle riding cannot be productive of aught bnt trouble. "While I base my denunciations of the exercise on the demonstrations I have seen of its effects, I even more strongly condemn its use for the sake of fatnre generations. I am fearfnl for the next generation if this bicycle craze keeps on, for it is then and only then that the foil effects of the evil will be absolutely demonstrated to the public. Now if Dr. Winslow had confined his strictures to the alleged bad effects of bicycle riding on the body of woman we should have been very read' to carefully examine his reasons and compare them with the reasons which other physicians give for thinking that the bicycle, discreetly used, of course, is proving a great benefit to woman physically. And we should have also examined them in the light of the experience of tens of thousands of women who are confident that the bicycle has greatly helped them. So far as professional opinion is concerned, it is doctor against doctor. On the very day that the English physician was giving out his interview, Dr. I. N. Love, of St. Louis, was reading a paper on the same subject before the Mississippi Vallev Medical Association, in session in Detroit. Dr. Love said that he had investigated the subject thoroughly and had come to the conclusion that the bicycle was the greatest thing known for exercise when properly used. The other doctors agreed with him. So it is Dr. Forbes Winslow vs. the Mississippi Valley Medical Association. Is there any evidence that the women of savage tribes who ride in that wray have been rendered incapable of bringing into existence well-formed and vigorous offspring? Is there a scrap of evidence to show that the women of certain country districts in the world today here and across the water, who ride much on horseback are more addicted to special diseases and weaknesses than are their millions of sisters who never put their feet in stirrups? Further along in his deliverance he declares that both exercises produce conditions that "lead to abnormal appetites and desires." This is enigmatical. The only rational explanation of it is that the general improvement in health attendant upon indulgence in these forms of exercise, and the mildly stimulating effect of currents of pure air, have a tendency to increase the strength of the amative impulses. THE PENY DREADFUL. Everybody seems to be agreed in denouncing the penny dreadful. Now and then some worthy magistrate, sentencing an unfortunate young scamp to the birch rod or the reformatory, solemnly lectures the court on the iquitous effect of these publications on the youthful mind. The newspapers are prompt to take up the cry ; indignant correspondents join in the protest ; and sometimes even a Parliamentary candidate gets heckled on this weighty question. It may, however, be reasonably asked, are these strongly stigmatised works in reality so desperately wicked ? Is it quite fair to insinuate that because some very naughty boyoccasionally endeavours to imitate the achieve ments of the Buccaneer King or the Terrible Brothers of Tabasco, every reader of these gory volumes is likewise affected ? A sweeping con demnation of these books, like most other sweeping condemnations, is emphatically unjust. Something, we beJieve, can be said even for the much-abused "penny blood." We have before us a volume containing some incidents in the career of a person known as "Ballarat Bill." Now " Ballarat Bill," does not seem to have been altogether a bad sort of man. In the first chapter of the work relating his ad ventures among the Patagonian giants, we find him rescuing a virtuous female in distress. No body, we tliink, can find any fault with this. THE ADMIRAL, SOME CABMEN, AND THE BICYCLE. Speaking at a Conservative dinner at Eastbourne, Admiral Field said he lost the support of the railway employes because-the minds of the men were poisoned against him. There was another vote, he had it on good authority, that he lost: that was the cabmen's vote. What was his iniquity, filled up to the full, which led to this vote being lost? Why, some emissary went about among them and poisoned them against him by saying that he was a man who rode a bicycle to save cab hire. (Laughter.) He supposed they believed it; but he would tell them that he intended to ride a bicycle whenever he could. He had a liver, and so had they, and it wanted shaking up, and so did theirs. (Laughter.) They shook theirs up by hard manual labour. He could not do that ; he worked with his brain, and must shake his liver up by riding a horse or a bicycle. It seemed that a poor slave of a member was not to be allowed to walk or ride a bicycle, but only to ride in a cab, and he must therefore ride in cabs till he rode in a hearse to the cemetery. (Renewed laughter.) He would not give up his bicycle for all the cab votes in the world.

j ITALIAN IMMIGRANTS. MANY NOW ON ELLIS ISLAND WILL BE DEPORTED. New York, March 27. At least four hundred of the 2,000 Italian immigrants who were landed on Ellis Island on Sunday and Monday will be deported, as they have not the means to subsist upon for thirty days. The law requires each immigrant to have at least $30 or to have some relative In America before he is admitted. Commissioner Senner attributes the large migration of Italians to the Italian invasion of Abyssinia, to which most Italian peasants are averse. They do not wish to be drafted into the army and so to avoid becoming conscripts they emigrate. In many instances they have sold their household effects In order to raise their passage money. Of the vast number of Italian immigrants now on Ellis Island but a very small proportion are ticketed through to railroad towns.

LEARNING HOW TO RIDE CHAMPION BALD TELLS THE NOVICE ALL. ABOUT IT. Tlie Bicycle Is n Great Aid to Health and Pleusure, But the Pastime Mrst Be Followed According to the Dictates of Good Common Sense, Champion Eddie C. Bald writes for the the New York Journal the following article, 'which will be read with interest and profit by every one who Is learning or intends learning how to ride a wheel: EDDIE C. BALD. There has been ;a great deal of discussion of late on the part of medical men and women over the advantages and Injuries to health that come from riding the bicycle. The "monkey hump," the "bicycle face," "bicycle Insanity," Injury to various physical organ's from the jar of riding over rough roads or sitting upon improperly constructed saddles, and the thousand, and one other evils, whether real or imaginary, have been harped upon through the nress by these people. There are always cranks ready to attack any , Innovation that disturbs the routine of every-day life or jostles against their sensibilities, setting It down at once as a harmful and highly injurious practice. What I say upon this matter must be said from the standpoint of a layman, who knows as much about the practice of medicine as an old cow does about knitting work. But from the standpoint of a bicycle rider of a good many years' experience, both of road and park riding and race track competition, I am ready to defend the practice. When I first began to ride, as a puny boy, it was merely for pleas- FIRST LIEUT. R. T. LEVY, N. A. C. Wheelmen. ure, but during a single year I gained so greatly in health that I decided to enter race track competition, and almost continuously since I have followed the occupation of a racing nian. Dur Ing all that time my physical health has Improved vastly, .and I never experienced an hour's- Inconvenience or suffering as a result of bicycle riding. If doctors generally, or even the large majority, of them, were opposed to byci- cle' riding and could cite instances of injuries resulting from it, I would not expect that anything that I could say would be taken m rebuttal of such evidence. But they are not. In fact. : know of one physician who conducts a large sanitarium at Geneva, N. Y. where all sorts of nervous and chronic diseases are treated, who relies almost as much on the bicycle as unon his medicines and baths for the improve ment of his patients. On any fine day his bicycle brigade may be seen pedal ling, about the streets of the village or the-large park that fronts the lnstitu tion, and he says that in many cases Improvement dates from the day they begin to ride the wheel. And he Is only one of the many doctors who will say the same thing. For the first week do not ride more than a mile or two, or perhaps three miles, morning and evening, say at S or 9 a. m. and 4 or 5 p. m. If you master the wheel readily, you may be able to exceed this, but in no case ride long enough to get thoroughly tired out. The new rider tires before he realizes it; and great harm may be done by too severe exertion, at this stage. , Smooth roads should be chosen, where traffic Is light. The green rider is liable to lose his head and get a spill on . a crowded thoroughfare. Don't try any trick riding or hill climbing. You ought to be able to do five miles and return by the end of the week if the roads are entirely favorable and a good rest is taken before starting back. DON'T RIDE TOO FAR. 1 Having reached this point, don't think at once that you can break records either for time or distance. I can think of nothing more 111 advised than for a rider who has had experience of four or five milesof smooth pavement or level country roads setting out for a long, hard day's ride. By this I don't mean ai century run, either. I have seen riders used up for the season by foolishly attempting too much while yet green and soft. It will pay .you in the end. It will save physical wear and tear that cannot be estimated and much strain upon your. machine. It will also obviate much injurious effort of the heart.
