MONKEY HUMPS. They Ire Unhealthy, Unsightly, and Altogether Bad. Chat With a Reporter on the Correct and Sensible Thing in Wheel Riding. "The monkey hump is injurious to the health of bicycle riders, and if it is not corrected, within Aye years it will tell seriously on the health of this nation. No woman ought to ride a century, and I might also say no man ought to ride a century. It is extremely dangerous to one's health." These statements were made last night to a "Leader" reporter by Miss E. Marguerite Eindley of New York, a hcturer on physical culture. Miss Eindley is accompanied by Miss Carrie P. Purrus, formerly of this city, but now of New York. Both ladies are enthusiastic bicyclists, and both have made the question of the physical effects of bicycling a deep study. Miss Barrus assists Miss Eindley in illustrating many points. For a long time Miss Lindley was opposed to bicycle riding for women, and says that her lecture is the result of a challenge in which she was compelled to defend herself and give her views. The lecture met with much success, and she was compelled to repeat it. Since that time she has given it many times. The lecture was given in Association Hall last Monday evening. A "Leader" reporter called at the house last night, and Miss Lindley spoke in an interesting manner for some time on her favorite study. Among other things, she said: "That the wheel lias come to stay is a well-known fact. That wheeling is a national epidemic is another well-known fact, one which we must meet rationally and utilize as a blessing, and not allow to become a ban on figure and health. A noted author says of this pastime: 'That which might be an angel of light is transformed into a power of evil,' and so it must seem to the non-rider who sees the atrocities of bad posture ruling the pleasure. "The body is a living machine. The bicycle is also a machine, but it is for the use of the rider. We must see that it is fashioned to suit the requirements of the rider, and abandon the task of molding the rider to fit the wheel. "We need daily recreative exercise, and also systematic, corrective exercise. Health suffers when either is disregarded. The bicycle comes to us with the possibilities of untold advantage, providing- it is properly adjusted so as to suit the build of the rider. We cannot overrate the lieneiits that will be derived from proper outdoor life, whether for school child or parent. We need more fresh air. We need freedom from responsibilities. Bicycling is destined to be the recreative exercise that will supply these needs. "Besides the benefits mentioned, it Cures the fatigue of supporting the weight of the body on the feet, and the amount of energy put forth in propelling the wheel is much less than that employed in walking. Even the slow pace is more rapid than walking. And as a consequence, the rider experiences more exhilaration from the friction occasioned by the rapid motion. Respiration is sure to be increased, circulation stimulated, and digestion, in consequence, improved. "Excess in any pleasure la intemperance, and excess in bicycling tells its tale daily in the pallor and fatigue of many who undertake to keep a record equal to that of their robust friends. Individual conditions differ from day to day under the daily influences that shape one's life, so it is unwise to even gauge the amount of energy put forth in this or any othe*r exertion by the amount expended on previous occasions. Still more unwise is it to gauge one's strength by her neighbor's. "Incorrect posture and careless gait are daily before us, especially with men and children. Men, even on foot, habitually carry their heads forward and chests are in consequence flattened, shoulders become round, and abdomens sag. So habitual is this, that readymade clothing is generally shaped for such figures; and a man who can his head where nature meant it Should be finds that his garments wrinkle at the back of the neck and should' is. Just think how terrible for us women to feel obliged to adore such badly built 'lords of creation!' "Men seemed to have ignored entirely nature's magnificent plan of hitch chest and straight shoulders and to have shifted the prominent part of their figure to another plane. On the wheel this is exaggerated, not only In the eyes of the beholder, but in actual condition. A body, hung so disproportionately from its support, especially when its parts are connected with material of a wkldy nature, can't but become permanently misshapen from the continued joggling and from exercising the muscles in this and unnatural position. "What is the excuse for bad posture? The man says speed, and they proceed to go on all fours. And whut is the apology fur rc>ad racing".' Merely to imitate, and very poorly, track riding. A good authority says that not one of the road racers or scorchers is a ge-ntleman. When our gentlemen want to race they usuall> take the track, train for it, and dress accordingly. I must d.mounce the practice of gentlemen's racing when they are not in training from a physiological as well as an artistic standpoint. The preliminary training is necessary to make it a s indulgence. Even if they had that, there's no credit, and little satisfaction in it. "A comfortable nerve system and internal organs are much more to the purpose, and these are »H\er attained from scorching, hut always from riding. "Even Zimmerman denounce a the century runs. One harmful result of bicycling, unless supplementary exercises also enter into daily life, will 1" a loss of symmetry, and of flexibility of upper IllUtltia This is affecting many ali.ady. Incalculable harm la sure to : - j suit unless strict attention is given to correcting this baleful habit of posture. The cramped leg posture also retards the current of venous blood from lower l?mbs to the heart, which, with the continued hip and leg motion, causing excess of blood current in this part of the body, cannot but cause harm. "We need more health and happiness in these busy crowded lives. At best we are but a nation of semi-invalids. Do not take away any of our outdoor sports, but merely rationalize them. Study poise, symmetry, art in nature. Let. our women demanel that wheels be built to encourage pride of figure and health, to overcome invalidism, and at the same time let us discourage the race horse principle. Let us have jockeys to race wheels as horses, but let our men maintain their position as men. Wheeling must be made hygienic, both for symmetry and for organic health. One inipera- j tive demand is systematic exercise tol tiain or educate the muscles, not spe- | CificaUy employed in the pastime. She suggested in fact, a person who took gloomy views of the neighbors' morals, and would never be satisfied with this side of heaven. He called the lady every name he could think of and commented upon her character and appearance in terms altogether unfit for publication. The lady fainted, and a big policeman took the bird to the lock-up. They claim that a hitherto unheard-of malady, namely, the “bicycle eye,” has developed as a result of the great and unuspal strain on the optics of wheelwomen. The vigilant foe of the wheelwomen is still in the field, and will make a fierce and It is to be hoped final fight on the platform of the “bicycle- eye.’’ The worst feature of this malady, say those who have observed its development, Is that it Is chronic and Incurable. This makes the case well worthy of considera- tlon and cannot fall to suggest to over- zealous wheelw'omen that If they persist IrV cultivating the stare that seems to be necessary In order to acquire .speed and avoid other vehicles, they may actually be menacing the future of the human race. It Is easy to see that the falling off .n physical beauty will be swift and sure. When all women become converted to the wheel, as they soon will, the clash and confusion of bicycles will be so great A t cleverest will escape aHveJ As the most clever in taking care of themselves w’lll be those who have culti- iiicrinnui V Will 11« tllUS« WllU IlitV« CUJll- vated the biggest stare and consequently the most bulging eyes, the transmission of this undesirable characteristic will be as inevitable as It will be unlovely. John Brisben Walker, in the Cosmopolitan for July, speaks of the horseless carriage as a possibility of the immediate future. It may be a possibility, but hardly a probability. As a street or road vehicle it hns not demonstrated either Its practicability or Its desirability. tO'hus far It is an iridescent dream, hardly up to a disturbing nightmare. So far this season there are no signs that mankind is growing cold in horse love or panting to harness a machine In place of man's best animal friend. Nor is it evident that the omnipresent bicycle Is lessening the vim and vigor of the light harness horse devotees. A SERMON ON THE X-RAY. Ministers of the gospel are finding In the character and accomplishments of the X-ray apparatus used in The Herald's charitable work some new and apt Illustrations to adorn a sermon or to point the moral thought they would instil and fasten in the minds of their hearers. A most eloquent application of its powers occurred in a sermon delivered yesterday by the Rev. J. A. B. Wilson at the Garvanza Methodist church. His text was the opening words of the gospel of St. John: "In the beginning was the word, and the word was God. The same was in the beginning with God. All things were made by Him and without Him was not anything made that was made. In Him was life and the life was the light' of man. And the UgVit shineth in darkness and the darkness comprehended It not." "In the beginning was the word." That is to say before anything was formed, ere God began the great work of creation, the word or "Logos" was. Logos was no part of the creation. Logos antedated creation. Now, as what was before all creation must be eternal, and as what gave being to all things could not derive its being from anything, therefore "Logos," the word, Jesus, was before all things, made all things, and is the eternal God, upholding all things. Dr. Clarke says that "Logos," of which the literal translation is here used, signifying word, or spoken speech, or doctrine, or reason, or the faculty of reasoning, was as much an appellation of the Savior as "Jesus" or "the Christ." And it was an appropriate name for Him who is the true light which lighteth every man who Cometh into the world, the fountain of all wisdom who hati declared and revealed God unto mankind. In Genesis God is said to have created all things. In this verse, Jesus, the Word, is said to have created all things. The same unerring spirit spake in Moses and the evangelist. Therefore, Christ and the father are one, and to say that Christ made all things by delegated power is absurd. "In him was life," and Jesus imparted life to everything he created.whether animal, vegetable or intellectual. Yet the animal life held not the light of man. for "the world by wisdom knew not God." Therefore, the expression "in him was light," means naturally that light eternal which he revealed unto men. God created light. "God created two great lights."—Gen. 1. 16. And now we use a new light, the X-ray, and with it see through opaque substances. With "It turned upon the pocket books of this congregation your pastor can tell, when he appeals to you to emulate Its helpfulness in charitable work, whether It Is quite true that you have "lift all your money at home." At this witty sally a perceptible murmur of merriment and applause was with difficulty suppressed by the sedate congregation to whom the humorous predilections of the good parson much endear him. We are able with this new light to peer into the very heart of polld substance wrapped hitherto always in opaque gloom. If all I hear of the first steps of this groat discovery be true . I believe it to be only a short time until we can peer through the wall of your room and see your every act. whether you are conscious of it or not. But a little while till we can pierce the mountains surrounding us and see the plain beyond. \ How like the all-seeing omniscience of the omnipotent Gndjs tills great discovery! God is an X-ray, looking through your conscience, your motives, your faults, distinguishing between those sprung from hereditary environment and those of personal perversity in the secret sins of your life. In a way as mysterious to us as was the hesirt of solid substance but the other day, ere this new light made bright the gloom of Its hiding place, God, with the X ray of divine intelligence, can penetrate the innermost chambers of the tomb of time, where the buried centuries lie, or he can peer behind the veil of the future into the uttermost confines of the ages yet unborn. Verily, it is true as St. Mark hath said: "There is nothing covered which shall not be revealed, and hid that shall not be known." In this marvelous discovery, filling with translucency the opaque, we are finding out something old, not something new, although It may be new to us, of the great wisdom of the Almighty God, his power and his everlasting glory. *" In his divine omniscience he hath withheld from the minds of the children of men this new proof of his wisdom

Even the problem novel of this year has failed to attract the usual number of readers, and students of social questions are trying to explain this sudden change. The bicycle is blamed for this literary defection. It is said that men and womeh, youths and pr's, who nsed to send many of their evenings; scanning the pages of popular books, now enjoy scorching during the twilight and evening hours. This explanation may be partially true, bnt there must be other reasons that will partially account for the apparent indifference to literary relaxation. For one thing hard times have changed domestic conditions. Women do more household work these days. They also try to save expenses by sewing and re. modeling old garments to suit the prevailing changes in style that the modistes are constantly inventing. Men find it so hard, to make money that they either work more or worry when they should be enjoying some relaxation. Even the boys and girls are kept busy. This year's political unrest also con tributes to-the disinclination to read. The money question is being studied by many itersons who have been used to read novels'. Newspapers that devote considerable space to the expo sition of financial doctrines and theories are very largely read, as the ncreased and constantly growing circulation of such papers as the New York Journal sufficiently attests. Therefore the public library figures do not necessarily imply that the people of this country are becoming less fond of reading; they simply tell a story of decreased ready money, increased work and general pre-occu- pation.

TOO MANY WHEELS. Official Report Says England Had an Over-Production of Bicycles Last Year. WASHINGTON, Oct. 22.-Consul Bar ker, Birmingham, England, In his annual report to the State Department, says that the one marked development in that district during the year has been the cycle trade. It has been so great that there has been a great over-nro ductlon. The trade with the United States has not been greatly affected, but no complete bicycles have been sent to the United States since 1894. The British foreign trade in bicycles amounted in 1895 to $6,747,012, in 1896 to $9,056,420, and in 1897 (estimated) $7,877,275. So many men have been drawn into bicycle making that other branches have been Injured. An increase of 10 per cent. In the wages of skilled labor has resulted, but a decline Is expected for various reasons, Including the Introduction and use of the best American machinerv. In the last two fiscal years, the exports from the United States to the United Kingdom of cycles and parts of cycles was as follows: For 1896, $613,592-for 1897, $2,375,675.

Another side to the question is that it is the girls who refuse to enter the bonus of wedlock since the all-pervading wheel brought them independence. Whichever side is right, the fact remains that many good people on marriage bent are driven to the desperate expedient of advertising for partners. Home and Bicycles, i A couple of years ago a great many people exclaimed that the horse would go out of use as a source ot pleasure, and that the bicycle would take hit place, and to prove their assertions, drew attention to the fact that bicycles were selling for more money than horses, says a writer in the American Horse Breeder. That was at the time when $100 was the standard price of a bicycle. How is It now? The price of horses, particularly of horses suitable for pleasure use, is steadily going up, while the same bicycles that formerly sold for $100 are now down to $50, and in some cases to $40, while a second-hand wheel that cost $100 two years ago can be bought for $10 or $15 now. Did the price of horses drop In as great a proportion as that? Not much. True, some fancy and really absurd prices were paid years ago by men who had money to burn and wished to advertise the fact, but the legitimate value of horses never dropped over 50 per cent, and is now on tho rise, while the bicycle is down, to remain down. Any man who can afford to keep a road horse wlH keep one, regardless of all the bicycle and horseless-carriage fads.

CONCERN: Sales on pause since forbidding horseles carriages
OCR: AUTOMOBILE ORDERS Sales Held Up Because of the Course of the Park Commission X x X X X X X X X X 2-inch a un-till MUST FINALLY CONSENT The Horseless Carriage and Other Similar Vehicles Growing in Popular Favor Rules Easy to Adopt "I have not had my atuomobile down town for nearly a month because of the refusal of the Commissioners of Fairmount Park to allow4 the use of the East River Drive for horseless carriages." So declared Robert E. Glendinning, the banker and broker, to an Inquirer reporter yesterday. The two were discussing the seemingly inexcusable delay that has, characterized the action of the Commissioners in dealing with the automobile question. "I live in Germantown," Mr. Glendinning added, "and the Wissahickon and the East River drives would afford me a direct route to the. city. I. expected when I purchased my horseless carriage to be able to ride to business in it every morning and ride back home again when business was over. I was one of the first applicants for permission to use the Park drive, but I have never been able to obtain any satisfaction one way or the other. On the contrary, I have simply been put off from time to time, although I have signified my willingness to undergo any kind of an examination or submit to any kind of a test to demonstrate my capability as a handler of an automobile." Purchases Held in Abeyance Mr. Gleiidinning's experience is that of other Philadelphia automobilists, and upon the delay and dodging which have been such prominent features of the Park Cora-missison's treatment of the question of admitting automobiles to Philadelphia's great pleasure ground is their dissatisfac tion and that of The Inquirer founded. From one or two automobiles brought to this city as an experiment the number, in cluding public and private carriages used for pleasure only, has reached over thirty. Orders have been placed for several others and orders would be placed for many more were it not tor the unwarranted opposition of the Park Commission. A dealer who handles horseless carriages told the reporter yesterday that he had a number of sales depending upon the early admission of automobiles to the Park. "Persons contemplating buying norse- less carriages come here and look over my catalogues. Then they ask me how long I think it will be before automobiles will be allowed in the Park. Of course, I can't answer the question, and the natural re.-fult is a postponement of the sales in mr.ny instances. The delay of the Com missioners is absurd because of the universally acknowledged fact that the horse less wagon has come to stay, and that next year at the farthest the Commissioners will have to yield. Why, the factories are now turning out, in addition to horseless vehicles for pleasure purposes, automobile ambulances, delivery wagons, patrol wagons, trucks and even sprinkling carts. The horseless wagon has gone beyond the experimental point. It is an accomplished fact, and I am surprised that our Park Commissioners do not gracefully bow to ths inevitable and gain the favor of the public by admitting automobiles un-der proper restrictions."., Will-Not Frighten Horses Jules Junker, another Philadelnhia hi-l oneer in the introduction of the automobile, will within a very short time have three horseless pleasure carriages, in addition to three horseless delivery wagons. "I have ordered two additional pleasure carriages," he told the reporter yesterday afternoon, "because I feel confident that th admission of the automobile to Fair-mount Park is only a, question of time. I have ridden all over Philadelphia in the carriage I now have, and I have taken many drives with it in the Park. My experience has demonstrated to me, as it has to others, that there is not the slightest element of danger to anybody or anything from an automobile. Properly handled an automobile will not frighten horses any more than a properly-handled horse-drawn vehicle will. That fact I have endeavored to impress upon the Park Commissioners, but still they will give me no satisfaction. "As far as proper rules and regulations are concerned, it would be but the work of a few hours at most to draft all that are necessary for the Park. In France, where more automobiles are in use than in any other country, the rules followed the vehicles. What I mean by that is, with the first coming of the automobiles they were permitted to run without any regulations. As they became more and more numerous, however, it was deemed advisable to have some restrictions, as much for the safety of the automobilists themselves as for anybody else. But, even to-day, it is not considered necessary to have special rules for the parks. The same rules govern there as on ordinary thoroughfares, and nobody is endangered." Capability of the Driver In the opinion of several prominent futomobilists but one point other than those embraced in the rules governing the admission of the horse-drawn vehicle into the Park would be necessary in the case of the horseless carriage. The point is capability of the driver, to be determined by examination and test conducted by an expert. The wording of this regulation ought to require considerably less than three hours, let alone the three months and more which the committee, of which Colonel A. Loudon Snowden, of the Park Commission, is the head, has had the matter under consideration. As for the rules governing speed, style of carriage, right of way, bells for sounding warnings, etc., those now in existence for governing bi-cicles and horse-drawn vehicles will answer every purpose. It was rumored yesterday that several prominent members of the Park Commission were warmly in favor of holding another special meeting and voting to admit automobiles to the Park at once, but the rumor could not be verified. POLICE UNABLE TO LOCATE THE LONE FOOTPAD Captain Seymour Believes That He Is a Victim of Dime Novels. Detectives Swarm the Western Addition in the Hope of Catching Him While at Work. The lone highwayman who has been terrorizing the Western Addition Is still at large. The police have been unable to secure the slightest clew that might lead to his Identity. Referring to the case, Captain of Detectives Seymour said; "I think the fellow Is crazy. His actions while holding up a victim show that he Is mentally weak. I am satisfied that when we land him he will prove to be a pervert, whose mind has become unbalanced through reading dime novels and other trashy literature." Last night a number of detectl\'es and policemen in citizens' clothes were falling over each other In the Western Addition, all anxious to capture the robber. They were specially Instructed not to take any chances with him, as it is believed that he will not hesitate to shoot In case he Is cornered: Captain Seymour compares the recent hold-ups with those committed by a Swede named Peterson. Peterson was a constant reader of dime novels. After studying the exploits of Captain Kidd the famous pirate of fiction. Peterson resolved to emulate him. Buying a cheap revolver and some cartridges he started out on his career of crime. After holding up a number of citizens and creating a reign of terror he ran afoul of Policeman Duff, who with nearly all the available members of the department was out looking for him. Duff saw the fellow hold up a citizen. After he had relieved him of his valuables he quietly walked up to him and showing his star told him he was under arrest. Peterson promptly drew his revolver and fired at the officer. the bullet striking him in the calf of the leg. Before he had a chance to shoot again Duff, who had fallen to the ground, managed to draw his pistol, and pointing it at the robber fired. The bullet struck him in the forehead, killing him instantly. A search of Peterson's room revealed a large quantity of cheap novels, which he had been In the habit of reading. It was afterward ascertained that prior to becoming a bold robber he was a hard work- Ing fellow. The methods employed by the Western Addition burglar. Captain Seymour says, are not those of an experienced criminal. Chief of Police Sullivan, realizing that the robber would not hesitate to commit murder, sent for Captains Wittman and Spl'.lane yesterday and had them give him a list of their best men. When they appeared at police headquarters at 5 o'clock last evening they were given a description of the highwayman and Instructed to arrest him. Special Instructions were given to the officers to shoot him the Instant he attempted to reach for his revolver.

THE HORSE HOLDS ITS OWN, Despite Modern invention the .Horseless • Age Seems Still Far Distant. That a horseless age is at hand has been the cry for several years both in America and Europe. The frequent and confident statement of academic military men that cavalry could no longer be counted a useful arm of war, owing to the great power of modern artillery, hardly less than the success of the electric street car, the extensive use of the cycle and the boom pf the automobile, "have made this cry seem plausible. But as yet the cry is not justified by the facts. It is true that electricity is rapidly monopolizing the urban transportation of passengers, and that pleasure carriages moved by motors are every day becoming more popular, but nevertheless the horseless age is still a long way iti the future. The military sharps whose beliefs were based on theory instead of practice, have discovered through the bitter experience of the British in South Africa that cavalry is by no means an obsolete branch of the army. Indeed, lack of horses has been by all odds the most serious drawback Lord Roberts and the other British generals have had to encounter. At this moment British agents are scouring the world for remounts, and often paying exhorbitant prices for the same,mmply because the "cry of a coming horseless age was taken too seriously a few years back by the breeders. But while the current military demand for horses has much to do with the present stiffening prices, it is only one of the causes responsible therefor. The passing of the demand for car horses which caused the ruthless slaughter of tens of thousands of animals of that grade, inaugurated a permanent condition, but today in New York, Chicago and other large cities of the United States/,there is a more pressing call for horses of the better grades than has been known for years. General prosperity is responsible for this, and its influence on ths horse market is twofold. Unprecedented business activity calls for great numbers of draft horses, and an abundance of money, well distributed, naturally increases riding and driving for pleasure, and the demand for harness and saddle horses. The bicycle and the automobile have their places and are certain to remain in favor, but nevertheless there is a large and growing element that cannot be satisfied with steeds of steel.

E0?S ON STRIKE. Blue-Coated Messengers Want More iloney. Movement Concerns Two Companies and is Jot Organize! Officials Say That the Dime Novel Habit is Eesponsible. 1 The spirit of dissatisfaction with ex isting conditions that has been sweeping over China and the rest of the world has evidently taken possession of the boys employed as messengers by the Postal telegraph company in this city, for today a large section of them repeated last year's experience by going on strike. About 11 o'clock the boys employed at the Broad st and Atlantic av offices of the postal and Boston district messenger companies refused to take calls, and soon the word went round to the other local offices and by midday something like 50 or 60 of both district and "commission" messengers were enjoying a respite from their arduous labors. There appeared to be no definite leadership to the movement, and for a time both boys and management were pretty much in the dark as to the cause of the strike. As time wore on, however, it began to dawn upon the former that they were out for more "mon," the district boys desiring a raise to ?5 a week, instead of the $4 at present received, and the commission boys, who deliver telegrams wanting 2 cents a message Instead of the 2 cents which they now get. The district boys appeared to represent the more strenuous element in the movement, many of the others appearing to have gone out more in sympathy with them than with the desire or expectation of bettering their own financial condition. The whole enterprise appeared to be lacking in leadership, however, and up to noon the officials of the companies had received no definite word from the strikers as to their wishes in the matter. When this omission was called to the attention of several of the older and more intelligent looking boys, they admitted that they had no leader or committee, and the Idea of formally presenting their grievances to the management apparently had not hitherto occurred to them. One of the boys bravely volunteered to go up and see the officials himself about It, but his ardor was somewhat dampened when one of his companions exclaimed, warnlngly: "Don't ye do anyting of de sort. Ye'll get pinched If ye do!" As soon as the fact of the strike became known to them the officials of the companies, having vivid recollections of the almost riotous Incidents that accompanied last year's strike, notified police headquarters, and a detail of officers was sent to each office. The boys gathered in knots of half a dozen or so from time to time, but were not allowed to remain very long. The main office on Devonshire st was visited by delegations of the strikers early in the forenoon, but there were no boisterous demonstrations of any kind. Supt G. H. Yetman of the Boston dis trict messenger company said that he was entirely In the dark as to the reasons that had led the boys to stop work. He had been presented with no list of grievances and waited upon by no committee, up to midday, and was Inclined to think that the whole thing was engineered for the purpose of giving the boys a little excitement and an other dose of newspaper notoriety. At the Broad st, Atlantic av and Congress st offices the clerks and superin tendents were obliged to hustle around with messages themselves. As soon as the strike took place the patrons of the district company were notified, as far as practicable, of the difficulty in which the company found itself. No effort was made to employ new boys, as past experience has proved this to be rather impracticable. In addition to the difficulty of breaking them in, they are pretty sure to be subjected to serious interference from the strikers If what some of the telegraph officials say is correct, the dime novel is really to be held responsible for the present trouble. All messenger boys are more or less addicted to the dime novel reading habit, but the company recently had In the employ of its Broad st office one boy who was a perfect record-breaker along that line. He habitually carried around with him not only one novel, but three or four, some of them, no doubt, dealing with the rise from poverty to steam yachts and champagne suppers of messenger boys like himself. A week or two ago, apparently as a result of the kind of literary pabulum on which he had been feeding, he conceived the idea that the messenger boys of Boston were being ground beneath the heels of a financial despotism, and forthwith began to sow the seeds of disaffection among his fellows. He made several determined efforts to get the boys to go on strike, but before he could quite get them around to his way of regarding their situation his missionary efforts had become known to the officials, and there was one messenger boy out of a job. It Is now believed that the young man forthwith constituted himself a walking delegate and set in motion a prop aganda that eventuated in today's strike among his former associates.

emphasize THE COMBING MANIA Some few years ago the edict went forth that if we desired good-looking heads of hair we should apply the brush religiously; indeed, it was whispered that we should even count the strokes. So the women who brushed twenty-five times stood a chance of gaining their objective point sooner than the one who only covered ten strokes. This was not all; we were highly recommended to use a metal brash, and here came the rub. Now. very few scalps can stand the painful effects o the metal teeth in these brushes.. It makes the skin tender and frequently causes irritation which hai been found very hard to remove. Many women took it for granted that when the skin became red a fine circulation was being enforced, and bravely did they continue to brush their locks and inflict pain, believing they were on the high road to success. The consequence is that the women who employed this heroic treatment have very thin heads of hair, and in certain parts very nearly bald. Their scalps are delicate and tender, and will require a deal of care before restored to their former condition.

Only a Day of Wedded Bliss for the Groom, When the Fair One Departed Leaving Some of Her Clothes Behind Her. BY DIRECT 'WIRE TO THE TIMES. 1 TACOMA. Dec. 11. Exclusive Dispatch. John Aust of Bolstfort is having a hard time to secure possession of his wife, whom he married the day after Thanksgiving. Her maiden name was Olene Oveson. For several months she has been living with friends at Napavlne. She set the wedding day for Thanksgiving, but refused to go with him to Chehalis and be married on that day. Aust had previously secured the marriage license and the written consent of both her mother and stepfather. The day after Thanksgiving Aust went back accompanied by friends, who persuaded the girl to marry him. The ceremony was performed by the Rev. Monfort of the Presbyterian Church at Chehalis. Aust took his bride to the Hotel Relge at Chehalis, as she did not care to go on a wedding trip. The next day she returned to Napavlne, telling Aust she would secure her clothing and return. Up to today she has not returned. Several days ago she sent friends to Chehalis to obtain clothing and other things she had left there, but the hotel proprietor would not give them up. Last night Aust went to Napavlne, and served legal notice on John Curtice, in whose family the girl is living, directing him to stop the illegal detention of Aust's wife. As Aust and Constable Baker were driving away from Curtice's house, four shots were fired at them. .

FOURNIER ON THE AUTOMOBILE FACE. Say Successor to "Bicycle Face" Iff the Resnlt of Nervous j 7 Tension . The "automobile face" is the sue-sessor to the "bicycle back," the "bi-,cycle face" and the "board walk foot." Henil Fournler speaks as follows on this latest physical peculiarity: "The most careful chauffeur cannot avoid being shocked every time he " takes a spin. I do not think that any other sport known to man affords so much excitement One needs a stout heart and a strong nervous system as well as keen eyes to indulge in this most modern pastime, for I do not believe that navigating a flying machine brings a man into contact with more perils. . "The automobile face is no joke. It is the startling presentation in the human physiognomy of the record of thousands of dangers passed or, rather, close escapes from danger. I have never been in but one accident that was really serious, and in that case we were wrecked and bruised almost before my mind had time to form a picture of what threatened us. I refer to the time when my machine was run down by a locomotive on the Long Island (X. Y.) railroad. We wore caught like animals in a trap by reason of the lack of protection at a blind grade crossing. I had barely time to whirl the steering wheel in an effort to get oil the track when the engine was upon us and tossed us and the heavy machine -into the adjoining held like so much clmll. When a man begins to run an auto-1 bile, he is timid that is, assuming i mob that ho is a man of sound and normal mind. Only fools do not know tlie meaning of the word fear. But every ride the chauffeur takes adds to bis confidence in his machine and in himself.. When he becomes an expert, he is really as much a part of his machine as a good yachtsman is of his yacht or a cavalryman of his horse. He goes flying along the road, exhilarated with the sense of swift motion, feeling like a greyhound or a swallow in full flight. The idea that he may be hurt never oc curs to him any more than it does to the greyhound or to the swallow. "Only one fear haunts him that he may possibly .run down some other vehicle or run over a pedestrian. The "greatest source of danger lies in small boys at play, especially in suburban cities, where boys play at will about the streets with no thought of being run down. "No animal in the world is so reckless as a plas-ing boy. No other creature causes the nutomobilist so much horror. I have been running along an outlying road at the rate of twenty-five miles an hour with an absolutely clear track ahead of me and no indications of any one crossing the road for a mile or more in advance, and yet from some unknown place a boy or a group of boys would dart out, it seemed to me, right under my wheels. "I know of no other shock in auto-inobiling that is equal to this. One's lieart becomes constricted by fear until a ItsS few is or ' a l'OUliNIim S li.VCINU EXl'IiESSION. it feels no bigger than a marble. Every nerve in the body seems tied in a knot. The eyes protrude, and the chauffeur in hi3 mind contemplates the awful spectacle of the mangled and bleeding little body on the dusty roadside. The chauffeur's hand flies to cut off the power, to apply the brake, to swing tlie reverse lever. As if by a miracle the boy escapes. The rush of air with the machine perhaps blows off his hat. He has been within one-hftieth of a second of n horrible death. "This is tlie sort of experience that produces tlie automobile face, which the doctors are beginning to write learnedly about. Of course the con stant attention one has to pay while automobiling to the road, to the machine and nil its parts and to the distances which separate tlie machine from dangers of collision tends to produce the tension of tlie muscles about the eyes, the mouth and even the ears which, upon becoming fixed, produces the characteristic automobile face. The .petition for an inquisition as to the sanity of Joe Stipes -was not filed yesterday because Judge Hammer was busy with the trial of a law suit. Queen Bess' Bill of Fare. Dinner was a substantial affair in the reign of the maiden queen, who was by no means indifferent to the pleasures of the table. The first course on great occasions would probably be wheaten flummery, stewed broth, spinach broth, gruel or. hotch-potch. The second consisted of fish, among which we may .note lampreys, stockfish, and sturgeon, with side dishes of porpoise. The third course comprised quaking puddings, bag puddings, black puddings, white puddings, and marrow puddings. Then came veal, "-beef, capons, humble pie, mutton, marrow pasties, Scotch collops, wild fowl and game. In the fifth course all kinds of sweets, creams in all their varieties, custards, cheese cakes, jellies, warden pies, junkets, syllabubs, and so on, to be followed perhaps by white cheese and tansy cake. For the drinks ale and beer, wine sack, and numerous varieties of mead or metheglin, some of which were concocted out of as many as five and twenty herbs, and were redolent of sweet country perfume. She put them up in dainty boxes and placed them on sale in the Woman's exchange of the big city in which she lived. Today she makes sandwich making a business. She, has her private customers, and takes orders for teas, picnics, and other occasions, which demand the toothsome dainty she makes to such perfection. Ever since instantaneous photography demonstrated 'that the movements of animals are ready quite different from the impression which, they gave to the eye, the suggestion lies been made with more or less persistence that artists should change ilieir representations in confoiniity with the verities recorded by the camera. Kecently, ia a contemporary, writes the London Telegraph, the Earl of 2Jount Edgeumbe has proposed that a cinematograph should be mounted on a motor car and used in taking a scries of photographs of horses in motion, so as to show which positions are the least fleeting, ami therefore give the truest? The artist would then be enabled to sidect those attitudes most suitable to his purpose; but while achieving truth in a mechanical direction, would he not be forsaking it in another? To take a kindred case, we know that a revolving wheel is actually precisely the same as one at a standstill. Put no one would dream of suggesting that 1'i wheels of a moving vehic le should be depicted with every spoke distinct. J hit a drawing by a skillful urti.-.t would have conveyed the impression of rapid motion by rendered what his eye actually saw. Photographs attempting to represent motion seek refuge in making some part of the foreground of the picture out of focus. This demonstrates the canicrisl's appreciation of the failure of his instrument to do I'.istice to movement.

FOURTEEN PAGES. THE FUSION REFORM CAMPAIGN. The most striking thing- in the situation of city politics now Is th power of organization, cohesion, and co -operation that has grown up in the Fusion Party during the past "two years. For this credit Is due alike to the Republicans and to the Citizens Union. The Republican leaders have acted with sincerity and sagacity, and. despite some wayward gibes by Mr. Platt at various stages' of the negotiations, they have consistently pursued the larger Interests of the city and have refused to be misled by the spoilsmen among their followers. "When it became necessary to replace Messrs. Grout and Fornes on the ticket, they not only accepted but made and adhered to the proposition that two well-known Democrats should be selected. The Citizens' Union, In the same spirit, has met the larger requirements of the problems presented and has acted on the whole with extraordinary good sense and with a political efficiency that had not before been shown in the same degree. " -' " In other words, there has been a distinct gain for. the higher and more disinterested -politics in this city. It is proved that men . of energy, experience, and standing wlil devote their time and labor to the promotion of good government without the- incentives that have been held indispensable In ordinary political affairs. We do not assume that the Republican leaders have surrendered their party . aims entirely, but clearly they have learned that their party cannot persistently thwart reform in this city without incurring penalties which it cannot afford to have to pay. And . this lesson they have learned under a Mayor who, though Republican in National matters, has steadfastly refused to treat employment under the City Government as a reward for or inducement to party service. Exceptions there may hare been in some departments, but the rule has been general and has been faithfully enforced. For the first tims In the recent history of the city an administration seeks' re-election without depending on the Influence of place holders or place seekers. It is Its strongest claim to continued confidence. The selections by the Fuslonlsts of candidates for Controller and President of the Board of Aldermen axe admirable. "DIME NOVEL" FIENDS CONFESS' TO THEIR MURDER BARTBOLDO BALZANO. Charges of murder in the first degree have been preferred against Herman Heinberger, aged 17; William E. True-man, aged 19; William Draper, aged 16, and John Rousslet, aged 15, the four boys who have confessed to having been parties to the murder, of Bernardo Balzano, the grocery man, whose place of business was at Walden and Wood avenues. Detective Chief Taylor made the charge yesterday. This has proven to be one of the most heartless crimes ever perpetrated in the criminal annals of this country. A widow with three baby children is now destitute,, four families, those of the self-confessed murderers, are fairly crazed by grief, and an upright citizen, a thrifty merchant, has been cut off in the midst of the benefits derived from early industry and saving. - - They have all confessed to having pent the entire day of Friday planning the robbery. They have confessed to having carried either a revolver, a stiletto or a slungshot for the successful completion of the crime or the effecting of; their escape, as developments should require. Heinberger and Trueman were armed with 28 and 32-caliber revolvers, respectively; Draper was armed with the slungshot and Rouaslet with the atllleto. The boys have not yet been informed of the death of Balzano, a fact which makes their confessions all the more valuable. Trueman and Draper have stated that Heinberger; fired the shots, two In number. Rousslet was on watch outside the store and does not know which of his pals did the firing. Heinberger, in a braggadocio manner, has admitted having flred the shots, but claims that he did so in a state of excitement. The facts of the case as given by the first man to appear on the scene contradict the theory that the shooting was the result of a scuffle, and indirectly the same authority blames the police for this unfortunate occurrence. Dr. Edward Bodenbender. who was summoned Immediately to the house of Mr. Burrows, just opposite to Balsano's store in Wood -Avenue, where the murdered man fell In his efforts to secure assistance, spoke to a Courier reporter yesterday as follows: j NO SIGNS OF SCUFFLH. "There was not a sign that would lead to accidental shooting or even to the theory that Balzano was shot in a scuffle. The crime was downright murder, pure and simple, without any modification. The coat was not scorched. Had the shot been flred at close range from a 38-caliber revolver the coat would have been scorched. The hole through the garments into the body was a clean-cut one, indicating careful aim. I believe that when the murderer saw that Balzano would not submit to a robbery they shot him down in order to effect a sure escape. A small piece of clothing was carried by the bullet into the wound. The hole was as perfect as one made by a cookie-cutter in a platter of hardened dough. Had the shot been fired by one who was excited or In a scuffle the wound would not have- been so nicely made.N The shot would have been a slantlng-or a glancing one and it would certainly have torn the clothing- in a different manner and made a different impression in the flesh. These ruffians I believe to be members of the same gang that attempted to break Into my barn a week ago. The police "have been very negligent in this matter. LAXITY OF POLICE. "They have received complaints time and time again from residents of this district. They have ignored these complaints, even those made against these very ruffians who committed: this crime. It is not safe for a woman to go out here after dark. So bold are the members of the rough gangs out this way that they will insult, hold up and assault men, to say nothing of 'their conduct toward the other sex. These fellows have become a terror to -the community and the police have allowed them to flourish. It is hig-h time that our citizens in this district received protection and it is too bad that a peace-abiding merchant has to sacrifice his life to bring about a reform that could have easily been made long ago had the police done their duty. Even last night, the police apparently took their time In getting out here. Inspector Martin came along with the patrol wagon nearly three hours after the crime had been committed and had the murderers been) anything but foolhardy . boys, they would have made good their escape without leaving a clue behind them." TRUEMAN , THE "SQ.UIB AtEB." Trueman appears to have been the main "squealer." After .he .had told considerable, no difficulty was found in getting the others to talk. Detective Sergeants Holmlundj. and Burkhardt went to the pond on William Street, where the tys said they had thrown the revolver and they dragged up a 38-caliber weapon. The 32-caliber has not yet been found. Tb chambers of the revolver found were empty ive for the . discharged thells. But all this evidence cannot Incriminate the boys aa much' as their own confessions have done. ' TOUGH QUARTETTE. ' - They have admitted having spent an entire day plotting the crime, ? having gone , to the store : fully armed and equipped, having attempted the ; robbery, and having fired the shots. .The only modification attempted is the one given by Heinberger, and that Us that he "fired during the excitement.' All four of the boys are described by the police as "looking: the part." Heinberger is very profane and Trueman and he, the oldest members of the quartette. , talk as if their plots had been hampered by the youth of their younger accomplices. -'n, The families of the young desperadoes are all highly respectable and they are completely prostrated with grief, excepting in the case of Rousslet, whose parents have been kept in ignorance of their son's deed and consequently do not know where he is. All this has long since been lived down, and the Trappists of Loddis-v.ell are regarded with unfeigned respect and admiration throughout the whole arcadian district in which they live. A Living Death. The Order of La Trappe is one of the most rigorous in the Papal faith. Its"rnembers literally consign themselves to a living death so far as communication either' with the outer world or "with themselves is concerned. The solitary exception when they break the mournful silence is at tho morning greeting. "Memento morl!"-"Remember death!" They sleep in their own coffins upon straw. These cofl'ms are placed slantwise. A Trappist monk never knows the bliss of slumbering supine, unless he be ill. In the gray of the dawn they steal forth like shadows, for manual labor forms one of the great ethics of their creed. A long spell of inarticulate prayer heralds in thfr-'muto tasks of each day. ,A frugal breakfast is followed by one of the sternest of the daily obligations-each man digs one shovel tul of earth from out of his tutus c grave. And when the Trappist monk breathes his last he is laid to rest In the same robes in which he. passed his everyday life. Their habit consists of a dull white robe or cassock, a black scapulary (the cowl can be pulled up over the head), and a woolen girdle. Yet, watching the members of this devoted band at their toll, It Is impossible not to believe that they are happy in their intense self-denial. An indescribable air of peaceful serenity seems to rest upon the features of one and all. They believe that the most austere abnegation is the surest road to eternity, and they live up to their simple ideal earnestly, perseveringly but always silently. Most usefully do they fill their place, on earth, however, despite the almost incredible se.lf-ccmtainment of their lives. They not only support themselves by the honest sweat of their brow, but they give abundant alms to the poor who present themselves at the monastery gates. Surely an order to admire and respect by men of all creeds are these monks of La Trappe. The transformation they have effected in their Loddiswell estate is a source of marvel even to the sturdy Kingsbridge husbandman themselves. When they took over that demesne it was wild and neglected in tho extreme. The restoration of and additions to the buildings will not be quite completed until about July next. Meanwhile the gloomy old manor now looks like a typical monastery. Their I,n nds. But il Is mainly In the lands sur rounding their abode that .these ever- j silent, sombre-looking men have wrought such striking changes. No model farm can compare with the perfect order and high state of cultivation which mark every rood of those six hundred acres; and they have- reclaimed tracts which throughout living memory have been waste and barren. They possess the foreigners' secret of making such cheese from the yield of their sleek herds as no Devonshire press ever yet turned out; and the local farmers laughingly admit this as they vie with one another in their efforts to secure the savory produce. Tho monks are venturing upon the cultivation of vines in the open, and though the farmers shake their heads half sceptically, the Trappists may yet vindicate their faith in the mellow Devon climate by rearing grapes. They are a beneflclent community to the neighborhood, these Trappists, for the money they earn by their own ceaseless toil they spend almost entirely in the district. A strange conflict of widely diverse phases of life, this admixture of the rigorous self-imposed discipline of the monastery with the homely labor of plowing and tilling and digging. But the work of this community, which numbers near upon half a hundred members,' is not confined to tolling in the fields. There are various domestic offices grouped around the monastery, consisting of stables, stores, shops for carpenters, metalworkers, painters, and the like, in all of which you will see. those hcayily cloaked men following their avbca' tions. Almost all manufactured articles of food, together with domestic and agricultural implements, clothing, shoes, and many varieties of woodwork are produced upon the premises. The, verv carts in which the monks fetch and carry they make themselves. The Guest Master. It may very reasonably be asked how, since silence is one of the Inexorable rules of this most stringent order, they manage to come in touch at all with the outer world. For example, If a stranger call at the monastery gate to make, an inquiry or solicit charity, may not tho monk who responds to his pull of the deep-toned bell speak to him? He may. But he is the solitary exception to that stern rule of silence. The "guest master" Is the only member of the whole pious gathering who is free to use his tongue, save under the sheer stress of necessity, and so weighty is this habit of speechlessness that even he is as sparing of his words as courtesy will permit. For the Trappists are men of courteous manneirs, and brimful of the milk: of human charity. Great is the power of a faith that can breed up such a race of earnest and ardent disciples. Whatever may be one's secret thoughts as to the ethical virtues of such a profession, all right-minded men must admire the devoted manner in which this band of believers, who have renounced all the mundane joys of life, show the courage of their convictions, and lead lives that are noble alike in their sincerity and their utility. Thus, In this last place, the lawyer finds his compensation in the salutation of Cicero. in' the trial of Milo: "If to his country a man give all, he becomes entitlid to what all money cannot buythe eternal love of hie' fellow man." , 111 a Prophesies End of Lawyers - Finally I return to my prophecy that the lawyer is soon to be a thing of the past. I mean as a professionallcalling for hire. I pause to note what his present position is. The Lawyer is no longer ,the first cititen of the community because he is a lawyer. No longer la the profession of law the " open sesame " to polite society. Therefore; the modern age is rapidly discinsing that there is no necessity for the lawyer. 'newspapera and 'magazines, colleges and educational opportunities. What is the-use Cf. education if it shall not serve the purpose of eliminating obstructions and burdens which' have existed as the result of ignorance? 'EachMan His Own Advocate. As the lawyer was necessary as a middleman and advocate in order that the rights of the ignorant might be presented by one learned in what those rights should be, why shall it not be that, when the ignorant becomes learned of is own rights 'he should present those rights himself? He certainly understands them best and feels them keenest. Therefore, where is the reason, in the progress of enlightenment and learning, for the intermediate man, who possesses no more knowledge than the client. generally speaking. to be called in and paid a sum of money to do that of which the client is equally - as capable? Next, in these days when clients mutually, instead of being clients, can present between themselves as combatants their respective rights and reach a conclusion, the lawyer is unnecessary. TOO MANY TOYS Mrs. Cochran . Sounds Warning? to Mothers "The modern child has. entirely too many toys given him. This stunts his resourcefulness and self-dependence. Take away your child's tops and make him learn to amuse himself. Most of, the great men of the past we're without playthings as boys. Lincoln, lacking toys, would walk eight miles .after his day's work was done to borrow a book. Do you think this quality of sturdy self-reliance would ever have been developed, if as a child he had had a nursery full of costly tops to break and tire of at his own sweet will. It is the mother's duty to help her child by teaching him to help himself." Thus spoke Mrs. Joseph W. Cochran in her address on "Resourcefulness" before the Mothers' Club, at 1227 Arch street, yesterday . afternoon. . Continuing, Mrs. Cochran said: . "A child's character is forever shaped by the mother's influence and she cannot expend too much time and thought in bringing up her offspring. A child's mind is like a sponge, it soaks up everything, and on the mother devolves the development of those little potentialities, which will become good or bad traits when the child grows up. Exercise guidance, but don't let your child know he is being guided. And above ell things instill into the child a great ideal, "with faith to hold it and courage to seek it through his whole life. For a true ideal is the lodestar of our destiny, and the splendid glorifier of all our daily work.

FALSE CLAIMS FOR VACCINATION EXPOSED ITS FAILURES AND DANGERS ESTABLISHED Repeal of All Compulsory Vaccination Laws " Demanded ' flEPLV OF MR. HIGGINS TO DR. H1GOWS irther regret the entrance of a namesake in the field 6f controversy the opposite aide because the significance ot the name 'Wiggins' Belies characteristics of most of the Doctor's arguments in this case. In TO the Editor of The Item: 1.1 doubtless owe The Item and its readers an apology for the long delay in answering the interesting article of Dr. Higgins in your issue of last May the 4th, in which, by a compilation of extracts from several medical sources, he endeavored to establish the pre-eminent value of vaccination and tried to refute the facts that I had already brought against it My apology is that I left the city on a prolonged vacation soon - after this article appeared, and have but recently returned for permanent residence, and I hope that this delay in responding has led no one to suppose that the Doctor's article was in any sense unanswerable or unrefutable. In one way I regret to find a namesake taking up the defense of this barbarous medical practice, as it will doubtless lead to an embarassing confusion between us which may be mutually disagreeable, for the Doctoi will probably find himself being quoted, much to his horror, as an enemy of vaccination, while I will be charged, much to my disgust, with defending the barbarous practice. MEDICAL CREDULITY AND DOGMATISM. I fi on the explanation of this point,- let me say that most family names have, of course, a derivative meaning or signiticance, and a uttie verDai rummage in tne Celtic, Norse and Latin languages seems to show that the name "Higgins" really means "forethought." Now, if Dr. Higgins had been really true to , this significance of his name if he had only shown a little logical forethought . in the careful pre-examination of most of the arguments, made and authorities cited he would never have made them, because they are mostly so bad, antiquated and absurd that they refute themselves on their very face. But this seems to be an all too common fault with many medical men who, not taking the trouble to carefully study the subject of vaccination on both aides, are content to take the mere dogmatic assertions of so-called authorities on one side, which they adopt as gospel truth with the simple faith of religious fanatics, without ever going into any careful examination or reconsideration for themselves, as an unprejudiced, scientific or logical man would do, or even as a man of ordinary common sense should do. And I regret to say that it is this kind of self-sufficient medical dogmatism, shown by certain authorities which the Doctor cites, that is chiefly responsible for the hold which vaccination has had in the profession, particularly that most barbarous form of the practice, COMPULSORY VACCINATION, and for the faith still placed in it by the oppressed and suffering laity who have been so long deluded and enslaved by this dogmatism. Let us now take up some of the arguments and authorities used by Dr. Higgins, and we shall soon find, I think, how true arid clear my charge of dogmatism and falsity will prove to be to every man of common sense, whether lay or professional. , STATISTICAL TRICKS ON SMALLPOX MORTALITY, At the cutset I would like here to remind Dr. Higgins of the' remark of that logical wit who said that there were three grades of liars ordinary or common liars, "damned liars," and STATISTICAL LIARS, the last being of course the worst and most illogical and unscrupulous of all. Now a good example -of this worst kind of fabricator may be traced in one of the Doctor's most triumphant quotations, as follows: "IN THE TEN YEARS FROM 1885 TO 1895 THE PERCENTAGE OF DEATHS A&iONG THE UN VACCINATED AT THE BOSTON SMALLPOX HOSPITAL HAS BEEN 75, WHILE THAT OF THE VACCINATED HAD BEEN ONLY 3 PER CENT.'V, This is a good sample of the stuff,! ""whhrwhlch lnnocenrTseHlifie 'D'Higgiffii'ireooleKlorlt can" be readily shown to be incredible and absurd on its face by attempting to prove too much, and is answered as follows: Careful students of the subject, who have studied the history of smallpox, have determined that in the days before there was any vaccination whatever the fatality of smallpox cases was not more than from 15 to 20 per cent., or about one death in five or six cases. This is clearly shown by Dr. Creighton in the great article in the Encyclopedia Brittanica, and by Professor Alfred Russel Wallace in "The Wonderful Century," and by many others. In a little book in my library on the History of Smallpox, by Dr. James Moore, published in London in 1815, the fatality of smallpox at that date and before vaccination was introduced is clearly stated on page 302, as being at this same ratio, viz., "about one in six." Now Dr. Moore ought to know something of the fatality of smallpox in . unvaccinated subjects at that time, and his word ought to be acceptable to us at this day and especially to advocates of vaccination because he belonged to the Royal College of Surgeons in London and was a Director in the National Vaccine Establishment, just then formed to introduce Jenner's scheme; and, furthermore, his book was dedicated to Jenner himself and was written partly as an apology for some of the failures of Jenner's doctrine which were even then becoming manifest. Yet even this great friend of Jenner and of vaccination could not credit a greater fatality to unvaccinated smallpox cases than one in five or six. SMALLPOX MORTALITY NOT REDUCED BY VACCINATIONA BOOMERANG ARGUMENT DISSECTED. Now what Dr. Higgins wants us to believe is that since the introduction of vaccination the fatality of smallpox has increased from twenty per cent to SEVENTY-EIGHT PER CENT., and he wants us to accept that fe a proof of the value of vaccination! Now, is not this a rich absurdity on its face, for, even if we accept it as true, is it not a flaming two-edged sword turned against vaccination itself? For if there were only twenty pet cent, fatality before any vaccination was used, and when the arts of ' medicine and nursing were comparatively crude, and sanitation nil, how can it be a good argument for vaccination to try to show that this fatality rose to 78 per cent, after vaccination was introduced, and when medicine, sanitation and nursing were greatly improved? Is not this argument, indeed, a terrible indictment and boomerang against all modern medicine, and against vaccination and the Boston hospitals in particular? V This argument of course kills itself, and it is therefore a dogmatic statis tical humbug and falsehood on its face, for a careful study of unprejudiced ' statistics of the last two centuries shows that there has been practically no - change in the average fatality of smallpox in all this time, being substantially the same in vaccinated and unvaccinated times, viz,, about one in five or six, no matter what special pleaders may try to show in special cases which , are evidently tainted with inaccuracy. Thus, in our own times, with hundreds of thousands of vaccinations, the fatality in the last great epidemic of smallpox in 1901-2 shows almost identically the same ratio as Dr. Moore pointed out in 1815 when there was little or no vaccination. The Health . Reports of New York City for 1901 show that the smallpox cases were 1964 and the deaths 410, which is about one in five. In the report of the Surgeon-General of the U. S. Army for 1899 it is shown, on page 244, that there were 236 cases of smallpox with 77 deaths among our soldiers in the Philippines, which is a mortality of over 33 per cent.) Now, perhaps there is no class of our population which is better provided with the alleged protection of vaccination and re-vaccination than our army. The facts of the centuries therefore clearly refute the fallacious claim constantly made that the introduction of vaccination has in any way materially reduced the mortality of smallpox as it has, if anything, rather increased it; and yet the very funny thing about the Doctor's argument from the Boston Hospital is that even if we accepted his point it would clearly prove that smallpox fatality HAS INCREASED TERRIBLY SINCE VACCINATION WAS INTRODUCED! Now, Dr. Higgins can take whichever horn of this dilemma he pleases and pull himself out of his illogical and statistical bog, if he can. , HOW THE STATISTICAL TRICK IS WORKED. It is, of course,, very easy to show how the statistical juggler works this ' aforesaid trick in favor of vaccination, and it has been clearlv shown by Wallace and others. It is done by putting ALL DOUBTFUL CASES,, those not having clearly defined marks, unbluBhingly, in the column of the "UNVACCINATED" and this class is ALWAYS VERY LARGE and to - this is also added the little infants under one or two years of age who are generally unvaccinated but who . would die in almost any case, whether vaccinated or not Smallpox is very fatal in young infants and this element of cases and deaths is always very high in every great smallpox epidemic. For example, in the epidemic in New York City in 1901, with 410 deaths, ' . 197 were under five years of age. When, therefore, your hear any doctor prating about the high death rate among the "unvaccinated" in hospitals as a proof of the value of vaccination, ask him to tell you how many little babies he put in the column of the unvaccinated and you will there find "the nigger ' in the fence." .. ; . . . - . " VACCINATION DEATHS CONCEALED. There is another point worthy of notice, which the Doctor has made, and which is not very serious, but is only amusing and shows he is truly a confiding and honest-minded man, to wit: "IN GREATER NEW vYORK, "UNDER DR. LEDERLE, OVER 810,000 PERSONS WERE VAC-"CINATED-BY THE BOARD OF HEALTH AND NO DEATHS FROM "VACCINATION ARE REPORTED UP TO THIS DATE, A PERIOD "OF OVER THREE YEARS." Of course, you dear, confiding man, no .deaths were "REPORTED" as occurring from any, vaccinations I That is one of the very things I object to, as deaths from vaccination are constantly being concealed and its dangers and fatal effects constantly minimized by. . the profession. With the present attachment of the profession to this dangerous and repulsive operation we will find no deaths reported as occurring from vaccination until we have a rigid law on the subject, as they have in ' England, where the records show a great many deaths from vaccination all through the years- (see Encyclopedia Brittanica), At present, among us, the last thing we need look for is the acknowledgment on the records from any vaccinator that his operation was the direct or indirect cause of his . patient's death, whether child or' adult He 'will not bring reproach or responsibility on himself or his beastly operation by putting down as the cause of death "vaccination" when he can so easily and. safely, and with - little or no qualm of conscience put it down under one of a score of headings, and more than half truthfully, too, such as "lockjaw," "gangrene," : "pyamcia," "plegmon," "erysipelas," "meningitis," "diseases of skin and . adnexa," and last, but not least, "ill-defined causes," under which headings we will find THOUSANDS OF DEATHS recorded every year. The Doctor . ,.; should really have caught on to this little conscientious trick or loophole in our "vital statistics" long before this. VACCINATION DISASTERS PROVED. I could, of course, fill a page of The Item with serious injuries and deaths occurring from vaccination, but I forbear as I cannot believe the Doctor is really so simple after all as to think that they do not frequently occur. .. I shall be content, however, to cite here the notorious case of the hospital nurse, Miss Buckley, killed by vaccination after terrible suffering, as re- " ported in the Eagle of June 20, 1906. See also the case of lockjaw following vaccination in a child, reported in the Evening World of September 29, 1906. This is, of course, a very common occurrence, although the Doctor seems never to have heard of it. In the New York Sun of November 16, 1901, there was reported a smallpox and vaccination panic occurring in Camden, N. J., with -these results: 14 cases of smallpox, one death only, from smallpox, and five deaths from lockjaw following vaccination! For an official record which the doctor can readily consult I will also here refer him to the Report Of the Surgeon-General of the U. S. Army, for 1900, where from page 204 to ' 209, he will find a whole chapter of deaths and serious injuries caused among our soldiers by vaccination. VACCINATION FAITH AND IGNORANCE DEMONSTRATED DANGERS IN VACCINATION. ' Now it is indeed sad that the Doctor should be so unacquainted with the subject of vaccination, and this doubtless accounts for his great faith in it, and the pitiable way that he has allowed himself to be fooled by some of the dogmatic humbugs of this barbarous cult. For example, here again is a monumental instance of his innocence and of the humbug which he ac- ' cepts as gospel truth. He-gravely quotes this "GEM" from "Brome," whoever he may be: "DISEASE IS NOT POSSIBLE FROM THE INOCULATION OF ANIMAL LYMPH." Now, any man who in the light of our ' present knowledge of vaccination could make that statement gravely, can only be classed among the "DONKEYS," and any man who accepts it seriously can only be placed among the "LAMBS." And it is nothing less than a professional scandal that doctors should allow themselves to be fooled with such ignorant antiquated and dangerous dogmatism when they could readily acquaint themselves with current medical literature which wpuld tell them a very different story; and the story it would tell them is this: That the various makes of vaccine virus, as found in the market for several years, have been demonstrated by government officials and experts of the regular medical school to be in fact not merely a culture of microbes of cow-smallpox known as "Vaccinia," but in addition are likely to contain a whole series of other germs which can and often do convey the most dangerous and deadly diseases imaginable, such as lockjaw, sepsis or blood-poisoning, tuberculosis, grave skin diseases, foot and mouth disease of cattle, also "lumpy-jaw" or actinomycosis which may also cause meningitis or its equivaent. For proof of this I refer him to: First Bulletin No. 12, 1903, Marine Hospital service, Washington, "Bacteriological Impurities in Vaccine Virus," by M. J. Rosenau. .Second Report to Department of Agriculture, Bureau Of Animal Indus- ' try, on Foot and Mouth Disease found in vaccine virus. This virus could infect children inoculated by it with an ulcerated mouth and throat which was very dangerous and could be confounded with diphtheria. This report is filed, but has not yet been printed, probably because it would hurt vaccination too much. THE TEDDY BEAR CRAZE. German and American Factories Cant Make Them Fa6t Enough. More than 20,000 nimble fingers were busy all year in Germany trying to make enough Teddy bears for the children of the United States. Several manufacturers in this country tried to help out. College girls and society women have taken up the fad, says The Boston Herald, and there is no telling where the craze will stop. The bearish tone of State street or Wall street is nothing to the bearish domination of the toy maiket. Toy dealers themselves can't explain the Teddy bear craze. But the bear is now in his second year and his hibernation has improved him. The craze seems to have started at Atlantic City. A child there, says one chronicle, saw a lovable looking little fuzzy brown plush bear in a shop window one day and had his mother buy it for him. It was a bear made by an old lady in Germany. Other 1 children saw the child with the bear, and copied. Visitors to Atlantic City took home with them the bear fad, and the bear craze was in the saddle. The German woman who had sent the bears over years ago, and had since then been making comparatively few, just enough to satisfy the small demand, wondered why the American toy dealers suddenly sent such large orders for the bears Teddy bears, as Americans began to call them immediately. The average German toy maker supplies orders as they come in, not eating to keep on hand a large stock of goods with only ephemeral popularity, so the German lady was hard put to It. This fall she had more than 2,000 girls at work on the Teddy bear, and the calls for animals were still insistent. As many of the ideas of the German toy makers came from France, and those in the United States from Germany, the American maunfacturer promptly fell in line for the bear trade. Hundreds of bears are being made every day in the United States, and the issues of the trade journals of toyland carry many advertisements of Teddy bears. Some time ago a man made visit after visit to one of the large department stores to get a Teddy bear for his child. He was finally told that there would be hundreds of them on hand a certain morning, as a cargo of them was about due. He reached the store about 9 o'clock of the morning named and found that he was barely in time to get one of the few remaining' Teddies. It cost him $8.50. The Teddy bears came in all sizes There are little cubs which retail as low as $2, if there is a little one in stock. There are big ones, five feet' high. It has been hard to get a fair sized Teddy for less than $2.50 or $3. It was hard to get them months ago when the wholesalers sold the present Christmas wares to the stores, and some of the big wholesalers them selves couldn't get the Teddies in time for the Christmas trade.

"Roosevelt hoist with his own petard: 'Teddy bear' responsible for race suicide,'' wrote a St. Joseph reporter when he went to the newspaper office, after listening to Rev. Michael G. Esper's sermon In St. Joseph's Roman Catholic church. For Father Esper declared that the "Teddy bear" was a national peril, threatening to result In race suicide to an unprecedented degree, in spite of all that the bear's distinguished namesake could do to make big families popular. Father Esper didn't call the president by name, or even hint reproachfully at him. But he did say that the "Teddy bear" was destroying all Instincts of motherhood in countless little girls, and in the future would be recognized as one of the most powerful factors In the race suicide danger. IXjIIs, the priest said, were a good thing and helped to implant iu little girls the Instincts which some day would make them long for children of their own. But the "Teddy bear" ! "Discard it. forever," the priest urged his congregation at the close of 15 minutes' earnest talk. Father Esper spolte seriously and strove to impress upon his hearers that, he meant what he said, and saw a real danger In the toys. "There is something natural," said Father Esper, "in the care of a doll by a little girl It is the first manifestation of the feeling of motherhood. In the development of those motherly Instincts Is the hope of nil nations. "It is a monstrous crime to do anything that will tend to destroy thes-i Instincts. That is what the 'Teddy bear' is doing, and that is why It Is going to be a factor in the race suicido problem if the custom is not suppressed. It is terrible enough that the present generation of parents in this country is leading us into grave danger by the practice of race suicide. If we cannot, awaken the present generation let us at least save the future ones."

MACON, Me-, April 18.--The placid life of a farmer wu sufficient for Frank Schollaert, who has become well off, until in an evil hoar a traveling man came along and sold him a phonograph with a number of records. When he brought his purchase home, and turned the records loose on his neighbors, his mother-in-law and his wife and six children, he found they were all the tenderest of love ballads, some of them so tender that they were almost mushy.
