Don't Read In Bed Peading in bed at 'night is, speaki .ni^ generally at all events, an unhealthy practice, and there is fortunately a tolerably nniversal consensns • of opinion among the public that the habit is better avoided. Probably the fear of its being the cause of a conflagration of the bed curtains and perhaps of the whole honse has had something to do with the feeling against it in the past. The chief danger is to the eyes, partly because the light used is frequently insufficient and so placed as to dazzle them, and partly because it is difficult to hold the book so that full benefit is obtained from the use of both eyes. This is more particularly the case when the reader is lying on one side. Again, there is generally a temptation to hold the book too close,to the eyes and this of itself tends to induce myopia. Especially is this result to be feared in the case of young persons whose eyes are not fiilly developed. For this reason boys and girls under 18 should be strictly forbidden to read in bei3. Of course, persons suffering from errors of refraction—myopia, hypermet- roDia, astigmatism and so on—are liable to increase the trouble. By DR. FEILCHENFELO, Botlon.

Mr. Cove demonstrates the success of bis invention by lighting his workshop at No. ,486 Somerville avenue, Somerville, with electricity generated from a simple apparatus on the. roof. ; , Ar a , - No electric wires enter his buildings, from outside lighting sources, yet the incandescent globes twinkle merrily day and night, and electricians from the Institute of Technology, who have watched with interest his experiments, have declared themselves enthusiastic over his success. . Cove's invention is designed to generate electricity directly from the rays of the sun and storing it for lighting and for small power plants. O sweeping statements about boys made in universal terms are true. There are some boys of whom some things are true, and there are other boys of whom very different things are true. Young boys do not play too much any more than they eat too much. They do both sometimes. But they are made to play as much as to eat. By both they live and grow City conditions restrict and hamper free play, and most young city boys get too little chance to run and climb and dig and Jump and throw things. Public playgrounds will help much, but after all they cannot restore the lost freedom of the country. With older boys under modern conditions the case Is different. A few play too much. Most spend too much time in watching others play and In reading and talking and dreaming about play. in older boys a certain amount of time spent In play Is useful, probably necessary, but time spent on play Is mostly wasted. No good comes of It either to body or mind. The amount of time so spent by boys and young men Is enormous. Public athletic grounds occupied day after day by professionals playing for a living and crowded with boys pay ing for admission to see the game are a public nuisance. They have taken most of the old-time zest out of play. No high school team of any sort would be willing to go off by itself and play for the sake of playing. They want to be surrounded by a crowd of cheering spectators, especially girls, and to have their pictures taken and their names in the papers. They work at play to earn applause. Most modern boys do too little real work. A few are fortunate enough to be obliged to work, some to help their families, some to earn thetr education. It has become fashionable to pity such boys. They are subjects for congratulation. There was a time when so many boys worked so much and played so little j and -play has become a business proposition. Whether business competition is right or wrong, it appears to be necessary under present conditions, but there is no excuse for carrying the competition and fierceness of business into the field of play. The modern boy, then, does not play too much; he does not play right he does not really play. He works when he plays, and in a treadmill often more injurious than that of business. Judging the modern boy by what I see of him in our high and Latin schools, I would say that I think he has less of good fellowship and pf social Intercourse than is obtained by the average successful man In business who dines daily at his club and who plays a restful social gamoaonce a day. Competition may be the life of modern trade, because modern trade is yet uncivilized, but competition is the death of modern play. THE ABUSE OF PLAY Albert E. Winship. The reat dominant instinct of young life is activity, and shows itself spontaneously In play. The play our children is the reproduction of the work of distant ancestors. Work one stage in man's evolution becomes play at a later period. At the dawn of adolescence the boy has a desire build a hut in the back yard or in the woous. This is play for the boy, but it was severe work for his savage ancestor. Nearly every boy has the wanderlust spirit to some extent. This can be naturally satisfied by cross-country runs or picnics. It is wise to provide as great a variety of play as possible swimming, running, games, group games, excursions to satisfy the boy's natural instincts. If the natural play instincts are checked, as they too often are by narrow streets and large districts without playgrounds, the ac- tlvity Is turned into mischief. Jon-son's a T DOES NOT PLAY RIGHT N. C. Fowler Jr. HE modern boy does not play too much; he plays too hard. Whe.i he isn't worii-ing or studying, he is sleep ing, loafing, or doing something which is suppo-3id to contribute wholly or largely to the pleasure side of bis life. Loafing isn't resting Mid is not a part of play or diversion. The average boy, whether at college, school or at work, makes a business of diversion and a hardship of play. Most, modern play as practiced goes beyond the line of sensible strenuosity and enters the field of fair or unfair competition. Practically all gam-.;s played, from questionable football 'o running races, are entered into prlnci pally for competition. The game is really not played for sport or for good fellowship, but that one may win. This sort of playing, then, becomes business neither diversion nor recreation. While competition and rivalry have their places, there can be no real play, no true diversion, no restful recreation where the element of competition is of more than secondary importance, nor where there is a test if physical endur ance beyond the normal. The social game of ball, for example, tends toward good fellowship, and is a healthful exercise; but make it merely a competitive contest and the participants in it have no diversion, rest or pleasure except the exhilaration experienced by the winning nine. But the side which wins today loses tomorrow One-half the players leave the Held in a more or less depressed state, for they have been defeated. Of course, in all games one side must win, but the game as played is a business affair for it is for comeetitive gain, and the good of the play part is lost. All play should be for pleasure, and it cannot be for pleasure when one-half the players leave the field sore over defeat, nor can it contribute to health or pleasure when either the physical or mental side Is strained close to the breaking point. Although I deplore the tendency o loaf, and condemn the street-corner lounger, I cannot help feeling that per haps the average boy would be as well off If he hung around the street, mingling with fellow loafers as he is likely to be on the field of strenuous com petition. The better part of play, aside from the physical exhilaration It gives. Is In the social side of it the good fellowship it engenders. Remove this good fellowship,, take away the social aide. i revolution when a rich man. whose son's amusement is a national scandal, tells me thut his chief ambition is to teach the sons of the poor to work 'Theatres and actresses for my son, but a bench and tools for yours,'' does not tend to America's peace of mind. There will ncv;er be less play with Americans, young or old. We have reduced the hours of work 20 percent, I evenings are being given over to diver sion, the "week end" has a day and a half for exhausting play, and our holidays have been doubled. So long as the chief function of adults Is to find i more time for play, there Is no prob ability that the youth will accept less. Whether youth play too mucMs not h practical question, since there Is no way to reduce the quantity. The problem relates to quality. The churches scold, the schools nag, reformers whine, but nothing is done except through the recent evolution of the playground movement, and this is for the poor man's children and not for the rich. Most of us play by proxy. Thirty thousand of us at a time shout wildly when one man in 18 makes a home run or one in 22 makes a touchdown. Millions enjoy suggestive displays before footlights, other millions unable to pay for the real thing, go to a nickel moving picture show and the still less fortunate take their pictures in a penny-in-the-slot machine. Those who do actually play take the fad of the day from flinch to bridge, from ping-pong to golf. What the world needs is healthy leadership in play. We need to have our boys and girls know what to play and how. The rich need this leadership even more than the poor. It is a scandal that the rich man's college toy bets on the play the poor man's boy makes. The danger signals should be put up to warn youth, by precept and ex ample, to avoid everything Immorally suggestive, whether it be on the stage, In the ball room, In moving pictures, or in the vaudeville parks. Warning is needed against all games of chance for gain, from craps and the slot machine to the gaming table, aird, against all betting, from ball games t& race tracks. There Is exhilaration In a game of chance. If there be no gain In the winning, if we can enjoy playing the hand we have for all there is to it. It is true sport, but the minute we are ready to profit by our luck, whether womerr play for a china vase or men for a pot of gold, it is vice. On the positive side let us all play, not too much but well. Let .us have time for recreation, for diversion, for developing skill, for learning to play square. Let us learn to be good losers. The playground movement as a boon to the children f of the common people is scarcely less than the common school itself. Now let somebody find a way to teach the children of the rich how to play right, to be square, to be corr-tent with real life in its sweetness and purity. Is it not as important that teachers and preachers, reformers and legislators seek to ennoble play as to And ways and means to make the poor man's son vvork? When we play right we shall work right. Play Is not worthy the name that does not give a relish for work. Play must never give a distaste for life, must never exhaust physically. Intellectually or socially, must never be an end in itself. One should play that he may work, and not work that he may play. Flay must be spontaneous, of the child's initiative and must have the halo of the imagination. To answer this question intelligently let us consider whom we mean by the "youth." Does the modern country youth play too much? Certainly not. The farm, village and even town communities of our land have hardly been leached by the newer play and playground ideas. Careless Reading and Thinking BY DR. C. H. PARKHURST TXT HAT effect is produced f Wupon people by the perusal of the usual contents of an American newspaper? Whatever may be here urged upon the topic Just nw in hand will not be designed as criticism upon the press. The press has selected for Itself its own line of work, and so far as it pursues that line in a clean and honest fashion we need allege nothing against it. It satisfies itself with noting and commenting upon what is transpiring to-day and in that way meets a legitimate and popular desire to know what the latest thing is that has happened and what its happening denotes. I The events so recorded may be of no possible interest or concern twenty-four hours hence, but they are Interesting at the moment and are what the great majority of people would like to know, and if the record of them is supplemented by some editorial comment pat to the occasion, that also will be relished if served up In a style that Is pleasantly flavored and easily digested. It is in the nature of people to-day. as it was with the Athenians in Paul's time, to want to hear and to tell some new thing. It is true that the apostle was not able to do much with his Athenian auditors, and they certainly heard more with their ears than with their understanding. Still if there had not been in them a touch of curiosity that makes even the most rational of men. Instinctively put his hand to his pocket when he hears the newsboys cry "Extra!" they would not have received from his preaching on Mars hill even the little that they did. But, granting the legitimacy of newspaper writing, the question still remains as to its effect upon the intelligence of newspaper readers. Lord Morley In the course of his address upon literature said: "It has been claimed by critics of democracy that the newer type of Journalism weakens the faculty of coherent attention, and I am bound to say that when I see a gentleman coming up of a morning in the suburban trains with a financial paper under one arm, a sporting paper under the other, a general paper written what is called 'crisply' If he is of an aesthetic turn of mind he has also an Illustrated paper and when 1 am told that this gentleman Is having his character shaped and his opinions molded and his views settled by this process, 1 confess I am very skeptical." That Is a strong way of putting a pretty serious truth. A man of whom It has to be said that he is "addicted" to newspapers is bound to be Intellectually an inebriate. It is nothing against the newspapers to say that whoever makes them steadily bis diet is on the certain track to mental indieestlon. And all of that ; - j quite apart from the' question as to whether the papers contain anything that is 'intrinsically contaminating. Bven though there be no poison in a man's bread, he will physically degenerate under a diet of innutrltlous bread. At our dinner table we indulge ourselves in certain dishes which, however innu-trlent, are palatable, ' and which, without being harmful, are at the same time gas-trically interesting; but to limit ourselves to such courses, and to omit the less piquant but more nourishing dishes, means dyspepsia. There is an analogous intellectual danger experienced by one who confines himself to the toothsome superficialities of very much of the contents of American newspapers. We need not object to their tooth-someness. We need not find fault with their containing matter that does not make brain and that is not brain stimulant. To no considerable extent is that the service they profess to render. They are "news" papers. , They claim to be that, and they are that, and we want them for that, with, however, as large a commixture of matter that is of more than evanescent value as they may find it possible to incorporate. Any process of intellectual "skimming," if habitually adhered to, is debilitating. It weakens the power of concentration and disintegrates the logical and sustained continuity of thought. In the existing condition of things "newsy" columnB will be read carelessly, and careless reading makes careless thinking. Things are quite different from what they were In the old days, when we, some of us, saw but one four-paged newspaper a week and read it thoroughly from the top of the first page to the bottom of the last, skipping neither news, editorials, advertisements, marriages nor deaths there were few murders then and no divorces. if the circumstances of the times and the present function of Journalism preclude that kind of fixed and consecutive perusal, then resort, for purposes of nn-ntal discipline and intellectual pabulum, must be had to literature, written matter carefully thought out, studiously composed, occupied with the permanent interests of all times, as contrasted with the evanescent concerns of this morning or this evening. All of this, however, while yielding unqualified tribute to the enterprise and genius, unequal.! In any other part of newppaperdom. wherebv, through the ministration of the American press, we are put in instant touch with whatever is of less or greater moment all the way from New York, t'hlcaao, tU. Louis, San Francisco to HonEkong and hourly admitted to the soi-iety of whomsoever we will, a wlt-neoa to his activities, a sympathizer with bis efforts and interests.

THE TELEPHONE FOOL. Has Cost Many a Good Fellow His - Position. Don't you do it, Gertrude, or Estella, or Gladys, or Irene, or Imogen, or what-ever your name is. Don't you do it. Don't run to the telephone every ten minutes and call up Elbert, or Harold, or Earle, or Aubrey, or whatever his name is. Don't you do it. You stick to your knitting and let the little fair-haired fellow you are expecting to make a pie-piece of for the remainder of your life call you up in case he wants to. But don't you go and call him up. If you do, you may lose your pie-piece, and Harold, or Eugene, or whatever his name is, may lose his job. I'll tell you why, if you'll promise never to mention it: When Eugene has a frantic desire to pay for your shirtwaists and thing for the remainder of your days, he wants most of his conversations with you when he is within reaching distance. Do you see the point? And when he is not within reaching distance he wants to exercise his faculties in getting enough money together to buy furniture for a four-room flat on the uneasy payment plan. There you are.! Perhaps I never should have thought of putting all this Solomon into print if I hadn't come across Joshua Dodd on the street car the other day. When I first knew Joshua Dodd he was struggling to acquire enough money, all at one time, to buy a marriage license, a frame to put the preacher's certificate in and two both-way tickets to Howard City. He had relatives at Howard City, so he thought that would be a fine place to spend his honeymoon. This in spite of the well-known fact that Jimmie Has-kins WTites up all honeymoon trips remorselessly in his newspaper. Joshua was saving up money for all these things when he came to work at Perkins' shoe store, where Itwas employed just for the novelty of finding out how long it would take me to learn the difference between a pair of patent-leather pumps and a bunch of shoestrings. Joshua was a good clerk. He could sell goods with the best of them. He was honest, too, and people discovered it, so he had a little personal patronage of his own. When Joshua came in one Monday morning and went to work I wondered why he had left the good job up at the Blake department store, where he was next to the head of the shoe department. I soon found out about that. Joshua wras on the silk carpet up in front selling shoes to a pretty blonde from the high-up precinct of the Fourth Ward when the telephone rang. The book-keeper lifted the receiver and called out: . "Mr. Joshua Dodd!" I thought that Joshua looked as if he had been shot in the ribs with a load of bird shot not fatally injured, but annoyed considerably. He went to the telephone, after asking permission of his customer, and something like this followed : "Never t(ta busy when you " Then he listened a moment. "Why, of course. Glad you called me up A long silence followed. "The blue suit? Why, anything looks well on " The other clerks began to snicker. early. If anything goes "Oh, yes, wrong call The customer waited a long time. She smiled. She would have been a dunce not to know that it was a love-talk going on over the telephone. I have no doubt she imagined the little bees out on the wire gathering the honey that was slipping out of the transmitter at the other end. The boss began to get nervous and Joshua saw it. So he rang off and went back to the blonde girl from the Fourth Ward. From that time on Joshua was haunted by that telephone. He looked at it with terror in his eyes morning, noon and night. He was afraid of it. As a usual thing Joshua Dodd was called to the telephone at 9 o'clock every morning. He used to stand right there so he would be sure to get the call. Then he would be called at irregular intervals all day. You never knew when Joshua's lovey-dovey was going to nestle down to the telephone for a good long chat with him. I guess Joshua was afraid he'd lose Clellie. He never said a word back to her when she called him three times an hour. I reckon she thought he was paid a salary for standing at the telephone listening to her voice. Joshua was a profitable man to have about the store, and so the boss put up with a lot of foolishness from him. Some of our business friends used to address the store like this: "If Joshua Dodd is not using the phone I'd like to talk with the manager." If Clellie hadn't had Joshua snared proper she would have lost him right there. However, the boss felt sorry for him and let it go on. He knew that Joshua trembled at the sound of his name, yet hadn't the nerve to tell Clellie to cut it out or go and snare another pie-piece. The telephone has knocked many a wTedding because silly girls could not refrain from calling up Charley and telling him all about nothing in seventeen thousand words. Many a lover has become so exasperated at being haunted by the telephone that ho has left both his job and his lady-love. Also, many a promising business deal has been spoiled by the too frequent use of the telephone. It is easy to take down the receiver and talk a lot of half-digested ideas into the transmitter. Now, it is not half-digested ideas that go in business. When a man talks business he must pick his words and say them forcefully and stand by them. That is business. The telephone fool does not seem to know this. It is exasperating to have any one call on the telephone just for the sake of a little chin-chin. It may be your sweetheart, your wife, your chum, your business associate. Never mind. If it is not business it has no place in the office during business hours. Many a good deal, many an advantageous business chance, many a friendship, has been lost because of the telephone fool. There is the telephone nuisance who talks a lot of nonsense with business, but he can be endured. He only delays business, does not block it. When a young man has to answer a lot of lovey questions before a roomful of associates, it makes him mad, and the girl is prying herself away from her meal ticket. NATURAL ICE IS FREE OF GERMS The first warm days of spring always bring hurried demands from householders for that great necessity of town and city life, ice. The local ice men are prepared to supply all orders. As to the quality, as that is particularly interesting to the heads of households where ice is used f ree- ly In drinking water it is a satisfac-I tion to the dealers in natural ice to be able to assure the public on the very highest authorities in public health and scientific circles in this country that there is no danger possible from the use of their ice for all domestic purposes. For instance, in a recent address. Dr. H. W. Hill of ths Minnesota state board of health said that after investigating thousands of epidemics of typhoid fever and dysentery, he had entirely, eliminated natural Ice as a source of disease, for he had never found a single case traceable to the use of natural ice as a factor In causing disease and devotes his time to othy possible causes. And Dr. W. T. Sedwick of the Massachusetts Institute of technology, at Boston. America's leading sanitarian, in a lecture last fall declared he had long used natural ice In drinking water for his own family, being convinced it could not cause any disease, but that on the contrary iced water as a drink in Ms opinion is a gentle and effective stimulant of high value in combating the physical exhaustlan occasioned by torrid weather. He also said of natural ice that "taken by and large It is one of the purest food materials of our time." These opinions are backed by the results of recent investigations of the effect of freezing on bacteria which may be present in water. Dr. E. O. Jordan, professor of bacteriology in Chicago university, in summing up the question, says: "The great majority of typhoid bacilli per- ish within a short time. AH Investi gators are now agreed that three weeks after freezing less than 1 per cent and probably less than one-half of one per cent, remain alive." None of the natural ice offered the public now has been stored for less than four and most of It has been stored for six to eight weeks, when accord ing to Dr. Eugene H. Porter, health commissioner of New York state, the last bacteria is dead and the ice practically sterile. The conclusions of these eminent men that natural ice is not a possible source of danger to public health is of vital Interest to the people in this community where owing to our long warm summers with many intensely hot spells, the fear of using natural ice freely in water, tea and other Iced drinks, would cause needless discomfort, if not ac- tual suffering to thousands of people.

Too Much Reading as Bad as None By Charles P. Donoghue, Denver. Colo. I do not decry the reading of fiction. An old instructor of mine used to say that during the winter months everyone should read solid books for the most part and do light reading in the warm weather. His theory was that too much solid reading during the entire1 year tended to make one mentally stodgy. . The point I wish to make, however, is that mental intoxication, consequent upon too great indulgence in the printed page, is as bad as physical intoxication. If we read too much fiction our taste is apt to become vitiated. . . The summer is the time for fiction, but it is 'also the time for the country, for athletic' exercise, for botanizing, for getting acquainted with -that wonderful nature which is all about us. It was Lord Bacon who said "reading maketh the full man," but he failed to tell his public that too much reading of a certain sort might make the reader "too full."

BARACH. The following are extracts from n address on "What Constitutes Physical Fitness'" delivered under ' the auspices of the Allegheny County Medical Society before the members of the 8ection on HyRlene of the Pittsburgh Academy of Science ana Art: mHB question of the evening, "What Constitutes Physical Fitness," is- a direct question, but one which can be answered indirectly only. Physical fitness does not even mean perfectly normal health. In a large series of physical examinations for life Insurance, etc., carried on by an institute in New York, It was found that only 3.6 per cent of the applicants who it may be said were representative of the great mass of American people only 3.6 per cent were in such a state of health that they needed, no advice nor medical attention. I call attention to this to show you how rare a thing is perfect hearth and that the world's work is now being done by persons far from the perfect health line and that the perfect man is as yet an ideal rather than a reality. Let us focus our attention upon man of the twentieth century and see with what kind of a body he has be come fit to accomplish all that he has to do, what it is that ia necessary for his existence, his physical welfare and his survival. Thus, indirectly, we shall answer the) question: ""What is physical fitness." Bar to Progress. The- laziness of the present day is our crowning sin, how we do love to ride rather than walk, and how we do prefer the thick well-upholstered cushions of the street cars or automobile to the jolting buckboards of our fathers and grandfathers. Luxury and physical self-indulgence means the toboggan, for you, while work and effort means physical fitness and the pennant at the end of the race. I could write a wonderful chapter on "The Modern Laziness." I could depict to you the modern man or woman whose chief aim in life it is to get others to do the work for them while they would look on and perhaps direct. Kach tyro would be a general if he could in these modern days. How the very antithesis of physical fitness is the man who rides to his work In an automobile behind his chauffeur, who gets shaved y a barber, who has his nails manicured, his boots blackened, whose hardest work consists of sitting at his desk and using the pen or the telephone; the man who overeats three times a day, who underworks all day long, and unfits himself by living in the glare of electric lights till long after midnight, tilling his stomach with liquor or his lungs with the smoke of dried leaves from a plant called tobacco. How abnormal it all is when we hold it up in its true perspective! As bad as man is in this respect, the modern woman is infinitely worse. "With help to do the upstairs and downstairs, basement and outside work of her home she goes about ordering and directing and complaining. The Modern Woman. With one woman to do her scalp, another to massage her muscles, an-' other to manicure her nails, an automobile to take her about, with teas In the afternoons and nerve-racking entertainments in the evening, lectures to occupy her idle hours,, clubs at which a professional reader does the reading and thinking for her, with all this it is easy to see how every voluntary function in life is taken away and there is nothing left for these individuals but to be witnesses to what in going on about them. The result is that removal of effort weakens every faculty of these persons ami finally produces complete physical unfitness. S6 much for the muscular system. We now come to the nervous system, which comprises the brain, the spinal cord, the nerves proper and other jierve tissues of the body. The nerve impulses issued from the brain go forth along the complex system of nerves which intertwines with every muscle, every organ and gland of the body. These impulses control, impel and direct all the movements and all functions. a The nervous system, like all the tis sues of the body, while under normal conditions is well capable of performing its functions: likewise is subject to wear and tear. One of the greatest advances in our knowledge of the nervous system has come about through the studies of the effect of shock, Huch as fright, fear, anguish and distress. It has. been shown that if, of two foxes in a cage, one is let loose and chased by the hounds and the other left undisturbed in the cage, upon examining the brains of both of these, the brain cells of the one which has been hunted will show certain degenerative changes, while the brain cells of the other one will be found normal when examined under the microscope. Mental Strain le Real. What is true of the animal is likewise true of man. Thus the intense emotions, pain, fear, anguish, distress, the stress of work or play and such others all have their ill effects upon the nerve tissues of the body. We all know and all have said at one time or another that we would rather be disappointed than go through a period of anxiety over being disappointed: that anticipation is worse than realization. Another example. Let lis take the outfielder in a game of baseball. Ilia actual time of playing throughout the game may be only a few minutes, yet at the end of tho game he comes in "dead-tired." From what if not from anxiety, from the effects of emotions vpon his entire system? Nerve strain comes from work and Continual nerve strain sooner or later manifests itself by a reaction, sometimes mild, sometimes in a complete nervous breakdown. This condition, call it by whatever name you wish, often i3 designated neurasthenia. Neurasthenia is a condition We meet with in pvprv walk of life, and wherever it creeps in we find j lamentation and failure. We see the neurasthenic sick-a-bed woman that burdens her family and eats away at the very core of home life. We see it in the pessimistic, fault-finding, crabbed, incompatible business man. We see it in the artist and the professional man or woman who has left the main field of his or her work to tread in the vapid bypaths of science, literature and art. This neurasthenia is one of the modern sins. It comes to a nervous system which has been abused and exhausted. Point 'of Balance. There is a fine point of balance between the proportion of nerve force and muscular energy that one may expend without ill-effects: so long as the proportion is maintained all is well and good, but just as soon as the demand upon the nerve enersy becomes too great, then one is inviting trouble. It is very pleasing to sit in the cozy chair of the theater or movies, not moving an inch perhaps, and with our mind and eyes to be going through all the experiences of excessive emotions, daring feats, perilous escapes and escapades. But like all other stimulants or intoxicants, it is very trying and wearing and harmful to the nervous system. The lesson from all this is that to be physically fit one must give his nervous system work as well as ample time lor recovery from the work after -each day's effort. That we must njaintain a normal proportion betweeu the energy expended bv the nm-vnno tem and that by the muscular system. ine circulatory system: We now come to the very center of life for the human body, the heart. As the motor is to the automobile, so is the heart to the human body. Under normal conditions the heart beats with perfect regularity 72 times a minute in man and about 76 times a minute in woman.v As you have all noticed, there is a pause between each heart heat. This pause is the period of rest for the heart muscles. and also during this period the heart muscles absorb from the blood what nourishment they need. It is readily seen that the normal man has just so many heart beats in the course of a lifetime. My calculation shows a count of 2,649,0L'-i,40O. Coat of Indulgence. We all know that over-indulgence in food, in drink, in work, in play, and that all the emotions that man is heir to, all these quicken the pulse and cut short the momentary period of rest for the heart muscles, and that in these happy or unhappy indulgences one may use up his allotted 2.649,0:4,400 pulse beats at a much earlier period of life than three score and ten. While these figures may not be exact. let me assure you, ladies and gentlemen, that the underlying principle" of this calculation is most eminently true. The respiratory tract: What I have said of the nervous, the muscular system and circulatory system also applies to the respiratory system, the lungs. One may practice breathing exercises. Improve his lung capacity and be benefited. Certainly this is the proper procedure for the thin and narrow-chested individuals. Increasing chest expansion, in many cases, produces better aeration of the blood, rids the system of harmful poisons and would ward off many cases of pulmonary tuberculosis, aside from increasing physical fitness and physical efficiency. On the other hand, the man who overuses his lungs, as does the public speaker or the man who plays the trombone, distends his lungs to such a point that they lose their normal elesticity and remain balooned out. All of which results In a condition which produces asthma. The digestive tract: There are three kinds of . food substances meats, starches and fats and normally we should partake of them in certain proportions. . When man becomes too fond of his food and indulges into excesses natur repays him in her own coin. Perils of the Fat. There was a time when men and women in the very best society considered it perfectly respectable to indulge quite excessively in the use of wines and liquors. But that time is past, no man or woman may drink to intoxication and be well thought of; it is now considered a sign of lack of self-control and an evidence of self-indulgence, no longer tolerated t.nd even looked upon with disgust. The time is coming when it will be Just as disgraceful to be a glutton. Up to the present, it may be said, that we even a,dmt-e the big f3t man, though society and the feminine styliHts have begun casting doubtful glances' at fat women. I predict a time in tht near future when the big, fat mar. or woman will be looked upon as a selfish, self-indulgent creature. However, it is not for you to wreak your vengeance upon them; nature'wiil get them sooner or later and usually sooner. The law of compensation is ever at work and if you eat as much food in 40 years as you should in a lifetime, then nature will see tovit that you do not get much more than is coming to you by an early dismissal after the age of 40. A very unscientilic idea with some mothers is that the more the child eats the stronger it will be. The fact, however, is that after one has eaten the necessary amount of food for bodily needs, all over that is excess baggage, carried about in one's intestinal tract, undigested and a source of disease. The Normal Man. Now let us construct our resume of what we have just discussed and, that done, we shall have a fair idea of what constitutes physical fitness. First of ail, one should possess a body free of debilitating disease. The body height or weight matters little so that it is not t far removed from the average, a muscular system of fair development, with especially good development of that portion of the body most used in work or play. A heart that beats at normal rate; lungs which expand fully and are not "5 jday. from exceswes of pleasure as well cramped nor stretched, and a digestive I U3 from suffering, from lack of occu- tract not overloaded. i '

Too Much Artificial Light, White Ceilings and White Clothes. By DR. R. KENDRICK SMITH. Ei KS were not designed ror modern city life. Artificial light dirt not exist when human eyes nssnmed their present .state of ieriec-tlon. Animals do not have to wear glasses. Neither do mirage peoples. The eye Is possibly the most donate yet the most perfect and most wonderful organ in the body. It stands an. enormous amount of abuse without breaking down, but there is a limit to everything. , A lifelong habit of misuse is bad enough, but when you sue- eed one life after another in an end less row, generation after generation, is it any wonder that more than half of our school children are found to have serious defects of risiou? " Our eyes get too little exercise of one important kind and altogether too much use of an undesirable sort, rre- quent alternation of near and distant rlew is absolutely essention to maintain the health and efficiency of the normal eye. What chance has the ordinary inhabitant of a civilized community who siiends most of his time within the confines of some sort of a room, with occasional journeys in a street or road where his rision is blocked by brick walls? What chance has such a one to exercise the distance capacity of his eye by searching the distant horizon of the sea, prairie or mountain? ' A group of important nerves and muscles have the exclusive job of sud denly changing the roc us or the eye from long to short distance, and vice versa, just as you do with your opera glasses or telescope. You know that nerves and muscles become weak and MODERN inefficient If they are seldom used, and If neglected long eiioinjdi beenuie powerless. Tills happens In the eye just as truly as It does in the biceps. Try yourself some .lime to compete with an Indian in an attempt t see some minute object on a mountain, or with a sea captain In an endeavor to discover a distant sail at sea. You will then discover the difference between muscles and nerves of the eye which are regularly used and those which are neglected in their exercise. Babies should not be dressed J in white. The glare is too much J for their eyes. White ceilings are injurious to the eyes. They diffuse too much light. Indirect illumination is preferable. ' Indians do not wear glasses. They are an outcome of civilization. Our houses are overlighted. Books should not have white pages. t g One remedy which may be utilized in the home in a practical attempt to off set as much as possible the lack of dis-, tant vision which urban life denies to most of us consists simply of getting into the habit of frequently and regularly removing our gaze momentarily from the reading, writing or other work which we may happen to be doing and looking intently at the most distant point possible. This may also be reversed, as, for Instance, when you are at the movies turn your head frequently to look fo'r a moment at your companion. , While the eye of the Indian has become adapted to withstanding the glare Exercising the Eyes by Alternately Looking Far and Near Will Aid Them Greatly. of the noonday sun on the prairie, because of all the equalizing influences of outdoor environment, it is not equally true that the eye of modern civilization is competent to put up with the constantly injurious effect of the excess of artificial light which so many of us have. Most residences, public buildings nnd amusement houses are overlighted. The old fashioned Idea used to be to caution one against straining his eyes by reading with insufficient light. Nowadays .the danger Is reversed, as most of us read with twice as much light as we need. This is a distinct injury to the eye and a strain on the nervous system. The page which we read should not be white, as white reflects too much of the light into the eye. A light tint of color would be much better. Ceilings, should not be white, particularly in hospitals and nurseries, for the same reason. Babies should never be clothed, in white, as their eyes in particular are not able to receive so much light without injury. The eye should never be considered by itself alone any more than any other, part of the body. A good oculist always warns his patient that it is impossible to maintain healthy eyes when there is disease or weakness or abuse of some other part of the body, and the good osteopathic physician goes even further and adjusts the neck and the upper part of the back whenever he finds any mechanical interference there which brings pressure to bear upon those nerves which control the nutrition or function of the eye. Cleanliness and fresh- air are also vital for the eye. The eyes should be examined just as regularly as the teeth.

Reading in Bed Strains the Eyes It is Comfortable, but Very Detrimental. T is a comfortable habit, we all know, I that of reading In befl, and one In which a great many of. us Indulge without realizing Its detriments. For Instance, have you ever though that a good deal of the eye strain in this world originated right In this luxurious practice of reading In bed? Yet this Is a fact, to the truth of which more than one doctor -will attest. As you lie there surrounded by conv fortable pillows, an exciting novel In hand a lamp by your bedside or perhaps far removed, you only know that you are per fectly comfortable In your present position and enjoying one of the real luxuries of life. A good book, comfortabU pillows ! What more could one ask7 Only one thing but that Is the most Important one of all a brilliant light which fall on the reading matter at Just the right angle Without this necessary adjunct reading In bed Is sure to prove disastrous, perhaps not at first, but undoubtedly in the long run. "But I always read In bed." perhaps you protest, "and there is nothing at all the matter with my eyes." May be not, but that is not saying that If you continue the practice your eyes will keep their brilliancy and good sight. This is the. flrt heeded by all 'Tint how," perhaps you ask, "ran on indulge in reading in bed and still do the eyes no harm? Surely it Is unnecessary to givft up thi delightful practli-o." It Is unnecessary, provided you take all TOU EALL AfLEiLP OVLRSOtTIC BOOR the necessary precautions. These are that a brilliant light shall be so placed that its rays fall directly over the left shoulder and onto the reading matter. The lst way to arrange this Is to placp an electrlo bulb over the lop of the hodMead. so that it falls In Just the right position for reading. A night lamp on the left side of the bed will not do, as the rays from a lamp placed In this position will fall too low ion the book to do much good As for the reader who has only gas by which to read, there Is only one thing to do In order to preserve the eyesight. Place the bed so that the light from the Jet falls over the left shoulder when slU ting up to read In bed, or If this is not convenient, then prop yourself up In a position which will catch the right rays. But after all these precautions have been taken there still remains dangers attached to this delightful custom. Not dangers to the eyesight, but dangers to other parts of the body. IN PRAISE OF HAND MIRRORS. . Proud Beauty! Consider the hand mirror. Contrary to its undeserved reputation as a symbol of vanity, the hand-mirror is, instead, an instrument of humility. The coifure and complexicn which appeared so flawless under the flattering electric light besido the full length mirror In the dresser are shown at their true value by a ses sion with the hand mirror in a window's cold daylight. As Insurance for a dignified and well-gromed appearance, and ad guard against the perils of over-indulgence in cosmetics the hand-mirror is a veritable beauty policeman. Take the little matter of powdering the nose. 'Tls a delicate art and much abused as an observant person may see by the feminine riders in street cars. A full sized mirror will cry "More, more" to the powder puff, when the more honest hand-mirror held up to the light of day will warn "Enough lest you look like a clown!" And when the complexion and hair are deemed ready for the stieet tho hand-mirror, if consulted, will confirm the decision that their condition wil'. bear a "close up" in full daylight. It should be every woman's fina rite of the toilet to subject herse'd to the Judgment of the hand -mirror This little friend alone can be depended upon to tell her truthfully if her powder is on straight, if the unbecoming white grains are properly brushed out of the eyebrow?, If the rouge is in proper place and balance to 'varn against that tragedy of one cheek pinker than the other or the horror of ripe red lip3 looking over-ripe. In the hand-mirror too are found the first whispered warnings of tiny wrinkles-r-in time to ward them off, the danger of freckles or punburn, or the intimation that pastry and chocolates are poor cosmetics. In the hand-mirror also Is caught and foiled the anti-beauty plot of the straggling lock, the ill-adjusted net or false hair, the loosened pin v or comb. And there is one fatal foe to fern inine beauty and charm that the hand-mirror alone is able to conquer. Have you the gum-chewing habit, fair lady? What has that to do with beauty? All right! pick up a hand-mirror and face it for ten minute when next you are enjoying a chew. Gen on. We dare you!-It will save you many nickels in the future! and how it will improve your appearance!

" moas-uro is Will Science Develop Phone Photography? By N. P. Babcock. THE tremendous enthusiasm with nfrich radio development has been accepted, leads naturally to the dreadful thought that mankind mlgnt regard with favor a promise of telephone photography as science's latest achievement. Already pictures have been sent over electric wires, and it Is by no means inconceivable that a time may come wlien through the mere act of lifting the receiver, one will be transmitting one's features rs well as one's voire to if le party at the other end of the line. It Is, In fact, easier to Imagine a day when every telephone will auto-roj.ticnlly photograph the user the moment he or she takes the receiver from the hook, than it Is to feel confident that such a condition of affairs would be welcome or even tolerable. In tde first place, if a photograph of yourself were transmitted over the wire every time you essayed to use a telephone, your Image would of necessity first present itself to the eyes of "Central." I have never seen "Central." but Judging from her voice Blie Is a young lady whom It were not wise to offend. There Is sometimes ,a note of impatience in her tone that inclines one to believe she had red hair and snappy eyes. Can you complacently think of thrusting a portrait of yourself upon "Central" while In one of her im-pullent or apparently preoccupied moods? For my part I do not feel I Know" her weH" enough. Ii Is one l.ing to shout "Hello!" to a girl under cover of the dark, and quite another to be suddenly il lumined before her eyes In the act of uttering that familiar salutation. Far better for all, it would seem, that "Central" remain an Impersonal medium In the transaction of telephonic business, but If there Is to be any presentation of photographs, it is hers that should be given to us, net ours that should be given to her. Being at her regular daily occupation, she presumably Is properly attired; called to trie phone In the midst et a toilet it Is obvious we are not. Nobody can catch her with suspenders hanging down her back and one side of her face lathered, nor In a faded wiapper with her hair In curl papers. But another question arises through this proposed amalgamation of photography and discourse. What would be the period of duration? Would the urjiooking of one's telephone-receiver flash a portrait that would stay "fixed." and unchanging until the receiver was returned to the hook, or would the process be akin t ) that of the "movie" film, permitting of a variety of facial expressions? In the former case, would not a new duty be added to life's burdens? Would we not, all of in, be obliged to cultivate a "telephone face?" There Is perhaps no word in the F.ngllsh language more susceptible of conveying various shades of feeling, from contemptuous indifference to boundless enthusiasm, than the one which has become the customary salutatory of telephone users. You may say "Hello!" to a yellow dog or t i a long absent friend, hut with fai different intonation. In fart, the word can be uttered in such manner as to leave little doubt its utterer lies mentally dropped the final vowel. Now It Is evident that if a photograph of ourselves is to accompany each telephone visit we pay, our halos for civility wrtll more than ever depend upon our "hellos," Do you. madam, suppose for a moment the merchant will be as prompt In delivering the article for which you are waiting. If a scowling, sour "telephone face" thrusts itself Into his vision, as, had you furnished a glimpse of that irresistible smile for which you are famed? And if you, my dear girl, must call up that good-looking young man at Lis office, and ask if he has lost or mislaid your address, do you not know the kind of "telephone face" that may help him to And it? It seems certain at all events that if this photographic attachment Is ever made to our phones, the rates for service will rise, as the Inevitable result of clogged wires. If women in suburban sections find difficulty In limiting their telephone conversations to 15 minutes, what will they do when, added to all the rest of their discourse,.- must be a preliminary somewhat as follows: "CI i, my dear, how well you are looking. What have you done to your hair? Oh. yes you have, and It's very Jiecomlng. And that's a new lace-piece you're wearing; I never saw it before. Really? Oh do tell me all about It. Ho you suppose I could have mine done over the same way? Charley likes your hair done that way. you say; well, I don't blame him," etc., etc. All Tilings considered, tele-photography may In course of time become, like this radio business, a need, but there Is no doubt It could ho. a nuisance.

INJURIOUS MENTAL HABITS It is now stoutly contended that children read too much fiction, also that they are compelled to carry so many studies that no stable impression results. Images are blurred, the child becomes tired, then nervous. The grill of study becomes repulsive and he seeks surcease in the stimulating narcoitc of poor fiction. An old Baltimore school teacher who retired a few years ago has been studying the reading habits of young men and women in particular, with some general attention to the reading of older persons. He concludes that much of our modem reading is injurious rather than benefiicial. We believe that almost any person of ordinary patience might soon verify this finding by making rather careful inquiry among his friends. Reading thoroughly is an art that requires training. Is it not true that the overwhelming majority of those we know scarcely possess a dictionary? Those who chance to own a fair one seldom use it. We know hundreds of persons who are averse to consulting a dictionary even if it lies on the desk before them ; yet a prime rule of careful readng is to permit no word to pass unless it conveys its exact meaning. If or.e has a vague idea what a word means he should focalize the picture and gain accuracy. Disorderly reading is like hapazard conduct in general, which destroys efficiency. Devouring a book, a magazine, or even a newspaper, is to clog the brain and leave the problem undigested. Turning column after column or page after page of idle reading is as wastifully useless as to he on ones back and count the fleecy clouds in a South Sea sky. Such desultory reading destroys the incentive to vigorous mental effort. The very best way to read is when the zest for information fairly possesses and drives one to his book or newspaper. Then reading is never a lash, but a pleasure -nor is it mere trifling when thus indulged in. Indohnt inclinations too long induldged in case a dul-ness of the mind, throttling the will power and causing the reader to lose control of his thoughts. Any idLr who believes he is vvoiking on even acquiring knowledge by lacing through a story is Lkely to be d.sillusioned as soon as he is put to a test and asked to summarize what he has learned. The mania for hop-skip-and-jump reading is a species of mental mixed drinking comparable to gluttony in the abnoima! eater A great observer says many nervous readers ramble or race over a page as if they were biting the-r nails. That rapid reading, with no moment for real absorp-and weakens the interlligence, is a habit which scatters and weakens the intelligence, there is hardly a question. Excessive disorder and transient mental stimulation are undoubted evils to the mind. When the great Cervantes sought to drive Don Quixote insane he drove him to excessive reading. A rapid succession of impressions weakens attention, destroys analysis, and leaves the will power unhorsed. A swift run through a sensational novel leaves the reader weary mentally and physically. Knowledge caught by skimming and skipping is of fleeting duration. Memory cannot retain what is necessary until propositions are formulated, compared with experience, and classified by reflection. Dr. Jules Payot, Frances greatest educator possibly the worlds greatest says that fast reading leaves no more trace than does the countryside we see through the car window of a fast train.

The transatlantic telephone, recently called a failure by a member of the British Parliament was used from the date of Its opening on Jan. 7, 1927, to Dec. 20 last for a total of 2,173 calls, 90 per cent of which were completed, according to an announcement by the American Telephone and Telegraph company. The corporation is joint operator of the telephone with the British General Postoffice. By November last, the" reeords show, calls were averaging seven and three-quarters each business day. They had an average dura tion of five minutes for & toll of $125, the rate being $25 a minute. Almost half of this de luxe con versation was purely social. One- fifth engaged bankers and brokers. The remainder was miscellaneous, with merchants, newspapers and theaters to the fore. Originating traffic was heavier at the American than at the British end by a score of 1159 to 1014 and quite a few of the calls from England during the summer were made by American tourists. The member of Parliament called the transatlantic telephone a failure both as a convenience and a necessity, because, he said, calls from England between Jan. 7 and Nov. 14 averaged less than 12 and one-half minutes a day. He also criticized U 3 1 1 ! it 1 hibitive ' in cost and uncertain as to time of completed connections. But mere figures are not the point according to American Telephone and Telegraph company officials. Engineering and science, they say, do not necessarily reckon the success of an enterprise, particularly one contributing to the welfare as well as convenience of mankind, by it3 showing the firsts year. It is not necessarily expected to "carry" itself. The only reward, thev sav. might conceivably be the establish ment of a potential value, the benefits of which would accrue only grad ually and cumulatively. Furthermore, the A.T.4T. neonle say, the record of the transatlantic telephone is only repeating the history of. the development of other long distance telephone facilities. They cite the transcontinental telephone. The first line was opened between New York and San Francisco in 1915. For a year or so calls averaged only two or three a dav. Yet the gradual development of through and intermediate business along the coast-to-coast trunk line eventually exceeded its capacity. Trans-Atlantic Telephone Calls Total 2,173 in First Year of Use Now there are two eoast-to-coast trunks, and a third line from Chicago to Seattle. The three lines average 350 to 400 calls a. day. Pre sumably the telephone engineers an ticipate comparable gain3 eventually on the Transatlantic telephone. Such confidence does the A. T. & T. corporation appear to have in the Transatlantic telephone that one hears discussion in the communications field of greater things to come. A report is current that the Transatlantic telephone will sooner or later be made the backbone of a wider development, one which will link by telephone the entire Hemisphere . with the entire Continent of Europe from Spitsbergen to the Mediterranean. Test calls between Stockholm and New York have already been successfully completed. The Transatlantic telephone started with a daily four and a half hours' service, but has been in operation for 10i hours a day since May 23 last The scope of the service was widened until by March 26 it included all points in the United States and In England, Scotland and Wales. Ottawa, Montreal, Quebec, Toronto and Hamilton were added on Oct S last The uses to which patrons have Put the radiophone have been various. An American patient of a French specialist suffered a relapse on reaching- his homo in New Orleans. It was Imperative to consult the specialist again and the patient cabled the French doctor to telephone him. The doctor took the first train to London. There telephone communication was established with New Orleans, the physician learned first hand of the developments and successfully prescribed the proper treatment American song hits have beea played and sung into the United States end of the overseas telephone their words and music taken down at the London end and, In one case, the song itself actually put into rehearsal in twenty-five minutes at a West End threatre. In speaking over the transatlantic telephone the American volcce now goes by radio from Rock Point L. I to Cupar, Scotland whence land wires relay it to its destination. The English voice comes by radio from Rugby, England, to Houlton, Me.. whence land wires are again employed. In other words, at one stage the two "speech paths" are allowed to come as closely together as the mouth and the ear, but in the main they are kept hundreds of miles apart

The next six .weeks will determine the crisis of a gigantic struggle between capital and labor on the question of working hours, according to Ethel-bert Stewart, United States commissioner of labor statistics. The outcome which may be postponed until 1929 or 1930. will direct the future prosperity of the country. Stewart believes. For 41 years, Stewart has sat In the labor department and watched employment charts rise and f alL More than 46 years of his life have been devoted to the study of labor statistics, and he is credited with a knowledge of employment conditions held by no other person. MACHINES TAKE JOBS. "Every machine that is built to do the work of four men throws three men out of work. Of course new industries are created and production increased to absorb part of the surplus labor but sooner or later we win reach the saturation point. "Whether we have reached that point now will be determined by the middle of April," he said. "And if we have, there is only one solution-shorter working hours.' "Anything else will be suicidal." Stewart pointed out that national prosperity depends upon, domestic marketing conditions. If the purchasing power of the masses is curtailed by unemployment, then the very foundation of the nation is undermined, he said. MUST FACE ISSUE AGAIN. Tf we have reached the saturation point of labor," Stewart emphasized, "then we must have shorter hours to give more persons employment. We faced it when the eight-hour day was apoted and we must face it again. "This is not an ordinary unem ployment situation, it is scattered, not only geographically, but by industries. When we are in an ordinary working slump everything everywhere is hit more or less alike. "Today we have workers laid off in some industries and taken on in others and, while unemployment is increasing, production also is in creasing. To me this is an indica tion we are reaching the crisis. fcome of the unemployment is seasonal. A great many men will probably be given work as soon as spring sets in, but many more will probably be left unemployed because industries cannot absorb them. "Some capitalists and employers of labor see the change coming. They are preparing to accept it. Others will be forced into it by economic pressure." Secretary of Labor Davis also believes present industries have reached the saturation point of labor. WE ARE LIVING TOO FAST "People in this modern age are living too fast to die an old age" is the opinion of Dr. J. C. Anderson, 69 state health officer. "They're cutting down their lives an average of ten years," he said. "The men who in an earlier age would have lived beyond the seventies are passing out in the early sixties or late fifties. "This is due to the high tension un der which they work and play. "Business has speeded up. It is more cold-blooded than in the earlier days when competition was not so strong. "Today business is a hard game, ex acting its toll on man's, health. One business man is trying to out scheme the other. "In the earlier days Jhis competi tion was not as strong since there was enough business for all. The executives played the game in a more leis urely manner. "But today the business man works under a high nervous strain, fails to eat regularly and doesn't sleep as much as he should. "When he goes home at night after a day of work he doesn't alwavs rest. He has a dinner appointment to keep with some business opiionent or as sociate. He talks business while eating. " "Or iterhaps, if s a social affair a bridge party or dance. He plays hard. He talks business at these functions. "To live and enjoy a long life peo ple must eat three meals each -day and eat them at regular times. One, and no more, of these meals should be a meal. People should have at least three quarters of an hour for each meal. "Eight hours sleep is necessary for a long life. "There should le less running around at night and other times." Use some of the spare time in rest and sleep; not all of it in discussing business or having a good time," he said.

NOWY SONCH, Poland, July 14. iJF) Peasants of the mountain regions near here have destroyed all their wireless sets in the belief that radio has attracted the unusually cold weather during the present summer. Last year the peasants of central Poland did the same when the month of May was very cold and rainy. By a freak of fate the month of June brought, much better weather which had confirmed the peasants in the belief that wireless attracts bad weather. News of the improvement of weather after the destruction of the apparatus evidently reached the Tatra mountain region which was suffering from the coldest June weather in more than a century. On June 20 in Zakopane and other villages near Not J Sonch there was snow, and the thermometer was at freeslng point.

There Is no doubt that the "talkies" have come to stay. The pessimists and the conservatives, of course, have declared that they are only a "craze," and that after a time people will gladly turn from them to look again upon the silent screen. But pessimists nnd conservatives raised their eyebrows scorn fully at wireless when It was In Its early stages. Now, wireless telephony Is being carried oo across the Atlantic. One of the most notable examples of an Invention that has hai to struggle against overbearing conservatism and short-sightedness is the moving picture Itself. In a recently-published life of Adolph Zukor. Will Irwin tells how for year after year the "movies" were housed only In the less savoury quarters of New York; how producers deliberately Ignored the possibilities thnt lay In them: and how there ruled nn unreasonable Idea that no film more than two reels long could hold the attention of the public. In VjZO, It Is by no means uncommon for a Mm to be twelve reels long, and for the spectators to be Jut as Interested In the twelfth reel as In the first; and the films are screened In theatres more magnificent than those which house the "legitimate" drama. "TALKIES" AND THE STAGE. But In the case of the "talkies' the chorus of doubts and denunciations expressed simply for the soke of oouhtlng and denouncing has already begun to die away. More and mors people hnve experienced the "talkies" for themselves, and realised the vitality that lies ln this new form. Of course, there will always be people who say they "don't lke talkies," Just as there have always been people who said they "didn't like mnvjnir pictures"; but with them It will be tho rub-Jert and not the technique that has no appeal. They will not really dislike talkies. Their dislike w be for drama; or nt least the sort of drama that the producers give us. Unless he were entirely devoid nf any lnterodt In human nature as expressed through dramatic art, or else Insanely prejudiced, no one could fall to be Impressed, say, by the last scene in "The Doctor's Secret,' which whs shown last week at the Capitol Theatre. Here one found dialogue written by Sir James Barrio (for the picture had been adapted from the Ilarrle play. "Half an Hour"), superb acting, a beautiful setting, and exquisitely enunciated words reproduced so that they seemed inseparable from the person of the speaker. What more could one have for the perfection of drama? Only two things. First, colour. And, second, the real presence of the actors. Now, colour Is not an essential element in drama. On the theatrical stage It often proves distracting and blatant. Is the bodily presence of the actors essential for the highest effects In drama? Lovers of the theatre, of course, draw together In a defensive body at this question, as at the sound of a bnttls alarm, and cry, "Yes!" On the other hand, mnny Intelligent people claim that they can be Just aa much moved by a shadow on the screen as by a living, breathing figure 'in the stage, now that the "talkies" have endowed the shadows with speech. Everything seems to depend on the ability of the spectator to support an Illusion. And at this point it may be as well to say that the term "shadows," which has always conveyed a feeling of mild contempt, Is no longer strictly applicable. "Shadows" Imply flatness; whereas the latest methods of photography have given scenes stereoscopic depth, so that one feels one could easily wak Into the pictured room and move about among the actors there. In fact. one feels one really Is In tho room with them. A MORE INTIMATE STYLE. It Is In this feeling of greater intimacy with the actors that the talking films have nn advantage over the theatrical stage. In the theatre, If you happen to be sitting towarJs the front of the dress circle, you see the figures of the actors from a distance of f:rty or fifty feet. If you are sitting In the gallery, you not only see them from an even greater distance, but you are looking down on the tops of their heads as well. In ether case, you feel yourself outside the "fourth wall' of the room on the stnge. And If you try to bring the faces of the actors closer by means of opera glasses. Oct. 10.—In the village where General Pershing had his headquarters during the war and which bears the high-sounding name of Colombey-les-Deux-Lff- lises but which means only the place with two churches, the saddest man to be found Is the town crier, old Jehan Bor'dier. Town crying isn't what it used to be. For more than ft quarter of a century Bordier has cried the news aloud night and morning to a grateful populace that has now become ungrateful. No one seems to want to hear his melodious voice agaJn. People pass him by without the glad greeting, the eager enquiries they once had for him The radio Is to blame for it nil. says the old town crier. Everyone, or nearly everyone in the village has a radio outfit and news which they were glad to receive from Bordier twelve hours late, or maybe even two days late, they now get red hot over the wireless waves. “Man and hoy,” says the old town crier “I have sounded on my drum and given out the news to an appreciative public—when to sow. when to harvest: who’s come to town, who’s going to the city; who's going to sell something by auction and so on and so forth. “But now the days are dull for town crying. I blame hoth newspapers and radio for the big change, especially the radio. "If you ask me,” added the old town crier, “I don't understand it, don't undersl md it at all. How' anyone can talk without any wires and to so many people all at once beats me." Jehan Bordier bemoans the passing of General Pershing and the American doughboys. “They were a fine lot of poopte for my business.” the old town crier declares. “They would gather round me when I beat my drum. They didn't understand me, perhaps, but nevertheless hey list* ened to me all the time, right until I had cried out everything I had to say. Almost never do I write an article, like a fisherman casting hi3 net into the sea, hoping for a catch f opinions in letters. But when early in September I wrote an article about radio and children I had a lingering hope that the thinking mothers would have something to say. Because it's the .mothers who are going to have the real thing to contribute on thi3 subject for a long time to too e n o t the professional or scientific student of children, whose laboratory is not the home. It is the wise use of radio in the home that we must develop, and who has an opportunity to collect data on the subject equal to a mother's ? Radio is assuredly something that bears thinking about. To go back then. As I said, I didn't deliberately spread my net when I wrote about radio and children, but a remarkably fine and thoughtful letter came to me as a result of the article. Here is a woman who thinks and talks to great purpose. This is a letter that every person who has a radio and children should ponder carefully. "Dear Mrs- Bevans: Reading your article about the effect of radios on children, I am moved to write a few suggestions, based on a little experience I have had with my own children. "One day when there was a beautiful program to be given by the Chicago Symphony orchestra, I called my two boys to me and told them I wanted them to relax on the floor and listen to the lovely ' music Result was that in about five or ten minutes' concentration was no longer possible, the restlessness -of the age overtook them, and mother's plan for them flew to the winds. "That set me thinking rather seriously about children versus radios. "1. Children being brought up with the sound of the radio ringing in their ears will naturally accept it as just another sound in the course of everyday life, on a par witn vacuum cleaners, automobile norns, street cars, and other noises of civilized life. "2. An adult who unthinkingly allows a radio to run incessantly as a background to every home activity is hindering the sensitive child (or even a normal one) in developing concentration, discrimination and fineness of taste. "3. It behooves every mother and father to study radio : programs, pick the finest, and then use it as an 'occasion.' It should be the unusual thing, not the usual thing." This is masterly. Some extremely worthwhile letters have come in on the subject of radio, and children. Instead of making a continuous symposium of them, as I had originally planned. it seems to me now that perhaps the opinions expressed will be more provocative of thought if they are scattered, and appear at intervals. One letter says: "Dear Mrs. Bevans: I am Interested to know the effects of the radio Upon other children, as I have often observed Our little girl when our radio is going and have really looked for comment upon this subject before you invited mothers' opinions on it. " When my 2 year old is busy with her toys and the radio is turned on to some jazz or exciting entertainment she becomes more active, getting too hilarious and is irritated at the slightest provocation. If she is more relaxed and not so occupied when an orchestra is playing music of a restful type, she seems to enjoy it. In a similar way, when I am working around the house and the radio is playing, it makes me nervous, too, while if I sit down and really listen to a program I thoroughly enjoy it. ' I really think the radio being played when the child is occupied with some other task or play is harmful to his nervous system, for while thus occupied the music stimulates the emotions so far diversified from the ones immediately occupying his mind that the conflict makes him nervous and he loses concentration on either, hence his nervousness and irritability. However, I think the baby should be accustomed to music gradually so there will not be such a marked effect on the nervous system. Born of Immigrants By .Glenn frank. I have been long fascinated by the perplexities that beset the firstborn generation of Immigrants I mean the first generation of American-born children of European-born Immigrant parents. So often they live in a kind of twilight zone between the land of their fathers and the land of their birth. It is no reflection upon the Immigrant fathers and mothers that they bathe their sons and daughters in deep memories of the ancestral fatherland. I am suspicious of the Immigrant who effects a complete and obliterating divorce from his fatherland the moment he sights the Goddess of Liberty. The man who lightly casts aside old and deep seated loyalties Is the sort of man who is likely to cast aside new loyalties even more lightly. One does not have to slander his fatherland in order to serve the land of his adoption with sincerity. But the first generation of American-born children of European-born Immigrant parents often have neither the stabilizing love of the old home of their fathers nor the stabilizing insight of a mature knowledge of the new home. They may become victims of an irresponsible sort of sentimental Internationalism.' They may become victims of an Irresponsible sort of swashbuckling nationalism. The first generation of children of European-born immigrants need above all education in the current realities of their fathers' homeland and the current realities In the land of their birth. Here Is a device I should like to see tried. f In every American university J should like to see. a dozen free scholarships or fellowships in economics and politics, six going to American-born sons and daughters of Immigrants, and Bix going to foreign students from the ancestral lands represented by the six immigrant sons and daughters. With students of the same blood and nationality for background, one to live his life in Europe, the other In America, study .ng together. 1 think both would find a stabilizing sense of reality far beyond dim memories or current passions. M 1931 by American Weekly, Inc. Great Britain Rights Reserved. ISS ANN LEE HILL was cooking a pot of beans on the stove in a ranch-house near Santa Barbara. California. As the water began to bubble the music from a violin sounded from the pot and then a voice began to sing Gounod's "Ave Maria" in French. There was no other human being in the house, no other musical instrument, and no radio set within a mile. When Mrs. A. W. Morrell, of Jackson Heights, Long Island, stepped in front of her bathroom mirror the other night a sneeze and a voice came from the mirror, saying, "Here's looking at you." Mr. Terry Turner, of West Seventy-second street, New York, sold his radio set and sent it out of the house entirely. And yet that evening when Mr. Turner came home a musical programme greeted his ears from the spot where the radio set used to be, near the steam radiator. A laborer who owned no radio set reached for his iron shovel one Sunday morning to do a little work in the garden. Suddenly the pious shovel greeted his astonished ears with the Lord's Prayer, and followed this with a hymn from a church organ. These are a few of the instances of what are known as "radio ghosts," which are discussed in more detail further on in this article. Scientists understand the reason why that pot of beans sang the "Ave Maria" and why Mr. Turner's radiator took up the job of giving the evening programme . after the radio set had been taken out of the house. These weird antics of the wireless waves are going on here and there all over the world. But in some localities they are exceptionally varied and uncanny. Iron stoves and radiators that talk, chicken-wire or tennis-court fences that give market reports, sink drains that reproduce a melodious symphony more clearly than a loud-speaker, antenna poles that arc and sing when touched, and music everywhere, are a few of the oddities at short-wave radio station W8XK, near Pittsburgh, Pa. The antics of this radio station are well known in the neighborhood and to farmers and school children for miles around. The whole atmosphere surrounding the radio 'building in Wilkins Township is charged with high-frequency currents, the strongest part of the electric field is the building itself, but its effects are felt in neighbors' homes at considerable distances. Visitors at the station are first shown the famous singing antenna pole. A tall wooden mast supporting one of the 49-meter aerials will give off a large blue arc when touched with a wire or a metal pole. This arc will sing, play or announce, depending on the particular programme broadcast from the station at the time.
