The human body furnishes sufficient capacity to build up a high frequency arc between a wire held in the hand and the charged pole. No shock is felt these currents are of such high frequency that they travel over the surface of the body instead of through it. The carrier frequencies on the antenna varying with the modulation of the voice or musical instrument will cause the arc to set up vibrations of audible frequencies in the air. The case of the stove and the radiator is likewise simply explained. Any poor connection at the station will cause an arc, and even though it be very small, if the stove is atune to it, signals will be produced. A "crystal effect" between dissimilar metals will produce music from a wire fence around a tennis court at the station. If the terminals of a pair of earphones of the type familiar to radio .pioneers be touched to the fence, the programme is heard distinctly music, song or market reports whatever it happens to be. All this is perfectly well understood by radio engineers. But such astonishing things seem uncanny to those who are not radio experts. It is not surprising that "supernatural" powers are attributed to radio waves and that many people have attributed illness, misfortune and hoodoos to the malevolent influence of radio black magic. Thus the mysterious waves of the radio have been blamed for droughts, floods, earthquakes, heat, cold, headaches, stomachaches, the withering of vegetation, and even death of animals and human beings. Mental hospitals are full of people whose heads are ringing with voices and music that nobody else can hear, and therefore they are convinced that they have become walking radio receiving sets. But people outside of institutions also suffer from the same delusions, and one man went to court because he was sure that waves from a New York broadcasting station gave him cramps every time he crossed Forty-second street. Fakers who are always quick to seize upon popular delusions are doing business here and there, "correcting" these mysterious and hostile forces. "Healers" send out "healing thought-waves" over the radio and credulous people have actually stuck their heads into loud speakers to "get the full benefit." Serious-minded physicians have a rather hard time with such patients. Auditory hallucinations, as these imaginary voices are called, were a common enough symptom of mental disorder long before radio. But if the doctor tries to tell a patient that, the victim of the delusions can mention the "radio ghosts," equally weird and mysterious phenomena that are real. In olden times delusions of "voices" and hauntings and invisible persecutions were common among people with unbalanced minds. The famous "Tom o' Bedlam," who wandered about the English countryside, was an example. The original Tom believed that moonbeams pursued him with malevolence, and bats and toads exercised magic spells over him. So common were these delusions of unseen influences that half-wits were called Tom o' Bedlams, and there were hundreds of them. They went about in wild attire. Dartlv naked with 'a collection of vegetables in their hats. They made strange grimaces, uttered wild cries, and wandered about town and country frightening or entertaining people. The unfortunates professed to see imaginary snakes, dragons, monsters and ogres and heard "voices" and felt unseen "influences." At times they would see blood on the face of the moon, dragons in the sun and other portentous phenomena. But nowadays very real voices are heard and other seemingly "supernatural" things are happening all the time. A radio fan turns off the switch and the set "goes dark" but keeps right on with music. The owner of a superheterodyne starts to tune in, but instead of a station finds he is listening in on a telephone conversation between a man and a girl. Cellars are haunted by ghostly voices and musical instruments; doors, faucets and bed springs suddenly burst into song. For instance, Mrs. George Lotterhoos, who was then Miss Ann Lee Hill, was cooking a mess of beans in the kitchen of a ranch house outside of Santa Barbara, as already briefly mentioned above. First they suspected it had gotten in through telephone or power lines from Los Angeles, both of which are connected with the house, but tests ruled these out. Finally they determined that the "ghost" sneaked in underground. From Los Angeles the waves traveled out along a metallic stratum of rock. At the ede of the kitchen is a deep, underground cistern in this stratum. Water is piped from the cistern to the kitchen and it was found that the pipes touched a brass tape running across the floor and making contact with the electric range. When one stepped on that tape sometimes he got an electric shock which turned out to be due to a short circuit in the range, which was also grounded to the earth. All these rather unusual circumstances brought the radio waves up to the bottom of the pot in half cycles. The loose contact between the electric burner and the pot acted as a condenser, cutting the radio waves down to a frequency low enough to be heard. Vibrating at that frequency, the pot-bottom sent out sound waves. As soon as any of these arrangements were disturbed the pot became silent. Too Many Books 1 By Aldous Huxley 1 LONDON. "Of making many books there is no nd." And yet in the Preacher's day, two thousand and some years ago, humanity was only at the very beginning of its book making. If Koheleth could return to the earth what would he say of the cataracts and avalanches of books which incessantly pour down upon us today ? He would say of tKem, no doubt, what he said of everything else: "Vanity of vanities." And the remark would be as true of books as it was and is of everything else in the world as true and as profoundly irrelevant. As one who contributes in a small way to swell the volume of the literary torrent, I feel a certain rather guilty concern about the almost frenzied book making of modern times. For surely there can be no doubt about the matter; there are too many books. Not too many, of course, to say all that might be said about this queer and astonishing universe; the world being infinite, it would require an infinity of books to do that. When I say that there are too many books, I mean that there are too many for any given individual. In order to qualify as a well-informed, up-to-date citizen of the contemporary world, a man must have read so many booRs that it is almost impossible that he should have read any of them well. We are in danger of sacrificing quality of reading to quantity, in danger of reading too much and too quickly to be in a position to pass judgment on what we read.

LOS ANGELES TIMES SUNDAY MAGAZINE November 6, 1932 AMERICA: "Sweet Land of Leisure!" With robots running things mankind faces the same kind of situation which put the ox, mule and horse out of business, says this writer. What we must do to keep our enormous overproduction of LEISURE from destroying US. ill a Machine Get Y our Job? INSTEAD of "Sweet Land of Liberty," we must learn to sing or, at least, think "Sweet Land of Leisure.". For we're in the machine age now, in the dazing dawn of it, shanghaied so to speak aboard a ship of state run by robots, with plenty of nothing to do. Meanwhile, whether we happen to be captains or gobs, rich or poor, men or women, we're expected to abide by the rules of the ship, and one rule hits below the belt. It says: "No work, no pay." With robots holding down the Jobs, mankind must face the same sort of a situation which put the ox, mule and horse out of business. No use fooling , ourselves: robots, are here to stay. Telephone girls have left the exchanges forever and trucks will continue to transport the burdens which used to break human backs.. Fitness always survives in the bitter end; and, as workers, machines are enormously more capable than flesh and blood. Ten Pounds Equal 100 Men Since last July, I have been wondering where robots are taking us. At that time I saw a ten-pound robot run a battleship the old dreadnaught Utah. This little robot was on a mine sweeper, the Robin, more than a mile away, and it might have been many miles away, for distance made no difference. After taking off the steering wheel, Commander Randall Jacobs ordered, "Abandon ship;" then for two . and one-half hours the little robot, no larger than a typewriter with nine keys, made 22,000 tons of steel behave as if hypnotized. Whenever touched, the keys started ether waves, which tripped throttles like so many invisible hands, causing the mist-shrouded battleship to turn right or left, to speed up or slow down, to whistle or flash searchlights to do whatever the commander wanted it to do Just as well as i! 100 sailors had been on their Jobs. If the guns had not been removed, the robot could equally well have broad-sided 10,000 pounds of shrieking shells into the heart of Los Angeles, twenty miles away. Fancy what a robot In a dirigible above the clouds might do with a fleet of floating fortresses, provided the brain in charge went mad as most brains do In . time of war! After the dynamiting, Al-phonse Boyer, the watchman, said the pair forced him to enter his shack while they made a getaway. CONCERN: Debate article on influence of technology & machines
OCR: THE MODERN JOSHUA: STAND STILL! How the Economists Fool Themselves 'Irrefutable logic" can be cited to prove technological unemployment . is impossible, writer says; however, thousands of jobless men, displaced by machines, are con . crete evidence to contrary; re'absorption by new industries is theory that doesn't work out in fact, as relief figures show, despite lofty reasoning of classical economists. Stuart Chase. Economist, in Harpers Magazine. I EMPLOY a skilled mechanic to mow my meadow and cultivate my garden. He .used to be employed, in a Connecticut mill, but a new machine was installed and he and some others lost their work, so he is keeping himself and his family alive as best he can at a fraction of his former income. He was a victim of what is termed "technological unemployment." A machine took his work from him, and for a considerable period he could find no other work to do. He might have left town, but he had bought a house, his children were in school, his wife liked the neighborhood. To take to the road was a risky venture, with machinists out of work on every hand. Now what do the classical economists do with my friend Roy Thompson? What they . do illustrates the sort of trouble that purely logical use of words can get people into. They prove by irrefutable logic that technological unemployment is impossible. I know what I am saying, for I have debated the matter in public with classical economists and can tick off the arguments with my eyes shut. The logic proceeds like this: A new machine is put into a 'pin factory to take the place of men. The cost of making pins is lowered. Presently competition lowers the price of pins as the machine is general-,, ly adopted. Therefore, housewives spend less money for pins and have more to spend for silk stockings. Therefore, the factories making stockings employ more help, and no . unemployment results. On the other hand, if the first factory has a monopoly of the new machine and does not choose to lower the price of pins, the not. Whether they do or do not, certain relevant human factors must be brought into the concept. Can one Roy, after 20 years of working at a lathe, shift his skill to qualify as a linesman if men are wanted in that field? . Can another Roy, after living 40 years in Middle-town, with his roots driven deep, pick up his family and move to Seattle if men are wanted on the docks? Can another Roy, now unemployed, hibernate like a wooa-chuck and live without eating because a year hence there is-to be a demand for machinists in the television industry? Can another Roy change from man's work in a machine shop to woman's work in a rayon factory? What kind of employment awaits him? Where does it await him? When does it await him? Talking about technological unemployment as a net statistical effect and observing Roy in his perplexity and discouragement are two different things. If new invention speeds up, it is obvious that more men and women per thousand are in transit from a job lost to a job hopefully to be found. And what happens if the owner of the factory does not care to buy a private airplane or to invest in a new pin plant? For the past eight years, new investments in private industry have been pitifully small compared with earlier , periods. What if we have as many pin factories as prospects for profitable investment warrant? - - These considerations by no means exhaust the question. But perhaps I have given enough to show that knowledge about technological unemployment, or, indeed, any kind of employment, is not advanced by the syllogisms of classical economists. Myers Wonders What Readers Think of Programs That Lure Tot, and What They Do About It "RADIO IS not to blame for all excitaWe children or adults," an executive of a broadcasting company said recently before the Federal Communications commission in defending the juvenile programs aired over his network. While he is said to have admitted that certain programs justified criticism at times, he allegedly insisted that others were not excitable or emotional. I wonder what my readers think of the radio programs which lure children. Have you written to your favorite stations to tell them what you think, not only ot the programs you condemn but also of those you heartily approve? It might be well to buy a £a'ck of 50 or perhaps 100 post cards and have them near the radio. Then immediately after hearing a children's program you liked or disliked you could write a note about it then and there to the station. Will Not Disagree Perhaps not a single one of my readers would disagree with the executive that "Radio is not to be blamed for ALL. excitable children and adults." He spoke safely. But many parents believe that certain programs can be blamed for SOME excitable children and adults, and that such programs contribute generously to jitters in the home. We •wonder if this man has watched many children from six to 12 sit or stand like statuary by the radio with a "thriller" on, or if he has checked on the dreams and general emotional health of these children. We wish studies of RADIO AND CHILDREN similar to those of MOVIES AND CHILDREN might soon be made. In the meanwhile, one wonders why the Federal Communications commission has not called upon those experts who are supposed to know about the mental and emotional health of children, such as representatives of the American Psychological association, the American Association of Applied Psychologists and other groups. Coincidentally, since then, you | probably have read the report of a very interesting national survey of the prevalence of chance-takin'f in the United States. It was found that on the average, every other person spent money on at least one gam* of chance last year; that church lotteries stood first, with the punch board second in popularity. These thefts occur In instances where no need or poverty has been indicated. He maintains that violence is glorified in the comic strips he studied and that they do violence to the American principles. SALNDERS Says Mr. Lynn: "The aensa-' tlonal exploits of individuals or groups engaged in executing masked and hooded Justice have, proved profitable for the purveyors of comic books, but this fact remains unshaken: No matter how despicable the villains against whom this "justice" Is aimed, no matter how triumphant the final defeat of vice by virtue, it is neither Christian nor American to permit the young to be taught in this way the. pernicious totalitarian doctrine that the end Justifies the means." He maintains that children often » forget the "good" but remember the technique used by the "evil" and points to the recent case where children playing "bad man" tied a playmate with a wire clotheslines to a tree, injuring the child's arms, while In another instance a small boy actually met death by hanging while trying to imitate the flying feats of a comic book hero. The word "comic" misleads parents, says Mr. Lynn, for these books are far from comic, humorous or laugh provoking. He charges: "Yet the parent who hands a child an uncensored comic book is literally saying to that child: Meet these murderers, sadists and degenerates, observe and study how these inhuman monsters torture and kill their helpless victims; notice how necessary it is to set up illegal methods to bring about law and order." Mr. Lynn maintains that "It is not enough that good should triumph over evil. The triumph must be gained by lawful, American methods." In the study of the comic books upon which this report is bused, there wore discovered 246 un-American plots or episodes of a vigilante nature, a total which indicates the extent to which the masked and hooded justice falsely appeals to those who produce the features in which these were found." Prevalence of reading comic books is commented upon: "Members of the American Association of University Women in Gary, Ind., during a week of survey, eiuestloned 696 grade school pupils with the following findings: These children had read 915 books of which 137 could be termed good. They had read a total of 2370 comic magazines or about 3.4 comic books per pupil. Thirty-five per cent had read nothing but comics. Reading is ones of the leisure time activities that can either add or subtract from children's mental poise and development. It is one measure of control that parents can usually exert and Mr. Lynn's findings are well worth considering.

Effects of Radio On Our Children Causing Concern BY RUTH MILLETT. Recently Ohio State University sponsored a panel discussion on the question: "Is radio meeting the needs of our children?" Judging from the opinions of the experts who took part in the debate, the main concern of parents and educators is whether the programs children are listening to are harmful or not. But isnt the effect of radio pro grams on youngsters as much a problem of quantity as quality? Isn't how many hours' the radio is on also an important factor in what influence it has on children and family life? In the morning the mother escapes . from facing her own problems by listening to the agonies and frustrations of one soap heroine after the other. When the father gets home he listens to his favorite programs. 0 Noisy Outsider. - The children also have their schedule of favorites. During dinner, news broadcasts reduce table conversation to requests for ; salt and pepper. Through it all, there is no real family closeness and companionship. Instead of sharing experiences of the day, they are all escaping each other. Radio makes thinking, good conversation, and concentration nearly impossible. Isn't that the danger pf the radio to children having a noisy out sider always in the house?

But we - have enough of them now to make. up for all past generations! 1 Comic books are with us. I be lieve they are here to stay. Does your son chase home from school and shut himself in his room for hours on end? He has lust traded with a friend for a new stack of comic books. Does your daughter spurn the Christmas books you so Carefully selected? Comics again. i In one small neighborhood store I, counted the titles -of the different series of comic books on display. An even 50 . different series were there.' Most of the series were rep resented by half a dozen different titles. , .. ' AVID READERS t There were many horror comics, Weird sub-human creatures tor tured the heroine, and fantastic machines made hash of the human warriors. There were the "character" comics built around "Archie," "Bozie" or "Gordo." There , were the teenage girl comics, teenage boy comics, grownup comics and even after-death comics. Many of our children seem to devour all types. Some studies have indicated that most, children prefer the humorous comics lull of lively fun. I do hope the studies are correct, but in years of watching youngsters read comic books, I haven't been able to observe oiucn aiscriminauon. 'Most of them are relatively harmless.; The damage they do "is in- direct They eep our children away from constructive things. .Our comic book addicts don't gel out and play when they ahould. They miss their Scout meetings. They skip their music lessons. - Many parents ration the comic books. They limit their youngsters to so: many minutes reading per day. . REDEEMING FEATURE - Our children's addiction to comics runs in a predictable sequence. Third, fourth and fifth graders are developing the appetite for them. Sixth, seventh, eighth and ninth graders read "them most continuously.' Then in the last years of high school the addiction lessens. Intelligent children read them about as frequently as the less intelligent ones. - s There is one good thing about comic books. It is that they do help some slow readers to increase their reading ability. The books are easy, the words are simple and the interest value is high. : The conclusion is that the comics are a mixed blessing. . They, are harmless if not carried to an ex cess. But many children do. carry them to an excess. And they are helpful with many slow readers. Editorial supervision by Call fornia Parent-Teacher. Reproduc tion rights reserved. OCR: BEDFORD DAILY TIMES-MAIL, BEDFORD. INDIANA Modern Housewife Must Be Electrical Wizard To Keep All Gadgets Operating By David G. Bareuther AP Newsfeatures Writer To be a successful housekeeper, the modern housewife is .obliged to be somewhat more of an electrical wizard than Thomas Alva Edison was at the time he invented the electric light. Modern households can be so packed with new electrical and other gadgets that a woman is expected to know .more about mechanical maintenance than any man needs to know about bis automobile. A man can usually Dull in at the nearest service station when something goes haywire under the hood of his car. But a housewife is alone and on her own with a veritable Frankenstein monster, which inventors have jokingly nicknamed the "labor saving house. -It may save physical labor, all right, but when it eo'mes to mental labor ask your wife. Matching her wits against the best brains among advertising men and salesmen, she is expected to be able to accommodate on a breakfast table more gleaming chromium and glass equinment than any ordinary table was intended for. There could be, for instance, an electric coffee maker, an automatic toaster on a tray with conserves, an electric egg cooker, a bacon grill, an electric fruit juicer, a waffle iron with tray for batter, an electric biscuit warmer, a radio, a table lamp, and in season, an electric fan and, if there still is room for a husband and some children nerhaps an electric cigarette lighter and electric clock would be handy. From this miniature breakfast factory, which todays bride knows how to run and keep, in working order, she moves into a larger plant something her grandmother never would .have recognized as a kitchen. Table scraps are dumped right 'nto the sin kto be washed down :nto the sink to he washed down All dishes go into an automatic dishwasher, where theyll be soaped, rinsed and dried till they glisten. The butter goes back into a special butter-conditioning compartment in the refrigerator, where a temperature control keeps it from getting too hard to spread. The food freezer is checked to see if there will be anything to order when the; butcher calls on the kitchen phone. There are chops and steaks galore and that big roast that was bought at a sale two weeks ago. And sure enough, there is plenty , of ice cream in case tle girls chop in for the afternoon. If they want chocolate malteds, theres the electric mixer with its drink-stirring attachment like a soda fountain's. The modern wife can do more things with an electric mixer than some men can do with a whole tool chest. Deftly changing attachments, she beats up cakes, sharpens knives, juices oranges, whips potatoes, polishes silverware, chops hamburger, makes candy and what not. None of those old hairpin and chewing gum expedients are used in all this kitchen magic. Today's boys who grow up to be mechanics will' learn a lot from their mothers. The ladies know how to mesh the thread on a bolt, how much of a load the electYie circuit will carry, how to replace a blown-out fuse and where to turn off the current when they want to splice an electric cord. Making one trip back to the breakfast table, they whisk off the linen and drop it into an automatic laundry machine where it is washed, wrung and dried to the right degree for zipping through an electric iron-er. The reast for dinner is placed in an electric oven. A clock is set to start the meat to cook at the right time and automatically turn It off when it is done. A kitchen television may demonstrate something like stuffed brusscis sprouts, which the housewife follows handily while she flicks a switch to start the kitchen exhaust blower to carry off the fumes. You'd think with all these wheels going around a girl would have to be a grease-monkey to make a success of her marriage. I Planning Living Area Of Small House Is Important Lafayette, Ind., To achieve a well-planned living area in a small house it is important to use a definite plan carefully worked out on paper before building or remodeling, says Miss Ruth Hutcheson, extension home management specialist, ' Purdue University. The living, or social area, of the house includes the space used for living, dining and recreation. This living area should be large enough to meet family needs. Lach tamily should consider the amount ot entertaining to be done, its own furnishings and amount of money to be spent. Perhaps, the living room should be at least twelve feet wide. An oblong room may be furnished to better advantage. A nice proportion is two units wide by three uriits long. Such proportions make it easier to group the furniture for activity centers such as, reading, hobbies, conversation or music. Unless the living room is large it probably is advisable to omit the fireplace. Window spacing should be planned with good location of the furniture in mind. An adequate amount of light, both artificial and natural, is essential for pleasant living. A front entry or vestibule gives protection to the living area irorn cold, wind and rain. It also provides good location for a closet to store outer wraps. When such an entry cannot be provided a closet may be located in the living room proper for such storage needs. Doorways should be placed so that passage through the room is across one end or across a corner when possible. Locating doorways near room corners provides usable wall space, routes traffic in short direct lanes and avoids confusion caused by people passing through the activity area. When the dining space is only partly separated from the living room it is possible to use the total space for two activities at once. This separation can be accomplished by making the dining area an ell or alcove off the living room. It may be partly separated by a partition or storage wall for general storage needs. If the owner can afford a separate dining room it usually can be worked into the plan for the slightly larger house. Latest Wonder- of Scicntific-Macliiiic Ajze Robot to Forecast Election Univac, $600,000 Electronic Computer, Will Be Used M. ember 4 in Video Election Test On Night of Nov PHILADELPHIA. Oct. 14 CP) Univac, an electronic robot eight feet tall, will forecast election results for television viewers when returns start coming in the night of November 4. The $600,000 electronic computer will be used by CBS television to see whether its prodigious capacity for making calculations and analyses will make it possible to indicate the final outcome with a fair degree of accuracy on the basis of incomplete returns. Officials of Remington Rand, which built the machine, emphasize that it isn't psychic. But they and CBS say it will make possible comparisons on a scale and at a speed that would be impossible by conventional methods. It will be the first use of one of the giant electronic computers on election returns. t Machine With a 'Memory Univac short for universal automatic computer is a machine with a memory. Figures fed into the machine are recorded electronically on metallic tapes and mercury tanks. From now until election night, the machine will be fed data on hour-by-hour election totals of 1944 and 1948 for each of the 48 states and more detailed data on eight key states. On the night of November 4 the machine then will he given, for instance, the 9 p. m. returns from Pennsylvania. Univac then will take the figure, compare It with the 9 p. m. totals of the 1941 and 1918 elections, and report on an electric typewriter its forecast of what the final 1952 totals will he from the Mate. . The Univac forecast will not be a mere projection of the 1952 9 p. m. figures on 'the same ratio, but will take in account Republican ratios that usually occur in later returns from Pennsylvania. Will Have to Wait Some Similar forecasts will be made on a national basis, although they will have to wait until returns from enough states are in to give a fair sampling probably at least 21 states. An operator sitting at a central control unit that looks like the console for a pipe organ will type into the machine the latest vote totals. By means of little flip switches, the machine will be told what to do with them. Tiny red lights blink as Univac goCs through the various stages of calculations. In a few; seconds, an electric typewriter Mill start writing out the results, which a closeup TV camera will show video viewers. Each succeeding vote total will cut down, the margin of error as Univac gets more complete material with which to work. .Actually,, Univac still will be dependent on the usual counting and reporting of election returns. CBS will use it - only as an adjunct to its telecast of election returns, but as an interesting experiment to see whether Univac can give fairly conclusive clues on the final-results earlier than the usual procedure. Latest and Fastest Univac is the latest and fastest in the family of computers developed by the Eckert-Mauchly Division of Remington Rand. Six of the , calculators have been built and a seventh is in the works. The Census Bureau has i been using Univac for develop jing numerous types of statistics ifrom the 1950 census. It also is i being used by other Government branches and basically is a busi ness machine. The brain of the device is an insulated cabinet eight feet high, eight feet wide, and 14 feet long, I containing a maze of vacuum tubes, crystal diodes, wires and other electrical apparatus. The control panel several feet away co-ordinates the central com puter with the reporting unit! called a uniprinter, several metallic tape units in separate cabinets, and a unityper which feeds data into the machine. Univac has more than 50 miles ; of wire, 500,000 soldered joints and 5,500 vacuum tubes. Skills Lost To Modern Technology Are Many By RAY fflGGINS And now a lament for the lost skills. . . the dexterity w i t h R-hich our forebears performed primitive tasks outmoded by modern methods. They are many. . . from butter making at home to the simple ac: of shaving, a function further complicated by the devotion of college students io beards. Tne lost skills, often time-consuming and difficult for home practitioners, have yielded to commercialism and mechanical methods, to changing tastes, to scientific improvements and short-cut nieihods and to technology. Already the trade of the bookkeeper is threatened by the computer. Soon the comptomet- er operator who felt safe in a special knowledge, will give way io these thinking machines which perform complicated functions at high speed. The job elimination which upsets the national-economy and alarms the labor force has been subject to this attrition f o r years in less spectacular forms. The railroad crossing watchman was replaced by electric signal controls in the more-or-less recent past The small boy who wore his cracked and dirt-stained knuck- les with pride because of his skill at playing marbles now fhds himself triumphant over a lost art. Who now can cut willow twig and fashion from it a marvelous whistle for small fry amusement? What housewife cherishes her ability in the long process of making sauerkraut when she can buy it ready-made in cans? Who takes the time to peel, slice and cook pumpkins when there are pies ready-made on the grocer's shelf? Does she compound the separate ingredients to make a Cdke or resort to ready-mix? Does she poultice a small boy's skinned knee with turpentine or apply a ready-made, self-adhesive bandage? Would her husband know where to start if told to harness up the family horse for a buggy-ride or where to find a blacksmith shop if the vehicle threw a tire? Or the horse needed shoeing? Maybe we're better off, giving ourselves more leisure time in a fast-moving era, but does the catsup taste as good as when conceived over a hot in a steamy kitchen? Although it may seem to the parents that the adolescent j talks about nothing for hours on end, the typical gossip, jok-' ing, teasing and scheming of teen telephone conversations ; help the youth become familiar with group standards of behavior and "try on" attitudes and opinions. Of course, the adolescent must also learn to respect the i rights of the rest of the family to use the teleohone or to simply have the telephone free for incoming calls. Deciding ' a reasonable limit on the length of adolescent conversations , on the telephone should be a decision reached by family. discussion, not an arbitrary edict. If the parents' business and social interests demand considerable telephone hours, the possibility of an additional telephone might be considered. Value of Measles Vaccine Is Doubted WASHINGTON (UPI) — Suspicion Is growing among some child doctors and virologists that the current massive vaccination campaign to eliminate German measles may be misdirected. The question being raised is whether it might not be better to let children get measles and develop a natural life-time immunity instead of immunizing them in childhood and leaving them susceptible to the disease as adults. IT IS AMONG the adult population that rubella poses its greatest threat. It is a major carrier of infection to suscepti- ,/ble pregnant women whose offspring -may suffer crippling birth defects or die. During a 1964-65 epidemic an estimated 20,000 to 30,000 childen were born with such rubella-caused_ H&H Materials Due Airport lob H&H Materials 'was the apparent low bidder today for developing 'tracts of airport land and to improve Terminal drive on airport property with a bid of $127,355. The City had defects as mental retardation, heart disease, blindness and deafness. The National Center for Disease Control in Atlanta stresses that the vaccine has been given safely to more than 13 million Americans, mostly children. And no one is seeking to halt the federally financed drive to immunize school-aged children. But a Nobel-Prize winning virus authority thinks it is time to' raise some serious questions about who gets the vaccine, and a Seattle, Wash., pediatrician told UPI he was not prescribing the vaccine because he is uncertain of its effectiveness. WRITING IN THE current New England Journal of Medicine, Dr. .John F. Enders of Harvard University expressed a concern that young girls vaccinated today may be more likely to get the disease when they grow up and start having children than if they had gotten it naturally in their childhood. Findings indicate that vaccinations may establish . only partial resistance that is not as long lasting nor as protective as a natural infection, Enders wrote.

Television addiction DETROIT Television has become such a part of daily life that 93 of 120 families spurned an offer of $500 to turn off the set for a month. The offer was made by the Detroit Free Press, which wanted to study the effects of "television addiction." For families who did accept the offer there were these results: All the subjects said they saw more movies, read more, visited friends and relatives more often and took more weekend trips.

Girls Most Likely To Succeed Sometimes Don't Everybody knows somebody like Tuttle, the brightest girl in my freshman class at college, and, it went without saying, the most likely to succeed. Up at 5 a.m. every morning, she would be fully dressed, brushed, combed, deodorized, lip-sticked and deep into a "review" of Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics by the time the rest of us began to stumble into the bathroom, recoiling at our green-and-purple 7 a.m. reflections in the harshly lit mirror. "GOOD Morning!" she would sing out to each of us in turn, simultaneously scaring us to death and blinding us with the gleam of her luminescent incisors. " 'G'morg," you would grumble between clenched teeth, wondering privately how ANYONE could be so damned efficient AND cheerful so early in the morning? Tuttle, who wanted to be a doctor, aced every course in which she was enrolled. And maddeningly, she seemed to do it without effort. But have you ever tried to express your admiration to a person like that? "Far out, Tuttle! NOBODY ever got an A from Coronius, the old geezer!" "Geez, Ash, I really faked him out, didn't I? Impressed him with a few arcane references to Diderot and Nietzsche! And the fact that I had read 'Remembrance of Things Past' in French! And by throwing all those four-syllable words into my term paper. I really fooled HIM!" "Um, no, Tuttle, I really don't think so. I mean, you really seemed to know your stuff in class . . ." "Yeah, well, that was only because I had YOU fooled, too. I never did understand a word he said." And whatever became of Tuttle? I wish I knew. She dropped out of college midway through her sophomore year to "find" herself and wound up marrying her high school boyfriend, in that order, none of us ever heard from her again. But I have often wondered about Tuttle, who seemed to have so much potential, and drive, but was so uncomfortable with her achievements, however splendid. Her behavior couldn't be explained away, I decided long ago, by the much ballyhooed "fear of success" syndrome. She had not only craved and sought success; she had experienced it, according to every objective measure scholastic excellence, the praise of her professors, the admiration of her peers and ought to have been able to revel in it, I thought. But it was as if she believed, deep down inside, that she owed her achievements to "luck" or some higher-up's error in judgment. Curious! And now, along come Pauline Rose Clance and Suzanne Ament Imes, psychologists at Geor gia State, with a theory that this sort of thing may be more widespread than is commonly believed among "high-achieving" women. They even have a name for it: "the imposter phenomenon." In a scientific study to be published later this year, based on five years of research, they report a recurring tendency among women of achievement to believe they are NOT intelligent, despite all objective evidence to the contrary, that they must have "fooled" anyone who thinks otherwise and that they are, of course, in constant danger of being "exposed." The origin of all this? Probably, they hypothesize, in the sibling rivalries and parental "expectations" of the woman's formative years. Its effect? To deprive her of finding satisfaction in any achievement, a never-ending cycle in which she is likely to drive herself progressively harder but less effectively. The cure? Well, wouldn't you know it? Although the authors advise sufferers to try repeating things like, "I'm bright, I'm bright," when those doubts begin to assert themselves, there isn't any known cure. On the other hand, Tuttle "found" herself and got married. And here I sit, juggling words and paragraphs around, well aware that it's time for an intelligent summation, but unable to come up with one. Why did I bring up Tuttle and the imposter syndrome in the first place? Beats me. You realize, of course, that I might just be an imposter, too. On the other hand ....

The Marketplace Sales of portable stereos boom, ushering in an age of isolation 1981 Washington Star WASHINGTON - The clerk in the downtown camera store didn't even look abashed. "I went on an airplane trip over the weekend and I took my portable stereo cassette player with me," he said. "I just plugged in my earphones and listened." But why? "Because I didn't want to be bothered listening to the other passengers," he replied promptly. Let it be admitted quickly: There isn't a one of us who hasn't had the discomfort of being belted into an airplane seat next to an insufferable bore blathering away at 33,000 feet. Of course not, of course not. Still, . . is this sort of thing the answer? Do we really need this sort of privacy, this sort of protection from genuine human contact? Apparently, we do. Salespeople in audio-equipment stores say that lightweight, portable stereo cassette players and similar portable radios, with their earphones that shut off the listener from the audible distractions of the outside world -dare we say the "real" world? - are flying out of the stores. "Can't keep them in stock," the salespeople say. "Sold 40 or 50 over the weekend. Selling 'em like crazy." "You should stand out here on Wisconsin Avenue (in Washington) on some hot Saturday morning and watch them go by," says Steven Goldstein, a salesman in the Audiokrafters store above Georgetown. "You see dozens of them." Seersucker Jackets from Haspel Wash & Wear Lightweight Comfort! Blue & White stripe sizes 38-50 regs, shorts, longs and extra longs $105 North at Summer St Downtown Pittsfield Dozens of people, that is, walking or running or bicycling or roller-skating down the main drag of a major city neighborhood, all of them plugged into their own worlds and oblivious to each other, to everybody else, to the world around them. Talk about a lonely crowd. Even some of the people who sell these things aren't sure of the social implications. "I'm not sure that I approve of it," says Steve Foster, a salesman in the German Hi-Fi Center store opposite the National Archives. Foster says the people who are buying these things are not spaced-out, zonked-out disco-hoppers. The young kids, he says, are buying the big, booming disco portable stereos, the kind you have to lug around, the kind that can blast passers-by into the next zip code.' No, the lightweight portables are going to a more mature set. An 'isolation thing' "Maybe it's because of our location, but we get a lot of government workers buying these things," says Foster. "People in the 25- to 30-year-old range, the three-piece suit crowd. They wear them under their suit jackets while they're driving home. It's an isolation thing." Goldstein of Audiokrafters -agrees that an older, settled crowd is buying the lightweight gear. For example, he sold one to a Rockefeller just the other day. Which brings up the matter of money. These things aren't cheap, though there are inexpensive lightweights, either AM radios or knock-down models of a cassette player, that sell for as little as $35 or $40. But the real sales action is at the other end of the price scale. The most popular models, like the Sony Walkman, cost in the neighborhood of $200. There are discounts, of course. W. Bell and Co. sells the Walkman for $169.95. . The better, and more expensive, models have first-class stereo sound, which appeals to those buyers who already have such sound in their homes and want to take it with them when they're away. The phenomenon isn't confined toWashington. "There's an entire range of buyers," says a salesman in a St. Louis camera store. "Old, young, black, white, everything. And they're all impressed by the sound on these things." 11-ounce Sony Sony was first on the market with its Walkman three years ago. Now it has just introduced a newer model that weighs 11 ounces when its cassette is inserted; that is down from the nearly 14 ounces of the original model. Most of Sony's competitors in other fields Toshiba, Sanyo, Panasonic now have entries in this field as well. "They make up 20 percent of our business," says Larry Brown, manager of the Federal Store in downtown Washington. Most of the buyers buy blank cassettes and tape their own programs to take with them, salesmen report; few buy prerecorded cassettes. Again, this indicates that buyers are sophisticated about sound and audio equipment; the salesmen say that the buyers are taping programs off their home stereo gear. For those who worry about the heavy demand for products that enforce isolation - Sony is reportedly back-ordered for 40,000 units a month there is this cheering note: some of these portable cassette players can accommodate a second set of earphones, so that a couple can get in tune with each other and totally shut out the outside world.

WILLIAM F. BUCKLEY Jr. Do We Really Need Home Computers? Stanley Marcus, the famous merchandiser responsible for the success of Dallas Neiman-Marcus, said recently that the art of selling is dead in America. Two years ago he took a pledge not to buy anything ever again on his own initiative. He would henceforth buy only things that were sold to him. In any case, Mr. Marcus said that it worked out that he hadnt bought a thing in two years, and has therefore saved himself $43,000 per year, the annual average cost of Mr. Marcus predatory appetite. In conversation with an executive of IBM the other day I said that I hoped before I died that someone anyone would devote a page of advertising now given over to home computers to explaining exactly how a computer can be useful in the home. Ones own imagination tends to be limited in these matters. I know of one use to which I would myself wish to put a home computer, but yearn to know of others, since it is difficult to believe that $1.5 billion is being spent idly by American homeowners. I'd like one that would hold the contents of a large dictionary, so that I could type out the word otiose and be reminded of what it meant. I said be reminded of what it meant because a communicable aphasia hit me. when I was 16. At that time a teacher told his class that most people have two or three words whose meaning they are forever forgetting, and he gave as his example the word otiose. I swooped upon a dictionary a half-hour later and learned what it meant. - Since then I have probably looked the word up 30 times. At this moment, I cant remember what I means. I dont suppose, though, the crowds will storm the store that advertises: "Learn instantly what otiose means ! William Draper, the president of the Import-Export Bank and an investor in small computers, told me once: Software is everything. There are no remaining problems of hardware. It took awhile before I understood that, which however I am now prepared to explain. What he meant was that the machine exists into which you can program the whole dictionary, or for that matter the whole encyclopedia. But somebody has got to pay for the time of the person who types out the 400, 006-odd entries in Websters Third into the discs that you then insert into the machine. Moreover, the capacity of the machine to memorize increases with some reference to its cost. A machine that operates a disc that will memorize, let us say, 64 bytes will give you 64,000 characters. Since the average word has five characters, then the disc is good for about 10,000 words, or about 12 times the length of this article. You can get a second disc and a third and a 300th. And the hardware exists that will search through your discs until it lands on otiose. But by that time you have run out of money and run out of time; so you resign yourself to the dictionary. Stanley Marcus is on to something. Some gadgets we know instinctively how to put to use: radios, say, or Waring blenders. But a $1,000 computer? The Pulitzer Prize belongs to the man who reveals what theyre good for. I mean, what theyre good for that the average newspaper reader wants to know.

U-lVrite 4W Cedar Rapids GazetteMarch 2, 1983 Mom confesses Pac-Man addiction She fills cookie jar with quarters instead of chocolate chips, spends Saturdays at arcades " MIDWAY im a il, n JMi & i OC3 V-7 Neighbors photo by Greg Mellis I've decided to come out of the closet and admit that Km hooked on Pac-Man. "So what," you may say, "so are a million other children and teenagers." Therein lies the problem ... I'm a 35-year-old housewife and mother! It's not natural! I should be home cleaning my house, attending PTA meetings and playing bridge with the girls once a week. But no, not me. My cookie jar is filled with , quarters rather than chocolate chips and instead of being afflicted with a socially accepted injury like "tennis elbow," I suffer from "Pac-Man arm" and sport callous fingers from gripping my joy stick too tightly. I'm hopeless. I've even passed my "illness" on to a few friends who join me in planning grocery trips and shopping expeditions around the nearest arcade! It all started innocently enough. I had always sneered at people who wasted their money in arcades and the few women I'd ' seen playing were .instantly classified in my mind as hoodlums. I mean, my stereotype of an adult female player wasn't complete unless she wore tight jeans, a leather jacket, had dirty fingernails, at least three visible tattoos and a lit cigarette dangling from her lips. I just didn't fit the image. I don't own a leather jacket, my jeans sag, and the closest thing to a tattoo I ever had was when my 6-year-, old son Jimmy drew anchors on my arms with a ballpoint pen so we could both be Popeye. Nevertheless, the occasion presented itself in the guise of a birthday party that I took Jimmy to at a local pizza parlor. To ' escape the screaming children, I wandered into the equally loud arcade area and watched three-foot-tall midgets rack up points in the tens of thousands without hardly crooking a finger. It looked easy. So with a furtive glance over my shoulder to make sure no one was watching, I put my first quarter into Pac-Man. A minute later and a quarter poorer, I was stunned to see the words "game over" flash on the screen. And my score isn't worth mentioning. Suffice it to say, I slunk away in abject shame amid titters from little kids grinning at me through their Pepsi mustaches. But I was hooked. I couldn't face my son again until I made at least a modest showing of success! After throwing away a multitude of quarters on machines around town, I discovered a place that gave me two games for one quarter and I started playing regularly each Saturday afternoon. Diarme Mills plans grocery shopping tips around Pac-Man games Somehow I felt less guilty knowing each game only cost me 12 cents. However, I did feel a little like a professional gambler and it was no small embarrassment being the oldest "child" at the machines. But I learned quickly after that and not only became a better player, but also picked up some arcade etiquette. (Fool that I was, the first time someone put a quarter on top of the machine I was playing, I thought it was one I had dropped and I almost grabbed it! Little did I know it was his "reservation" to be next in line when I relinquished the machine.) I've since graduated from Pac-Man to Ms. Pac-Man which is a bit more challenging and a figure I can at least identify with (after all, she does have a bow on her head). I can even modestly brag about my top score of 49,650 on Ms. Pac-Man and feel like all those quarters have finally bought me something. . However, I'm realisticenough to know that my folly has to end sometime. Dare I try to achieve 100,000 points? Will I be satisfied when I see my name taped to the top of the Ms. Pac-Man machine as having achieved the highest score to date? Can I quit playing even after that? That's the frightening part! I think the articles I've been reading lately in the newspaper on arcade addiction for our young people should also include a forgotten age group: the middle-aged housewife. I know what I'll do! I'll charter a "Ms. Pac-Man Anonymous" club fopthose of us afflicted with this computer curse and at our weekly meetings we can give our testimonies and then direct our energies to a more dignified pursuit ... like watching soap operas. Now there's a thought. I wonder if anyone has pondered combining the features of a soap opera with an arcade game: Eunice could chase John, gobbling up alimony payments along the way; then John could die halfway through the second screen and .... . Study links coffee to iron deficiency in women By ELLEN HALE Gannett News Service Coffee, the all-American staple that researchers think could be linked to cancer, heart disease, birth defects, peptic ulcers and high blood pressure, may also keep you from absorbing a crucial nutrient. When you drink your coffee, how strong you like it and how you take it may affect the way your body absorbs iron, the critical mineral that prevents anemia and keeps enough red blood cells circulating. For men, the finding probably poses no threat; for women, however, particularly those who are pregnant, it suggests potential problems, says nutritionist Timothy A. A study released by the U.S. Department of Agriculture says that women's diets are 33 percent below the recommended Intake of iron, and recommends that they eat more iron-containing foods like liver. Not getting enough iron, however, will eventually cause the body's levels of stored iron to drop, and that can lead to anemia, he said. it 'Dungeons & Dragons' addict's suicide gives rise to a lawsuit By MICHAEL ISIKOFF 9 Tho Washington Post WASHINGTON Irving Lee "Bink" Pulling II was a gifted high-school student who took an unusually keen interest in wars, science fiction and the popular fantasy game called "Dungeons & Dragons." His classmates were shocked when they learned that Pulling, 16, went home from school in Hanover County, Virginia, the day before final exams last year and shot himself in the chest with a pistol. When the local sheriffs office began to investigate, deputies found that Pulling's room was filled with paraphernalia from "Dungeons & Dragons," a game that has stirred up a whirl of controversy in recent years. Investigators found a "Dungeons & Dragons" magazine and a bizarre suicide note that one said contained "unexplainable-type things" mystical phrases that police believed were references to the game of mythology. Now, a year later, Pulling's parents have filed a lawsuit against the principal of Patrick Henry High School, charging that he was responsible for Pulling's death by allowing "Dungeons & Dragons" to be played as an "organized school activity." They have asked for $1 million in damages and legal expenses and interest on the $1 million from the day of Pulling's death, June 9, 1982. "The game was played in that school," said Lt. Clyde Futrell, a spokesman for the Hanover County sheriff's office, who described Pulling as a devotee of the game. "They had a teacher who was the 'Dungeon Master' or whatever you "call it." Hours before his suicide, the suit alleges, Pulling was playing "Dungeons & Dragons" at school when a "curse" was placed upon him by another player. This curse was "intended to inflict emotional distress" upon Pulling, the suit says, at a time when he was already under "extreme pschological stress and emotional pressure" from playing "Dungeons & Dragons." Robert A. Bracey III, the princi pal of Patrick Henry, said that "Dungeons & Dragons" was "not part of the school curriculum," as the suit alleges. He refused further comment. "Dungeons & Dragons," one of the top-selling games in the country with an estimated 3 million to 4 million players, creates an intricate fantasy world in which players take on the roles and mystical powers of mythical characters, such as medieval monsters, wizards, dwarves and dragons, some of them borrowed from J. R. R. Tolkien's popular trilogy "Lord of the Rings." The game has received publicity in connection with several bizarre incidents and deaths in recent years, most notably the disappearance and subsequent suicide of a brilliant 17-year-old Michigan State University student who was said to be obsessed with the game. Bracey's lawyer, William Smith, said he will argue in court that school officials are immune from such lawsuits. No hearing date has been set in the case. Dieter H. Sturm, corporate public-relations director for TSR Inc., the Lake Geneva, Wis.-based company that distributes "Dungeons & Dragons," dismissed suggestions that the game could be linked to Pulling's death. Sturm noted that the game is used in many advanced school programs around the country and that television personality Dr. Joyce Brothers, a psychologist, has been retained as a consultant by TSR to promote use of the game. Critics of games like "Dungeons & Dragons" have a different view. "This doesn't surprise me at all," said Robert Landa, a lawyer for a California-based group called SALT (Sending America Light and Truth) that has been campaigning against "Dungeons & Dragons." "I've got stories you wouldn't believe about people who have been victims of role-playing games like 'Dungeons & Dragons,'" he said. "This game becomes a lifestyle . . . that uses witchcraft and sorcery and black magic."

Apple wizard says computer 'fad' dying By Scrippt-Howard tit An astonishing blast of heresy casting doubt on the future of the computer In modern life has come from the very person who designed the first personal computer and is one of Silicon Valley's major heroes, Steven Wozniak. -Wozniak is the bearded genius who, with his friend Steven Jobs, started the fabulously successful Apple Computer Co. in a garage. He now has a personal fortune of close to $100 million. Yet he has Chosen this moment, at the peak of his wealth and fame, to put in question the whole notion of an endlessly expanding market and unlimited uses for computers, especially for the ordinary person. Specifically, Wozniak says: "The home computer may be going the way of video games, which are a dying fad. "For most personal tasks, such as balancing a checkbook, consulting CARPENTRY airline schedules, writing a modest number of letters, paper works Just as well as a computer, and costs less." Even engineers may not need computers as much as they think they do. When Wozniak designed the Apple models I and II he could not afford to rent time on a computer to type code. Instead he used paper and pencil and found it more efficient, engaging his Interest more strongly, because "I was part of the process." "If I'm right, a lot of computers will start being disused," Wozniak said. "For a couple of years every family had to have them. But you don't go to houses and see them played any more. Computers may be entering that stage. Nobody at Apple is going to like hearing this, but as a general device for everyone, computers have been oversold." , Wozniak, known to his friends as Woz, was the creative force behind Apple's giant success. He left to obtain a degree ln computer science at Berkeley, and has now rejoined Apple as an engineer, working in a small cubicle at the company's Silicon Valley headquarters. His return ln such a lowly capacity, with a cut in salary, is like Henry Ford taking a Job on an assembly line in his own factory. His interests are broad, and do not include the acquisition of power. Two rock music festivals he organized lost $25 million, but be thought the enjoyment worth it Anyone can call him up. Wozniak's ' chief Impact as a spokesman is as a sort of public relations man in reverse. He is fiercely' critical of his own company, which he thinks has succumbed to the vices of bureaucracy, especially the vice of secrecy. He says that a rival firm, Hewlett-Packard, is now a better company than Apple, because it is more open, allowing its engineers free access to components, whereas Apple "think they've got to keep everything locked up." The fall ln the price of Apple shares has cost Wozniak $100 million in the past four years. Experience has shown him that the usefulness of the computer has been exaggerated. When he went to Berkeley to study for his degree he found a computer a hindrance rather than a help. "I spent more time on my courses because I was trying to do all the neat things a computer can do, like beautiful graphs and nice spread sheets. Everybody else went to bed at midnight and I was still working at 6 a.m." Such subversive notions are not unique. Critics are exploring the myth that computers are "revolutionizing" education, as was once predicted, and saying they may be harmful, by crowding out the real substance of learning with time-wasting tricks and gadgets. The realization is dawning that people can easily pick up what they need to know about computers, If anything, after they leave school. One of Wozniak's new pet projects is far removed from electronics. He wants to start a children's suffrage movement, to enfranchise all family members, regardless of age. The headquarters, office may not even use computers.

I . ' ' . Until it can do dishes, home computer remains of little value to families Hawaii Tribune-Herald. Wednesday. March 6. 198S-2S By David E. Sanger NEW YORK For jnore than three years now, it has been the secret of the home computer industry, seldom whispered aloud: No one has figured out how a computer can be truly useful at home. This, after years of research and more than a billion dollars in losses by toy manufacturers and electronic giants. It should not be a surprise. Writing the occasional letter hardly demands a heavy-duty word processor. Balancing the checkbook, printing out labels for Christmas cards and keeping track of recipes seem to be tasks better suited to pen, calculator and file box than a $1,000 computer system. "What the world needs is a home computer that does windows," joked Esther Dyson, one of the personal computer industry's most influential observers, who was running her annual Personal Computer Forum several weeks ago in Phoenix. But window washing or, for that matter, drying dishes or vacuuming living rooms are the realm of robots, not computers. With the market for home computers the least xpensive machines are selling 1500 or less virtually dead lay, industry executives have to speak openly about their , most fundamental prob- Making the computer as pelling an addition to the home as a television set or a dishwasher. "A lot of myths about computers were exposed in 1984," says John Sculley, the former Pepsico executive who is now president of Apple Computer. "One of them is that there is such a thing as the home computer market. It doesn't exist. People use computers in the home, of course, but for education and too begun oldest leW com running a small business. There are not uses in the home itself." Two years ago, most people in the industry would have regarded Sculley's contention as heretical. They would have said be did not understand the growing multibillion-dollar industry that promised to turn the computer into an electronic hearth. But in the past six months, consumers have turned away from the inexpensive home computers, buying instead more powerful machines, like IBM's PCjr and the Apple lie, which are not really home computers at all. Rather, they are $1,000 personal computers to be used primarily for business or educational purposes, usually at home. This reality of the computer market was hinted at last year, in surveys such as the one conducted by Talmis, a Chicago market researcher. The homeowners questioned said their top priorities for computer use lay in preparing taxes, keeping track of portfolios and learning programming; that is, in business-oriented activities. So, when Sculley chastised the industry recently, pointing to the enormous difference between a computer used in a home and a home computer, almost no one challenged him. "He's right," said Trip Hawkins, whose Silicon Valley software company, Electronic Arts, has been one of the very few to survive the home computer shake-out. Speaking between sessions at the Phoenix computer forum, he added: "The primary use for home computers is still entertainment. No one has yet figured how to make the computer part of the social fabric of the home." Coleco Industries thought it had in the summer of 1983, with the introduction of the Adam home computer. The Adam seemed to be the perfect solution to the nag ging problem of what to do with a home computer use it to educate the children and as an easy-to-operate home word processor. Unlike other home computers, the Adam was even sold as a complete system: $700 bought a box containing a machine, printer, small tape drive for storing data and some basic programs. There was nothing to assemble; first-time users could immediately begin writing letters and running programs that taught basic mathematics and reading to their children. From the beginning, however, the Adam system was plagued by quality-control problems. Moreover, by mid-1984 consumers were tiring of its commercials, which depicted children who did not use computers as the illiterates of their generation, destined to trudge home from the freshman year of college in disgrace. By the end of the year , the writing on the screen was clear: Coleco would go back to pumping out cuddly little Cabbage Patch Kids. "We still think there is a market in the home for computers," said Arnold Greenberg, Coleco's president, a few months ago, as the company announced it was pulling out of the market. "But it didn't develop the way anyone expected." One reason may be that computers, at least today's computers, are not suited to ordinary tasks in the home. "Most people use computers to improve efficiency," said Doulgas Carlston, president and chief exeuctive of Broderbund Software, a San Rafael, Calif., home computer software house. Electronic spreadsheets, for example, greatly speed up a task that business executives and financial analysts must perform: determining how various economic factors might affect sales or profits. - But in the home, Carlston said, "people are not really looking for efficiency." Rarely do they perform the same, repetitive desktop tasks that make computers so useful in offices. Instead, home users put computers to a variety of different jobs, from electronic games to keeping track of grocery lists. Even in the beady days of 1982, when demand for small, versatile home computers seemed endless, there was talk of this kind of home computer neglect. Some retailers admitted that home computers seemed to be the center of family attention for two or three months. Then the novelty of electronic games wore off, and users discovered that the machines were unwieldy for more serious work. In time, home computers became what one IBM executive called "expensive doorstops," rarely turned on. The doorstop phenomenon eventually caught up with the industry's early leaders, who had hoped that once people started using home computers, they would find new uses for them. That happened in offices with higher-priced personal computers, but not at the low end of the market with home computers. As a result, companies such as Texas Instruments, Mattel, Timex and Warner Com-muncations' Atari abandoned their efforts, unable to weather the price-cutting war that constituted a last-ditch effort to sustain demand for the machines. Still, as late - as last year industry analysts were saying the market was far from dead, that American consumers would buy more than five million home computers in 1984. Although precise numbers vary, few doubt that the industry fell short of that projection by at least 40 percent. Even as 300 computer industry executives, software writers and retailers were gathering for the Phoenix meeting, evidence was mounting that consumers have lost interest in the current generation of home machines. The strongest survivor of the home computer market, Commodore International, announced only a few weeks ago that Christmas sales of its popular Commodore 64 model had plummeted; so had profits, more than 90 percent. , "What everyone is missing is that it has to be both convenient and cheap,'' said Daniel S. Brickli, the chairman of Software Arts of Wellesley, Mass., who six years ago helped invent the first electronic spreadsheet, Visicalc To Bricklin, the home computer cannot sit on the kitchen table: it must be the size of a spiral notebook and easy to carry around. "You need the computer all over the house," he said. "You are not going to go upstairs just to type in a quick query and get back an answer." Bricklin is one of several in the industry who are urging new research into what they call "Dynabook." The term was coined by Alan Kay, once the chief scientist at Atari and now a top researcher at Apple. Kay's idea was to develop a computer so portable that it could be carried anywhere, even to the supermarket, so that shoppers could ' compare prices as they cruised the aisles. It could also be used to sketch pictures, tap central data bases, even play music. The technology for Dynabook exists, but not at a price that would make the machine commonplace: the better quality portable computers start at $3,000 and work rapidly up to $7,000. Even these do best on small screens what business computers do on big ones; they are thus suited to the traveling user of a business computer, not the home user.

Study links coffee to heart disease BALTIMORE (AP) An person who drinks five or jtnore cups of coffee a day has arc almost three times greater risk of having heart problems than a non-coffee drinker, according to a study of more than 1.000 doctors released Monday. Findings from the study, which tracked 1,130 white males who graduated from The Johns Hopkins Medical School here between 1948 and 1964, were presented in Washington at the 58th scientific sessions of the American Heart Association. Information on drinking hab its was obtained from the graduating physicians at five-year intervals for up to 25 years. No information was obtained on whether the type of coffee was caffeinated or decaffeinated. A person who drinks at least five cups of coffee daily has a 2.8 times greater risk of having heart problems than the non-drinker, the study found. Even when other risk factors smoking, high-blood pressure, cholesterol levels and age are considered, the study determined there is still a 2.5 times increased risk, the researchers reported. Other studies into possible links between coffee consumption and heart disease have re sulted in contradictory findings, said Dr. Thomas A. Pearson, an associate professor and director of the Johns Hopkins Precursors Study. Some found a link, while others did not. A spokesman for the National Coffee Association, Bill Brooks, said 10 of 12 major studies found no relationship between coffee drinking and heart disease. In one of fhe two studies that did, the findings were later reversed, he said. "The bulk of medical literature does not support a finding that coffee is a risk factor in the development of heart disease," he said.

Industry: Will home video phones catch on? By DEBORAH MESCE Associated Press Writer WASHINGTON (AP) Nearly a quarter-century after visitors to the 1964 New York World's Fair were introduced to the Pic-turephone, the see-as-you talk concept is being offered again. The cost is lower, but so is the technology. ' Unlike the moving images of the Picturephone, which let fair-goers see as well as hear the person on the other end of the wire, the new devices produce only a freeze-frame shot. ; . And industry analysts still question whether the home video phone's time has come. ; "The issue is behavior," said A. Michael Noll, a professor of communications at the University of Southern California who worked for American Telephone & Telegraph Co. in new product planning in the mid-1970s. . Using the telephone is akin to "whispering in the ear. Seeing somebody almost destroys the intimacy of the communication," he said. "When we ask an audience whether they want to see on the phone, half or more say no." Mitsubishi officials recognize the psychological barrier Picturephone ran into, but the company believes its VisiTel visual phone display unit, introduced in the United States last November, will fare better. VisiTel, the only consumer product of its kind now on the U.S. market, has a camera lens that projects the user's image onto a black-and-white, 4.5-inch screen. The image can be transmitted to another VisiTel user in about five seconds. Since the unit uses ordinary phone lines, the same calling rates apply when the Visitel is used as when an ordinary phone is used. "This is a passive product," said Tim Beck, national sales manager for the visual telecommunications division of Mitsubishi Electric Sales of America. "It's not like picking up the phone and immediately your picture is there. It only transmits when you hit the send key," he said. Beck said VisiTels, retailing for about $400 each, are selling "very well." The company has orders for about 64,000 units and has delivered about 36,000 of them, he said. Two other Japanese companies, Sony Corp. and Matsushita's Panasonic division, are planning to put similar products on the market by Christmas. A variety of companies, such as PictureTel Corp. of Peabody, Mass., sell devices that transmit moving images, but those are more expensive and require higher-grade phone lines. They are mostly for businesses. AT&T's Picturephone initially was aimed at the residential caller. AT&T set up phones at central locations in New York, Chicago and Washington. People could place calls from a Picturephone at one of these locations to a Picturephone at another location, where family or friends would be awaiting their pre-arranged call. AT&T said it would extend service to other parts of the country if demand was large enough, and a June 1964 press release said, "There is no telling when Picturephone sets in the home will be as common as telephones are today." "The problem was the technology was just ahead of its time. There wasn't the demand for it," said Gary Whaite, manager of AT&T's corporate staff for teleconferencing application development. "People didn't want themselves seen in what you would call the private home environment. It just wasn't appealing to the public," Whaite said. It was also expensive to install and to use. Rates ranged from $16 to $27 for the first three minutes at one of the Picturephone centers. Installing a Picturephone in someone's home would have cost thousands of dollars for special wiring to connect the device to the phone network. AT&T eventually turned its attention away from residential prospects and focused on the business community. Businesses were more receptive to two-way video, but the growth of what came to be known as teleconferencing was also slow because of the high cost of equipment and the special circuits required. Even by the late 1970s, it cost about half a million dollars to equip a room with video monitors, cameras and special wiring, Whaite said. Technological advances began bringing the cost down significantly in the 1980s and by the mid-1980s, teleconferencing was becoming more attractive to companies trying to cut travel costs and open more lines of communication. Now, an estimated 150 to 200 companies have their own teleconferencing networks ranging in size from two to 45 sites, said Elliot M. Gold, a teleconferencing consultant based in Altadena, Calif.
